questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young male came with GI complaints like malabsorption, diarrhea. Cutaneous examination noted itchy lesions on the skin with blistering. On histopathology, cryptitis and flattened villi were noted. His condition improved with a gluten-free diet. What is the specific antibody in this condition? (NEET PG 2024)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tissue Transglutaminase 3 (ttg-3)

A patient with malabsorption, diarrhea, and itchy blistering skin lesions that improve with a gluten-free diet has dermatitis herpetiformis associated with celiac disease.

·         Skin disease: Dermatitis herpetiformis

·         Gut pathology: Villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia (celiac disease)

·         Key antibody in skin: IgA against tissue transglutaminase-3 (tTG-3)

Pathophysiology:

·         Gluten → immune response → IgA antibodies

·         These deposit in dermal papillae → cause pruritic vesicles

Related antibodies:

·         tTG-2 (tissue transglutaminase-2) → intestinal celiac disease

·         tTG-3 → skin involvement (dermatitis herpetiformis)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the finding marked by the arrow in the below image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vossius ring

The finding given in the image is that of a Vossius ring.

Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens. It is usually seen after blunt trauma to the eye and orbit.

It usually has about the same diameter as the contracted pupil. The force of the blow drives the cornea and iris backward and thus producing an impression of the iris on the lens. The resorption of the pigment results in discrete subcapsular opacities.

Other options:

Option B: Weiss ring is a floater which may be seen by the patient as a circle or other large solitary lesion. It is the detached former attachment to the margin of the optic disc. It is seen in posterior vitreous detachment and is not confirmatory. It is seen in the image below.

Option C: A Fleischer's ring is usually observed in keratoconus, representing epithelial iron deposits. It is seen best with a cobalt blue filter.

Option D: Kayser-Fleischer ring is observed in Wilson's disease, due to intraocular deposition of copper. A brownish-yellow zone is seen in the peripheral Descemet membrane of the cornea. Anterior capsular cataract, also knowns as a sunflower cataract may be seen in some patients.
questions.learning: Vossius ring — The finding given in the image is that of a Vossius ring. Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a population study, the value of the mean is 200. If the standard deviation is 20, 68% of the population will lie between?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 180- 220

68% of the population will lie between 180- 220.

In a normal distribution curve, 68% of the values lie within the mean +/- 1 standard deviation and the mean=median=mode. Since the mean = 200 and the standard deviation = 20:

68% of population will lie between Mean +/- 1SD, that is, 200 +/- 20 = 180-220

95% of population lies between Mean+/-2SD, 200+/- 2*20 = 160- 240

99% of population lies between Mean+/-3SD, 200+/- 3*20 = 140- 260
questions.learning: 180- 220 68% of the population will lie between 180- 220. In a normal distribution curve, 68% of the values lie within the mean +/- 1 standard deviation and the mean=median=mode.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The most common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rossenmuller which is marked 3 in the image.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking.

The WHO classification of three types of nasopharyngeal carcinoma includes

* Keratinising

* Nonkeratinising differentiated

* Nonkeratinising undifferentiated

The most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller. From here, it can spread extensively in any direction locally. It also can spread lymphatically to the cervical, retropharyngeal, or parapharyngeal lymph nodes.

Trotter's triad consists of ipsilateral conductive hearing loss (eustachian tube blockage), trigeminal neuralgia of the mandibular division, and palatal asymmetry due to invasion of levator palatini muscles may be seen. This triad occurs in malignant tumors of the lateral nasopharyngeal wall due to extensive invasion.

Diagnosis is made by high-resolution, contrast-enhanced CT of the neck. The treatment of choice is radiotherapy. Stage I and II can be treated with radiotherapy alone, while higher stages require combination treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

Given below is the labelled diagram showing the fossa of Rossenmuller, eustachian tube, and torus tubaris.
questions.learning: 3 The most common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rossenmuller which is marked 3 in the image. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presented with lesions as shown in the image below and later developed arthritis also. What is the treatment of choice for a patient who presented with the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Methotrexate

The patient has right knee effusion, dactylitis of multiple digits, sharply demarcated red papulosquamous lesions on both knees all of which point towards a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis.

Methotrexate and apremilast are the first-line drugs for the treatment of moderate to severe psoriasis associated with psoriatic arthritis.

Features of psoriatic arthritis are :

* Asymmetrical oligoarthritis

* associated with nail pitting/ onycholysis, or

* dactylitis, enthesitis

* Inflammation is prominent in the distal interphalangeal joints

* There is dactylitis with pronounced telescoping.

* Nail dystrophy (hyperkeratosis and onycholysis) affects each of the finger

* Axial involvement may occur

Radiological features:

* Pencil-in-cup deformity of DIP joint

* marginal erosions with adjacent bony proliferation "whiskering"

* small joint ankylosis

* Ray distribution of lesions

Note :

Indications for methotrexate (inflammatory conditions) include:

* Rheumatoid arthritis

* Psoriasis

* Psoriatic arthritis

* Ankylosing spondylitis

* Polymyositis

* Dermatomyositis

* Wegener’s granulomatosis

* Giant cell arteritis

* Systemic lupus erythematosus

* Other systemic vasculitis

* Graft versus host disease associated with organ transplantation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man with a history of long-term substance abuse presents to the emergency department. Which of the following clinical features is not commonly seen with chronic cocaine use?
options: Dilated pupils, rapid pulse and sweating.
Hallucination of insects crawling on the skin (formication).
questions.explanation: Chronic cocaine abuse is associated with several distinct physical and psychiatric symptoms. Black tongue and teeth (Option C) is NOT typically associated with cocaine; instead, this is a hallmark of "meth mouth" seen in chronic methamphetamine users or from heavy tobacco/cannabis use combined with poor hygiene. Characteristic features of chronic cocaine use include: Nasal or palatal perforation (Option A) due to chronic local vasoconstriction when snorted; Dilated pupils, rapid pulse, and sweating (Option B) resulting from the acute sympathomimetic effects; and Magnan’s sign—tactile hallucinations of insects crawling under the skin (Option D), which leads to compulsive scratching ("cocaine bugs"). Recognizing these specific "behavioral and physical signatures" is essential for clinicians and forensic experts to identify the hidden drug of abuse. While cocaine is a powerful stimulant, its cutaneous and mucosal damage patterns are distinct from other substances. Therefore, dental and tongue discoloration is the correct outlier for cocaine toxicity in this list

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match the following part of GIT with their histologic findings: GIT: 1. Oesophagus 2. Transverse colon 3. Duodenum 4. Terminal ileum Histology: a. Taenia coli and haustrations b. Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium c. Peyer’s patches and mucus-secreting goblet cells d. Villi and submucosal glands
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c

Each segment of the gastrointestinal tract has characteristic histological features that reflect its specialized function. Recognizing these hallmark findings is essential for identifying GIT sections in histology.

Correct Match:

• 1. Oesophagus → b. non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium
• 2. Transverse colon → a. Taenia coli and haustrations
• 3. Duodenum → d. Villi and submucosal (Brunner’s) glands
• 4. Terminal ileum → c. Peyer’s patches and mucus-secreting goblet cells

Why not the other options?

• Oesophagus does not have villi or Brunner’s glands.
• Colon lacks villi and Peyer’s patches; it is identified by taenia coli, haustra, and abundant goblet cells.
• Duodenum is distinguished by Brunner’s glands in the submucosa.
• Terminal ileum contains Peyer’s patches, which are aggregated lymphoid follicles.
questions.learning: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c Each segment of the gastrointestinal tract has characteristic histological features that reflect its specialized function. Recognizing these hallmark findings is essential for identifying GIT sections in histology.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-month-old baby presented with failure to thrive and delayed milestones. On examination, he had elevated transaminases and mild hypotonia without any organomegaly. Ophthalmological examination showed a cherry red spot in the macula. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tay-Sachs disease

The above clinical scenario of an infant with failure to thrive & delayed milestones, elevated transaminases, and cherry red spot on the macula without organomegaly points to a diagnosis of Tay-Sachs disease.

Tay Sach disease is an autosomal recessive disease. It occurs due to a deficiency of hexosaminidase A leading to the accumulation of GM2 ganglioside. It presents with progressive neurodegeneration, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages), a “cherry-red” spot on the macula, and developmental delay but does not have hepatosplenomegaly.

It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, and gradual loss of motor skills. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years.

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type.

The image given below shows the cherry-red spot on the macula.

Other options:

Option A:  Niemann Pick disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder due to deficiency of sphingomyelinase leading to accumulation of sphingomyelin. It presents similarly and also has hepatosplenomegaly.

Option B: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is due to a deficiency of Arylsulfatase A causing central and peripheral demyelination with ataxia, and dementia.

Option C: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder. Presents with hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, osteoporosis, avascular necrosis of the femur, and bone crises. Gaucher cells are lipid-laden macrophages resembling crumpled tissue paper.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with osteoarthritis has been taking ibuprofen for the past three months and has developed occult GI bleeding. Which explanation is correct for the cause?
options: Mucosal injury due to COX-2 inhibition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduced prostaglandin production

The clinical presentation of occult GI bleed in a patient with a history of chronic NSAID use suggests an NSAID-induced gastric ulcer, which is a result of decreased prostaglandin production.

NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, which form the rate-limiting step of prostaglandin synthesis in the GI tract. Prostaglandins promote gastric and duodenal mucosal protection via mucin and bicarbonate secretion and increased mucosal blood flow. NSAIDs impair these protective mechanisms, increasing the risk of peptic ulcers. COX-1 is present in the GIT and converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins in the stomach. Prostaglandins maintain the gastric mucosa and prevent its corrosion.

No dose of NSAID is completely safe. Most patients with NSAID-induced gastric ulcers present with complications such as ulcer perforation and bleeding without preceding dyspepsia symptoms. Concomitant use of glucocorticoids, anticoagulants, cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, or concomitant H. pylori infection increases the risk of complications in NSAID-induced gastric ulcers.

According to the Modified Johnson anatomic classification, NSAID-induced gastric ulcers are classified as Type V and may occur in any part/anywhere in the stomach. H. pylori and NSAID use are the most important factors in the development of peptic ulcer disease. The most common sites for peptic ulcers are the first part of the duodenum and the lesser curvature of the stomach. NSAID-induced ulcers can occur anywhere in the stomach.

Option D: All selective COX-2 inhibitors are less likely to cause gastric ulcers than nonselective COX inhibitors. Selective COX-2 inhibitors include drugs like celecoxib, lumiracoxib, etoricoxib, and parecoxib. They have analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects similar to those of non-selective NSAIDs but with better gastrointestinal tolerability, as COX-1 is not inhibited.

questions.text: A patient requires Ceftriaxone 180 mg. You have a 2 ml syringe with 10 divisions per ml. The vial contains 500 mg/5ml of ceftriaxone. How many divisions in the 2 ml syringe will you fill to give 180 mg ceftriaxone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 18

• 500 mg of drug is in 5 ml and hence 100 mg in 1ml. Thus 180 mg in 1.8 ml
• 10 divisions for each ml
• 1 ml = 10 divisions
• Therefore, 1.8 ml = 10*1.8 = 18 Divisions

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is your diagnosis from the below X-ray images?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell tumor

The given radiographs show the anteroposterior and lateral views of the wrist, demonstrating a solitary lytic lesion with cortical expansion and a soap-bubble appearance in the epiphysis of the distal radius, suggestive of a giant cell tumor (GCT).

GCT usually affects young adults aged 20 to 40 years, with slight female predominance. It is a benign but locally aggressive tumor. It is exclusively seen in adults and affects the ends of long bones, typically involving the epiphysis. The most common location of the tumor is the distal femur followed by the proximal tibia. Involvement of the distal end of the radius is also seen and the tumor is more aggressive in this location.

Important X-ray features of a GCT:

• A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis
• Eccentric location, most often sub-chondral
• Expansion of the overlying cortex
• Soap bubble appearance (the tumor is homogenously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance).
• No calcification within the tumor
• No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor
• Thinned out cortex, may be perforated

The classical "soap bubble" appearance of a giant cell tumor (GCT) is shown below:

Other options:

Option A: A solitary bone cyst is most commonly occurs in the metaphysis of the bone. On an X-ray, a bone fracture fragment may be observed resting in a dependent portion of the cyst, referred to as the fallen fragment or fallen leaf sign. This sign is considered pathognomonic of a simple bone cyst.

The image below shows a bone cyst in the humerus along with a pathological fracture and fallen leaf sign:

Option B: On an X-ray, an aneurysmal bone cyst is seen as an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion with well-defined margins in the metaphysis.

Option D: Osteoblastoma is a benign bone tumor usually occurring in the jaw and spine. On X-ray, a radiopaque central nidus with a surrounding radiolucent halo is seen. If occurring in the long bones, it involves the diaphysis or metaphysis, but never in the epiphysis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents with fever after returning from a forest trip. On examination, a black eschar is seen on the abdomen/trunk. What is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Doxycycline

In the above clinical scenario, a history of a forest trip followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus, which is treated with doxycycline.

Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.

Oral doxycycline is given in uncomplicated scrub typhus. In pregnancy, oral azithromycin is preferred.

In scrub typhus, both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free-living in nature; hence, they do not feed on vertebrate hosts. The larval stage (chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and picks up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below:

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. The Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains, OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus:

* Most widespread Rickettsial disease

* A mite is a vector

* Vector – Trombiculid Mite

* Causative agent – Rickettsia tsutsugamushi

* Incubation period – 10–12 days

* Typical clinical feature – Eschar

* Weil-Felix reaction is strongly positive with Proteus strain OXK

* Treatment – Tetracycline

Renal involvement is a common systemic manifestation of scrub typhus. The severity of renal involvement can range from minor urinary abnormalities such as albuminuria and active urinary sediments such as cellular casts, pyuria, and hematuria to acute kidney injury (AKI), necessitating the immediate initiation of renal replacement therapies.
questions.learning: Doxycycline — In the above clinical scenario, a history of a forest trip followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus, which is treated with doxycycline.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with right hypochondriac pain. He had an episode of diarrhea 1 week prior. CT scan of the abdomen reveals a liver abscess of around 25 ccs. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medical therapy

This patient with an abscess in the liver with a history of diarrhea most likely has an amebic liver abscess. The initial treatment of choice for an amebic liver abscess is medical therapy with metronidazole.

Ingestion of Entamoeba histolytica cysts causes intestinal diseases like diarrhea. Following this, the trophozoites reach the liver mostly through the portal venous system and cause amebic liver abscess. The common presenting features are right upper quadrant pain, tenderness, fever, hepatomegaly, and diarrhea.

CT abdomen is helpful in differentiating amebic from a pyogenic abscess. A rim enhancement is noted in case of a pyogenic abscess.

The mainstay of treatment for amebic abscesses is metronidazole, which is curative in more than 90% of patients. Luminal agents such as iodoquinol, paromomycin, or diloxanide furoate can be administered to treat the carrier state.

Aspiration of abscess is recommended in case of

• Diagnostic uncertainty
• Failure to respond to metronidazole therapy
• Abscesses larger than 5 cm in diameter and in the left liver, since they are thought to carry a high risk of rupture
questions.learning: Medical therapy — This patient with an abscess in the liver with a history of diarrhea most likely has an amebic liver abscess. The initial treatment of choice for an amebic liver abscess is medical therapy with metronidazole.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Weber-Fechner law relates magnitude of sensation to ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Log of Intensity of stimulus

Weber-Fechner Law states that the magnitude of sensation felt is proportionate to the log of the intensity of the stimulus.

Other Laws in Physiology:

• Doctrine of specific nerve energies - When the nerve pathways from a particular sense organ are stimulated, the sensation evoked is that for which the receptor is specialized no matter how or where along the pathway the activity is initiated.
• Law of projection - No matter where a particular sensory pathway is stimulated along its course to the cortex, the conscious sensation produced is referred to the location of the receptor. This principle is called the law of projection.
questions.learning: Log of Intensity of stimulus Weber-Fechner Law states that the magnitude of sensation felt is proportionate to the log of the intensity of the stimulus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5 year old patient presents to the OPD with dysphagia, dysarthria, and dysphonia. On examination, brisk jaw jerk is seen. What is the possible localisation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corticobulbar tracts

Dysphagia, dysarthria, dysphonia with a brisk jaw jerk indicate an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of bulbar muscles, localizing to the corticobulbar tracts (from motor cortex to cranial nerve nuclei (V, VII, IX, X, XII).

Features of corticobulbar (UMN) lesion:

• Dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia
• Brisk jaw jerk
• Spastic tongue
• Emotional lability (pseudobulbar affect)

Differentiation:

• LMN bulbar palsy → absent jaw jerk, fasciculations
• Corticospinal tract lesion → limb weakness, not isolated bulbar signs
• V3 nerve lesion → weak mastication, reduced jaw jerk
questions.learning: Corticobulbar tracts Dysphagia, dysarthria, dysphonia with a brisk jaw jerk indicate an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of bulbar muscles, localizing to the corticobulbar tracts (from motor cortex to cranial nerve nuclei (V, VII, IX, X, XII).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with ascites is found to have SAAG ≥1.1 . All the following can be the causes except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TB peritonitis

The serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) in ascites due to TB peritonitis is < 1.1 g/dL as it is unrelated to portal hypertension.

SAAG helps differentiate ascites caused by portal hypertension from nonportal hypertensive ascites. A SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension and suggests causes such as cirrhosis, cardiac ascites, hepatic vein thrombosis, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, or liver metastases. A SAAG <1.1 g/dL suggests other causes like tuberculous peritonitis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, or pancreatic ascites. For high-SAAG ascites, the ascitic protein level provides additional information. A protein level of ≥2.5 g/dL suggests normal hepatic sinusoids, while <2.5 g/dL indicates damaged and scarred sinusoids. Pro-brain-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels may help identify heart failure as the cause of high-SAAG ascites.

Additional tests may be conducted in specific clinical situations, such as measuring ascitic glucose and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels for suspected secondary peritonitis, ascitic amylase levels for suspected pancreatic ascites, and cytology for peritoneal carcinomatosis.

Tuberculous peritonitis may be associated with ascitic fluid lymphocytosis. The sensitivity of the smear for acid-fast bacilli and culture is low. Elevated ascitic adenosine deaminase > 30–45 U/L is highly sensitive.
questions.learning: TB peritonitis — The serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) in ascites due to TB peritonitis is 30–45 U/L is highly sensitive.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with multiple yellowish raised plaques on eyelids, xanthomas on the achilles tendon. What is the likely cause for the patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial hypercholesterolemia

The clinical presentation with yellowish, raised plaques on eyelids, and tendon xanthomas points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors and Apo B100. This decreases the uptake of Low-density lipoprotein and cholesterol leading to their increased levels in the blood. The increased LDL accumulates in the blood vessels causing atherosclerosis (premature coronary artery disease)and in the Achilles tendon causing tendon xanthomas. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and tendons. Patients can also have yellowish plaques around the eyes (Xanthelasma) and corneal arcus.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

The images below show Achilles tendon xanthoma and xanthelasma respectively:

Other options:

Option B: Tangier’s disease is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a mutation of the ABCA1 gene. Enlarged orange tonsils are pathognomonic. Low HDL levels are seen. There is an increased risk for atherosclerosis.

The image below shows enlarged yellow-orange coloured tonsils in Tangier's disease.

Option C: Xanthomatosis is the deposition of lipids in various parts of the body like tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, eruptive and tuberous xanthomas. This is a sign of underlying lipid metabolism disorders.

Option D: Fabry's disease is a lysosomal storage disorder with a defect in alpha-galactosidase. It causes angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis and characteristic Maltese cross deposits in urine.
questions.learning: Familial hypercholesterolemia — The clinical presentation with yellowish, raised plaques on eyelids, and tendon xanthomas points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A teenage girl presents to the outpatient department with delayed puberty, short stature, and widely spaced nipples. What is the most likely karyotype?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of delayed puberty, short stature, and a "shield chest" with widely spaced nipples is pathognomonic for Turner Syndrome. As discussed in Q.148, this is a chromosomal disorder where one X chromosome is partially or completely missing. The most common and probable karyotype is 45, XO. 46, XO (Option A) is a non-standard notation for Turner's. 47, XXX (Option C), or Triple X syndrome, usually involves tall stature and mild learning disabilities, but not primary amenorrhea or short stature. 46, XY (Option D) is the normal male karyotype; in a phenotypic female, it would suggest Swyer syndrome (pure gonadal dysgenesis), which presents with delayed puberty but normal height. Turner patients also frequently have webbed necks and cardiovascular anomalies. Management focuses on growth hormone therapy during childhood and estrogen replacement to induce secondary sexual characteristics at puberty. This specific physical triad is a classic board exam "spotter" for the 45, XO genotype
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of delayed puberty, short stature, and a "shield chest" with widely spaced nipples is pathognomonic for Turner Syndrome. As discussed in Q.148, this is a chromosomal disorder where one X chromosome is partially or completely missing.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most effective method for locating an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors. While 90% are in the adrenal medulla, "extra-adrenal" types (paragangliomas) can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain. The most effective method for locating these ectopic tumors is a nucleotide scan (Option C), specifically the MIBG (Meta-iodobenzoguanidine) scan. MIBG is a catecholamine precursor that is taken up by chromaffin tissue, allowing the scan to "light up" the tumor anywhere in the body. VMA excretion (Option B) (urinary vanillylmandelic acid) is a biochemical test used to diagnose the presence of a tumor but cannot locate it. X-rays (Option A) are not sensitive enough to detect these soft-tissue masses. Clinical examination (Option D) may detect hypertension or a rare abdominal mass but is not an accurate localization tool . MIBG scans are superior to CT/MRI for extra-adrenal cases because they identify functionally active tumors across a whole-body survey. Therefore, functional imaging via nucleotide scanning is the gold standard for localization
questions.learning: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors. While 90% are in the adrenal medulla, "extra-adrenal" types (paragangliomas) can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain.

questions.text: What will be the level of the anti-Mullerian hormone in low ovarian reserve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. <1

In low ovarian reserve, the level of anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) will be <1 ng/ml.

AMH is a glycoprotein secreted by the granulosa cells of the primordial follicle of the ovary. It helps in oocyte maturation and mono-follicular development. AMH is also used in assessing ovarian reserve.

AMH levels in ng/ml
Interpretation

2–6.8
Normal

<1
Poor ovarian reserve

>10

PCOD

Hyperstimulation syndrome

In women, AMH is always absent during embryogenesis and is secreted by the granulosa cells after puberty. It helps in follicular development and oocyte maturation. Estimation of serum AMH is used in the study of ovarian reserve in female infertility and secondary amenorrhoea.

In men, AMH starts to be secreted by the Sertoli cells in the testes by the 7th week of intrauterine life. It continues until puberty. It inhibits the development of the Müllerian system. The absence of AMH results in the development of hermaphroditism.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures will be present in the area marked below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pterygopalatine ganglion

The pterygopalatine ganglion will be present in the area marked in the image above which is the pterygopalatine fossa.

The pterygopalatine ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion located in the pterygopalatine fossa, a small, cone-shaped depression situated deep in the skull. This fossa is located posterior to the maxilla (upper jaw) and adjacent to the nasal cavity.

It is responsible for parasympathetic innervation to the lacrimal gland, nasal glands, and palatine glands. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers originate from the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) and travel through the greater petrosal nerve. These fibres join with the deep petrosal nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal before synapsing in the ganglion.

Boundaries of the Pterygopalatine Fossa:

* Anteriorly: Posterior wall of the maxillary sinus.

* Posteriorly: Pterygoid process of the sphenoid bone.

* Medially: Perpendicular plate of the palatine bone.

* Laterally: Pterygomaxillary fissure, which opens into the infratemporal fossa.

* Superiorly: Inferior surface of the sphenoid bone.

* Inferiorly: Palatine bone.

Structures surrounding the Pterygopalatine Ganglion:

* Maxillary Nerve (V2): A branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) that passes through the fossa, giving off branches to the ganglion.

* Greater and Lesser Palatine Nerves: Emerge from the ganglion to innervate the hard and soft palate.

* Nasal Nerves: Branches that innervate the nasal cavity, including the nasopalatine nerve.

* Pharyngeal Nerve: Provides innervation to parts of the nasopharynx.

* Arterial Supply: The maxillary artery's branches, including the sphenopalatine artery, which supplies the nasal cavity, are present in the fossa.
Foramina and fissures:

* Foramen rotundum: Transmits the maxillary nerve (V2) into the fossa.

* Pterygoid Canal: Contains the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve), which carries both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers.

* Sphenopalatine Foramen: Connects the fossa to the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following side effects are more commonly seen with carbamazepine than oxcarbazepine except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyponatremia

Hyponatremia occurs more frequently in the case of oxcarbazepine than carbamazepine.

Both carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are sodium-channel blockers that stabilize neuronal membranes. Oxcarbazepine is the 10-keto analog of carbamazepine and and cannot form an epoxide metabolite. Carbamazepine potentiates the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). It can result in water retention with decreased osmolarity and hyponatremia, especially in elderly patients with cardiac disease. Although hyponatremia may occur more commonly with oxcarbazepine than with carbamazepine, most adverse effects of oxcarbazepine are similar to those of carbamazepine.
Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can cause leukopenia, aplastic anemia, hepato-toxicity in the elderly.
Oxcarbazepine shows lesser hypersensitivity reaction. Hence, rashes (option A) are more commonly seen with carbamazepine than with oxcarbazepine.
Studies have shown that carbamazepine elevates enzyme gamma-glutamyl transpeptidases (GGT) more frequently than oxcarbazepine because of enzyme P450 induction. Hepatotoxicity from oxcarbazepine occurs less commonly compared to carbamazepine (Option D).
Side effects of carbamazepine therapy include: mnemonic: HEADS

Hypersensitivity reactions
Eosinophilia
Agranulocytosis: report symptoms like sore throat/fever
Aplastic anemia
Ataxia
Dilutional hyponatremia
Diplopia, blurred vision
Splenomegaly
Stevens-Johnson syndrome

Carbamazepine is most effective in complex partial seizures. It is also used in GTCS and simple partial seizures, trigeminal and related neuralgias, and manic depressive psychosis. Oxcarbazepine has been used to treat intractable trigeminal neuralgia refractory to other anticonvulsants.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions does the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) typically rise?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is a clinical estimate of left atrial pressure and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. In "Cardiogenic shock" (Option C), the primary problem is a failure of the heart's pumping mechanism, leading to blood backing up into the pulmonary circulation. This results in a "characteristically high PCWP" (typically mmHg). In contrast, "Hypovolemic shock" (Option A) involves a total loss of blood or fluid volume, leading to a "low PCWP" due to empty heart chambers. "Septic shock" (Option B) and "Anaphylactic shock" (Option D) are forms of distributive shock characterized by peripheral vasodilation; these also typically present with "low or normal PCWP" as blood pools in the periphery rather than the heart. Monitoring PCWP using a Swan-Ganz catheter is essential in the ICU to differentiate between causes of respiratory distress and shock, ensuring that patients receive the correct treatment—either fluids for hypovolemia or inotropes/diuretics for cardiogenic failure

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with abdominal distension, fasting hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly (liver palpable 8 cm below the costal margin). The liver is smooth on palpation. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucose-6-phosphatase

Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase causes Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (Von Gierke disease). This enzyme normally converts glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose in the final step of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver and kidney.

When this enzyme is deficient:

• Glucose cannot be released into the bloodstream, leading to severe fasting hypoglycemia.
• Glucose-6-phosphate accumulates, which is diverted into glycogen synthesis, causing excess glycogen deposition in the liver.
• This results in marked hepatomegaly and abdominal distension.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency: Causes hemolytic anemia due to impaired NADPH production in RBCs, not hepatomegaly with hypoglycemia.
• Myophosphorylase deficiency: Causes McArdle disease, presenting with exercise intolerance and muscle cramps, not liver enlargement.
• Phosphofructokinase deficiency: Causes Tarui disease (GSD VII) with muscle weakness and hemolysis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Given below is the demonstration of tetanization in the gastrocnemius muscle of a frog. Identify the tetanising frequency.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 30-35 Hz

Tetanizing frequency demonstrated by the muscle is 33Hz. In the above graph, we know,

• The speed of the paper is 1000mm/sec.
• The y-axis represents millivolts, the x-axis represents time.
• The scale on the x-axis is 10mm.
• The area under the graph represents the muscle contraction.

Contraction period (latent period to maximum force of contraction) includes 3 scales = 30 mm.

As paper speed is 1000mm/sec,

Contraction period = 30mm = (30/1000) = 30 msec.

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1000/30 = 33Hz.

Tetanization

The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways:

• by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple ﬁber summations.
• by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization.

When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventually fuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous, this is called tetanization.

Tetanization occurs in two ways:

• Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.
• Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.

questions.text: A 43-year-old male presented with right-sided rib pain and shortness of breath. A chest X-ray showed a significant right-sided pneumothorax with cardio-mediastinal shift to the left. Which of the following changes will be seen?
options: Increased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume
Decreased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume
Decreased lung volume, thoracic volume remains unaffected
Lung volume remains unaffected, Decreased thoracic volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume

A large pneumothorax with mediastinal shift indicates a tension pneumothorax.

Air accumulation in the pleural space causes collapse of the affected lung (decreased lung volume) and expansion of the hemithorax (increased thoracic volume).

The raised intrathoracic pressure leads to mediastinal displacement to the opposite side.

↑ Intrapleural pressure

Lung collapses → ↓ lung volume

Thoracic cavity expands outward → ↑ thoracic volume

Mediastinum shifts to opposite side

↓ Venous return → shock risk

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a protozoan parasite, that can be seen inside Kupffer cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leishmania donovani

The protozoan parasite, that can be seen inside Kupffer cells is Leishmania donovani.

Kupffer cells are a component of the mononuclear phagocytic system found in the liver. The amastigote form of leishmania also known as the Leishman-Donovan (LD) body (shown in the image below) is an intracellular form found inside macrophages, monocytes, and other reticuloendothelial cells. It contains a kinetoplast, which consists of a parabasal body and a blepharoplast. Flagellum is absent.

Leishmaniasis is a slowly progressing indigenous disease caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania.

The life cycle of Leishmania involves two forms:

• The promastigote develops and lives extracellularly in the sandfly vector, and
• The amastigote multiplies intracellularly in the reticuloendothelial cells of the host

It is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Phlebotomus sandfly which inoculates the flagellated promastigotes into the skin of the host. This condition causes fever with rigor and chills associated with splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. It lowers immunity, causes persistent fever, anemia, and liver and spleen enlargement, and if left untreated, death may occur due to opportunistic infection.

Diagnosis of leishmaniasis is mainly by demonstration of amastigotes within macrophages in tissue aspirates such as blood smears, bone marrow, splenic, or lymph node aspirate. It is the gold standard for diagnosis.
questions.learning: Leishmania donovani — The protozoan parasite, that can be seen inside Kupffer cells is Leishmania donovani. Kupffer cells are a component of the mononuclear phagocytic system found in the liver.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The Bragg peak effect is pronounced in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proton

The Bragg peak effect is pronounced in protons.

The proton is a heavy and charged particle that gradually loses its speed as it interacts with human tissue. It is easily controlled and delivers its maximum dose at a precise depth and can go as far as 32 cm. The absorbed dose increases very gradually with greater depth and lower speed, suddenly rising to a peak when the proton is ultimately stopped. This is known as the Bragg peak.

The behavior of the proton can be precisely determined, and the beam can be directed, allowing the Bragg peak to occur within the tumor site. Immediately following this burst of energy, the protons cease radiating and come to a complete stop. This property of proton therapy enables targeting tumors within the body, delivering radiation directly to the tumor while sparing the surrounding healthy cells, offering a much less invasive alternative to treat cancer.

The Bragg curve shown below plots the energy loss of ionizing radiation during its travel through matter.
questions.learning: Proton — The Bragg peak effect is pronounced in protons. The proton is a heavy and charged particle that gradually loses its speed as it interacts with human tissue.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old factory worker was brought to the emergency room with complaints of headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision after he consumed local spirit. Which of the following is used for the treatment of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fomepizole

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of methanol toxicity. Ethanol and fomepizole is used for the treatment of this condition.

Methanol poisoning is caused due to ingestion of illicit liquor which contains ethanol adulterated with methanol. Methanol is metabolized to formaldehyde and formic acid by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, respectively. The metabolites of ethanol are responsible for the toxic effects.

Clinically, patients present with headache, vomiting, abdomen pain, uneasiness, confusion, delirium, and coma. Formic acid specifically damages the retina and optic nerve and results in blurring of vision and blindness.

Elevated levels of formic acid and other organic acids result in metabolic acidosis in arterial blood gas analysis(ABG).

Treatment of methanol poisoning includes gastric lavage with sodium bicarbonate if the patient is brought within 2 hours of ingesting methanol to combat acidosis. Ethanol infusion since ethanol is preferentially metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase over methanol and helps by reducing the rate of generation of formaldehyde and formic acid.

Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase and the drug of choice for methanol poisoning. Folate therapy with calcium leucovorin reduces blood formate levels by enhancing its oxidation. Hemodialysis is used in severe cases of methanol toxicity.

Other options:

Option B: Flumazenil is the inverse agonist of benzodiazepine receptors and is used for the treatment of benzodiazepine overdose.

Option C: N-acetyl cysteine is used as an antidote for the treatment of paracetamol poisoning.

Option D: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist used for the treatment of opioid overdose.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Fishtail deformity is seen in the fracture of _____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Distal end of humerus

Fishtail deformity is seen following a fracture of the distal end of the humerus.

Fishtail deformity of the elbow is a rare complication that can occur in childhood after a distal humeral fracture. It is characterized by a contour abnormality of the distal humerus due to the absence or resorption of the lateral trochlear ossification centers.

Fishtail deformity of the distal humerus can be of 2 types:

• The first type is a sharp-angled wedge, which commonly occurs after fractures of the lateral condyle. It is caused by the persistence of a gap between the lateral condylar physis ossification center and the medial ossification of the trochlea. Because of this gap, the lateral crista of the trochlea may be underdeveloped, which may represent a small “bony bar” in the distal humeral physis
• The second type is believed to be associated with osteonecrosis of the lateral part of the medial crista of the trochlea.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Revised A nurse got an accidental prick from a needle used for an HIV+ patient. Which single test would lead to a confirmatory diagnosis in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Western blot assay

The single test that would lead to a confirmatory diagnosis in this patient is Western blot assay.

The Western blot assay detects specific antibodies against various HIV proteins in the patient's blood sample. It is considered highly specific and is used to confirm the presence of HIV antibodies after a positive screening test, such as an ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay). The Western blot assay helps differentiate between true HIV infection and false-positive results that may occur with screening tests.

ELISA even though is done as a 2-test protocol, one single test is not considered a positive case. The two-test protocol for the diagnosis of HIV needs two ELISA tests to be positive. (i.e. If the initial ELISA is positive, a second ELISA is carried out. If the second ELISA is also positive, only then, the case is reported to be positive).

Investigations involved in HIV testing strategies:

* ELISA/ rapid tests

* Confirmatory tests with high specificity like Western Blot and line immunoassays are used in indeterminate/ discordant cases of rapid tests.

In India, NACO provides Western Blot Confirmatory testing only to resolve indeterminate results on previous serological testing and not for routine confirmation after a positive result on screening tests. The drawbacks of Western Blot include low rates of detection during acute HIV infection and misclassification of HIV-2 infection.

Other options:

p24 antigen:

* The p24 antigen is a viral protein that is detectable in the blood during the early stages of HIV infection.

* It can be detected within a few days to a few weeks after infection before antibodies are produced.

* While a positive p24 antigen test suggests HIV infection, it is not considered a confirmatory test on its own and is often used in combination with other tests.

PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction):

* PCR is a sensitive molecular test that can detect the genetic material (RNA or DNA) of the HIV virus in a person's blood.

* It can detect HIV at an early stage, even before antibodies are produced.

* PCR is commonly used for early diagnosis in infants born to HIV-positive mothers or in cases where early detection is crucial, such as occupational exposures.

HIV ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay):

* The ELISA is a screening test that detects antibodies produced by the immune system in response to HIV infection.

* It is highly sensitive and widely used as an initial test for HIV.

* However, a positive ELISA result needs to be confirmed by additional tests, such as the Western blot assay, to differentiate between true infection and false-positive results.
questions.learning: Western blot assay — The single test that would lead to a confirmatory diagnosis in this patient is Western blot assay. The Western blot assay detects specific antibodies against various HIV proteins in the patient's blood sample.

• Two on the posterior vaginal wall

• The points above the hymen are described as minus and points below as plus.

Stage
Description

Stage 0
No descent of pelvic organs.

Stage 1
The leading edge of the prolapse is >1 cm above the level of the hymen.

Stage 2
The leading edge of the prolapse is <1cm proximal or distal to the hymen.

Stage 3
The leading point of prolapse is >1cm below the hymen but protrudes no further than 2 cm less than the total length of the vagina.

Complete eversion of vagina

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person who was mentally unsound at the time of committing a crime is exempt from legal liability if they were unaware of the nature of their actions or their consequences. What is this legal principle called?
questions.explanation: The McNaughton rule (or M'Naghten rule) is the foundational legal principle for the insanity defense. It states that a person is not criminally responsible for their actions if, at the time of the offense, a "defect of reason" from a disease of the mind made them unaware of the nature and quality of the act or, if they did know it, that they did not know it was wrong. Durham's rule (Option B) is a broader, less common standard stating that a person is not responsible if their act was the "product" of a mental disease. Currens rule (Option C) relates to the "substantial capacity" to conform one's conduct to the law. The Irresistible impulse test (Option D) focuses on whether a person had the power to control their actions, even if they knew they were wrong. The McNaughton rule remains the most widely used standard in many legal systems, including India (Section 84 of the IPC), as it places the focus on the cognitive ability of the individual at the exact moment of the crime

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presented to OPD of a PHC Watery diarrhoea having severe dehydration. Most likely causative agent underlying would be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rota virus

In children below 5 years, rotavirus is the most common cause of acute watery diarrhoea and is frequently associated with severe dehydration due to profuse fluid loss.

Rotavirus infects the enterocytes of the small intestine which causes destruction of intestinal epithelial cells, reduced absorption of fluids and increased intestinal secretion that results in Profuse watery diarrhoea.

Bacterial causes like Shigella and Salmonella typically produce inflammatory or dysenteric diarrhoea, while E. coli O157:H7 is more often linked to bloody diarrhoea and HUS rather than severe watery diarrhoea.

Rotavirus infection can be prevented by vaccination.

India includes the Rotavirus vaccine in the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).
questions.learning: Rota virus — In children below 5 years, rotavirus is the most common cause of acute watery diarrhoea and is frequently associated with severe dehydration due to profuse fluid loss.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A Patient had dietary Cu deficiency, which is required by lysyl oxidase to cross link the collagen, what is the diagnosis of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Menkes Disease

Copper is an essential cofactor for the enzyme lysyl oxidase, which catalyzes the oxidative deamination of lysine and hydroxylysine residues in collagen and elastin, allowing cross-linking of connective tissue fibers. Role of lysyl oxidase:

• Requires Cu²⁺ (copper) as a cofactor
• Forms cross-links between collagen and elastin fibers
• Provides tensile strength and structural stability to connective tissue

Menkes disease:

• X-linked recessive disorder
• Caused by mutation in ATP7A gene → defective copper transport
• Leads to systemic copper deficiency and reduced lysyl oxidase activity
• Weak connective tissue
• Kinky (steely) hair
• Neurodegeneration
• Failure to thrive
• Hypopigmentation

Differentiation from other options:

• Scurvy → Vitamin C deficiency → impaired hydroxylation of collagen
• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome → collagen structure/synthesis defects
• Scoliosis → spinal curvature disorder, not enzyme-related
questions.learning: Menkes Disease Copper is an essential cofactor for the enzyme lysyl oxidase, which catalyzes the oxidative deamination of lysine and hydroxylysine residues in collagen and elastin, allowing cross-linking of connective tissue fibers.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Of the following, which organism cannot be grown on an artificial culture media?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mycobacterium leprae

Mycobacterium leprae cannot be grown in a pure culture medium. It does not obey Koch's postulates and cannot be grown in vitro.

Mycobacterium leprae is an obligate intracellular bacillus confined to humans, armadillos, and in some locales, sphagnum moss. It is the only bacterium which invades peripheral nerves.
questions.learning: Mycobacterium leprae Mycobacterium leprae cannot be grown in a pure culture medium. It does not obey Koch's postulates and cannot be grown in vitro.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not involved in meta-analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Randomization

All the above steps are involved in meta-analysis except for randomization.

Meta-analysis is a set of statistical techniques for combining quantitative results from multiple studies to produce a summary of empirical knowledge on a given topic. It refers to a method of a systematic review.

Four basic steps involved in a meta-analysis are:

• Identification: This is the first step in a meta-analysis and it includes finding all of the articles or studies related to the topic.
• Selection: After assembling all the related studies, it is important to select the right or necessary studies by using inclusion (also called eligibility) criteria. Examples are minimum sample size (as very small studies may be unrepresentative), study design (controlled trials only vs randomized controlled trials only), etc.
• Abstraction: Once an appropriate group of studies has been identified, the author has to abstract the relevant data from each study.
• Analysis: This is the last step of meta-analysis.

Objectives of meta-analysis include,

• Summarize results from individual studies.
• Analyze differences in results among studies.
• Overcome small sample sizes of individual studies to detect the effects of interest.
• Determine if new studies are needed to investigate an issue.
• Generate new hypotheses for future studies.

Note- Randomization involves randomly assigning patients to different groups, like experimental and control groups. Clinical trials usually involve randomization and are hence called randomized clinical trials (RCTs). It is done to prevent confounding.
questions.learning: Randomization All the above steps are involved in meta-analysis except for randomization. Meta-analysis is a set of statistical techniques for combining quantitative results from multiple studies to produce a summary of empirical knowledge on a given topic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with gradually worsening difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. His muscle strength transiently improves with repeated activity but later deteriorates, causing frequent falls. A chest scan shows a hilar mass. Which type of lung cancer is most likely associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Small cell carcinoma

The patient most likely has Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), a paraneoplastic syndrome strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). LEMS is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) at the neuromuscular junction, resulting in decreased acetylcholine release. A characteristic feature is proximal muscle weakness that temporarily improves with repeated muscle use (facilitation), distinguishing it from myasthenia gravis. The patient has:

• Proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs)
• Transient improvement with repeated activity
• Hilar lung mass
• Frequent falls

These findings are classic for Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which is most commonly associated with small cell lung carcinoma.

Why not the other options?

• A. Squamous cell carcinoma: Commonly associated with PTHrP secretion, causing hypercalcemia, not Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
• B. Large cell carcinoma: May produce β-hCG, causing gynecomastia, but is not typically associated with LEMS.
• D. Adenocarcinoma: The most common lung cancer overall, especially in nonsmokers, but has no strong association with Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
questions.learning: Small cell carcinoma — The patient most likely has Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), a paraneoplastic syndrome strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A and B in the graph below represent which of the following ions, in terms of permeability for action potential generation?
options: A is Na+, B is K+
A is Na+, B is Ca2+
A is K+, B is Ca2+
A is Ca2+, B is K+
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A is Na+, B is K+

In the given graph, showing action potential generation in terms of ion permeability, wave A represents Na+ and B represents K+.

The sequence of events during the action potential occurs in 7 steps as described below.

1. Resting-state - Both channels are closed

2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters the cell. The membrane reaches threshold potential.

3. The sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs.

4. Sodium conductance decreases.

5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Repolarization occurs.

6. Sodium channels are reset, and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase, the potassium channels remain open and slowly return to closed state causing after-hyperpolarization.

7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP.
questions.learning: A is Na+, B is K+ — In the given graph, showing action potential generation in terms of ion permeability, wave A represents Na+ and B represents K+. The sequence of events during the action potential occurs in 7 steps as described below.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 7-year-old child post-tonsillectomy comes to you with complaints of snoring, palpitations, mouth breathing and a slight decrease in hearing. On examination, you notice a high-arched palate. His school performance has deteriorated as well. His mother is worried. What is the next line of management for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The patient is suffering from serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy causing eustachian tube obstruction. The best line of management is adenoidectomy with grommet insertion.

Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear is thought to happen due to either malfunctioning (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, palatal defects, tumors of nasopharynx) or increased secretory activity of the eustachian tube (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

It is often seen in children 5-8 years of age. They present with hearing loss not exceeding 40 dB, which is insidious in onset. Speech may be delayed and defective due to hearing loss. Mild earaches with a history of upper respiratory tract infection are usually seen.

On otoscopy,

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* If the tympanic membrane is transparent fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss. X-ray mastoid reveals clouding of air cells.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.

* Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion — The patient is suffering from serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy causing eustachian tube obstruction.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with exertional dyspnoea and a history of cyanotic spell. On examination, there is clubbing and a harsh systolic murmur heard at left upper sternal border. Chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond infancy, presenting with exertional dyspnea, cyanotic spells, clubbing, and a systolic murmur.

• Components (PROV):
• Pulmonary stenosis
• Right ventricular hypertrophy
• Overriding aorta
• Ventricular septal defect

Clinical features:

• Cyanotic (tet) spells due to increased right-to-left shunting
• Harsh systolic murmur at left upper sternal border
• Squatting relieves symptoms

Chest X-ray finding: “Boot-shaped heart” due to right ventricular hypertrophy

Differentiation:

• TAPVC: snowman sign
• TGA: egg-on-string appearance
• Coarctation: rib notching

questions.text: Identify the investigation shown in the image:

This characterizes mammography, a diagnostic tool that uses low-dose X-rays and breast compression to achieve high-resolution images of breast tissue. The MLO view is critical as it captures the upper outer quadrant and the pectoralis muscle. While mammography is technically a form of X-ray (Option C), "Mammography" is the specific clinical term for this specialized breast imaging study. CT scans (Option B) and MRIs (Option D) use entirely different cross-sectional technologies and do not present the breast in these specific compressed CC/MLO views. Therefore, the architectural detail and standard positioning confirm that the investigation is a mammogram

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus undergoes an exercise treadmill test for evaluation of intermittent chest discomfort. He has no ECG changes during testing. During peak exercise, his heart rate increases from 70/min to 132/min, and his mean arterial pressure rises from 95 mm Hg to 112 mm Hg. Which of the following hemodynamic changes is most likely to occur during peak exercise compared to rest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased total systemic vascular resistance

During dynamic exercise, several coordinated cardiovascular changes occur:

• ↑ Cardiac output (↑ HR + ↑ stroke volume)
• ↑ Systolic blood pressure
• ↓ Total systemic vascular resistance (TSVR) due to vasodilation in active skeletal muscles
• Blood flow is redistributed to muscles and skin

Despite increased cardiac output, TSVR falls because metabolic vasodilation predominates.

Why not other options?

A. Decreased cardiac output → Opposite; CO increases during exercise

B. Increased LVEDP → May remain normal or slightly increase, not a key change

C. Increased pulmonary artery pressure → May increase slightly, but not the primary expected change

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient was brought to the OPD with the following deformity. Identify the condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Genu valgum

The given X-ray of a child with abnormally approximated knees, divergent ankles, and increased intermalleolar distances depicts genu valgum.

A normal knee has 5-7 degrees of physiological outward deviation (valgum). Any increase in angle can result in Genu valgum or knock knee where knees are abnormally approximated and the ankles are divergent.

Intermalleolar distance has been used to assess the degree of genu valgum. It is the distance between the medial malleoli in a standing patient with touching medial femoral condyles. Intermalleolar distances greater than 8 cm are considered pathologic.

Children start developing physiologic genu valgum by age 2, and it becomes most prominent between ages 3 to 4. After that, it typically decreases to a stable, slightly valgus position by age 7 years. Other causes include

* Bilateral Genu Valgum: Physiologic genu valgum, skeletal dysplasia, metabolic bone diseases, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis.

* Unilateral Genu Valgum: Trauma, tumors, and infection.

Osteoarthritis of the knee
Rheumatoid arthritis of the knee

Genu varum more common
Genu valgum more common

Subchondral sclerosis
Periarticular osteopenia

No soft tissue swelling
Soft tissue swelling (pannus)

Osteophytes
No osteophytes

Hard and bony joint
Soft, warm, and tender joint

Rheumatoid factor negative
Rheumatoid factor positive

Knee deformities are:

* Genu valgus (valgum) or knock knee - Knees are abnormally approximated and the ankles are divergent.

* Genu varus (varum) or bow knee - Knees are abnormally divergent and the ankles are approximated.

* Windswept deformity - Abnormal valgus deformity of one knee with varus of the other.

* Genu recurvatum - Hyperextension at the knee joint with backward bending.

Pearl PF0382: Important Clinical Features of Rickets

Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices

* In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest:

* Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia

* Wrist: especially the ulna

* Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary

• If the patient's perception of depth in either eye is defective, then the image appears just like normal 2D image.

• Hardy–Rand–Rittler test: It is similar to ishihara test but is used to detect all three color vision defect.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are storage symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia? * Urgency * Enuresis * Hesitancy * Frequency * Dribbling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 4

Urgency, enuresis and frequency are storage symptoms.

Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) can be classified as:

Storage
Voiding

• Frequency (earliest symptom in BPH)
• Nocturia
• Urgency
• Urge incontinence
• Nocturnal incontinence (enuresis)

• Hesitancy
• Poor flow
• Intermittent stream
• Dribbling
• Sensation of poor bladder emptying
• Episodes of near retention

Clinical features of BPH:

* Urinary urgency

* Urinary nocturia

* Urinary frequency

* Urinary incontinence, terminal dribbling

* Abrupt starting and stopping of the urinary stream

* Splitting of the voiding stream

Physical examination reveals a smooth enlarged and non-tender prostate. Lab investigations reveal a normal PSA (prostate-specific antigen). Diagnosis is made based on clinical presentation and a lack of lab findings suggestive of malignancy (elevated PSA). A biopsy is rarely indicated.

Conservative treatment is recommended for men with mild symptoms, flow rate >10ml/s, and good bladder emptying with residual urine <100ml.

Medical management includes alpha-adrenergic blocking agents that inhibit the contraction of smooth muscle that is found in the prostate. Tamsulosin is an adrenoreceptor antagonist with receptor selectivity at α1A. It is used in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

The other class of drugs is the 5α-reductase inhibitors, which inhibit the conversion of testosterone to DHT, the most active form of androgen. Finasteride is a 5α-reductase enzyme inhibitor. It is effective in the treatment of palpable enlarged prostate. These drugs result in a 25% shrinkage of the prostate gland.

Indications for surgical management:

* Lower urinary tract symptoms that are refractory to medical therapy

* Refractory urinary retention

* Recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI)

* Hematuria

* Stone formation

* Hydronephrosis, hydroureter with renal functional impairment

Surgical management involves the use of the transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Laser ablative techniques using holmium YAG can also be done.

Storage symptoms are seen in conditions where the bladder is irritated. Voiding symptoms are common in conditions causing bladder outlet obstruction. In benign prostatic hyperplasia, both storage and voiding symptoms are present.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30 year old female is very talkative, hyperactive, doesn't sleep well and spends a lot of money shopping for the past 2 weeks. When asked questions she becomes irritable and angry. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Bipolar I disorder with manic episode
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bipolar I disorder with manic episode

This question describes a female who has mania as she is very talkative, hyperactive, doesn't sleep well and spends a lot of money shopping for the past 2 weeks.

Bipolar disorder manifests in two primary types:

* Bipolar I: This type is characterized by at least one lifetime episode of mania. Episodes of major depressive disorder may or may not be present.

* Bipolar II: This type involves episodes of hypomania alongside episodes of major depressive disorder. A key diagnostic criterion is the absence of any history of a manic episode.

Mania is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, elated, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy, lasting at least 1 week.

Other options:

Option A: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterised by repetitive intrusive thoughts, impulses or images which are not associated with compulsive acts.

Option C: Hypomania is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated/irritable mood, abnormally and persistently increased activity/energy, lasting for at least 4 days. It is similar to a manic episode wherein the patients can portray all of the above-mentioned symptoms but it is not severe enough to cause impairment in social or occupational functioning.

Option D: Cyclothymia is a chronic, fluctuating mood disturbance with many periods of hypomania and of depression.

Pearl PF1511: Bipolar disorder

Bipolar & related disorders

Manic episode

• Symptoms more severe
• 1 week unless hospitalized
• Marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or hospitalization necessary
• May have psychotic features; makes episode manic by definition

Hypomanic episode

• Symptoms less severe
• 4 days to less than 7 days
• Unequivocal, observable change in functioning from patient's baseline
• Symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment or necessitate hospitalization
• No psychotic features

Bipolar I

• Manic episode(s)
• Depressive episodes common (but not required for diagnosis)

Bipolar II

• Hypomanic episode(s)
• Major depressive episodes (required for diagnosis)

Cyclothymic disorder

• At least 2 years of fluctuating, mild hypomanic & depressive symptoms that
do not meet criteria for hypomanic episodes or major depressive episodes
questions.learning: Bipolar I disorder with manic episode — This question describes a female who has mania as she is very talkative, hyperactive, doesn't sleep well and spends a lot of money shopping for the past 2 weeks.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true about colon cancer?

1. Right and left colon cancers can behave differently
2. Colon cancers can be hereditary
3. Colon cancer risk can be reduced by metformin
4. Colon cancers frequently metastasize to the liver
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

All the 4 given statements on colon cancer are true:

• Right and left colon cancers present differently. Left-sided tumors commonly cause obstruction and present with changes in bowel habits or rectal bleeding. On the other hand, right-sided tumors typically present with iron deficiency anemia or a mass.
• While the majority of colorectal cancers occur sporadically, hereditary cases are also seen in patients with a family history of colorectal cancer. Genetic testing aids in early diagnosis for individuals with a positive family history.
• Metformin, a commonly used biguanide compound for diabetes mellitus, reduces the risk of cancer, including colorectal cancer. It achieves this by disrupting cellular energy supply through the inhibition of aerobic glycolysis.
• Liver is the most frequent site of distant metastasis for colorectal cancer, with metastases occurring via the portal venous system. The risk of hepatic metastasis increases with tumor size and grade. The lung is the second most common site of distant metastasis, also due to hematogenous spread. Carcinomatosis (diffuse peritoneal metastases) results from peritoneal seeding.

Note: Regional lymph node involvement is the most common form of spread of colorectal carcinoma and usually precedes distant metastasis.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 All the 4 given statements on colon cancer are true: • Right and left colon cancers present differently. Left-sided tumors commonly cause obstruction and present with changes in bowel habits or rectal bleeding.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The compound given in the image below can be used in the treatment of which of the following poisonings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phophorus

The compound given in the image is copper sulphate. It can be used in the treatment of phosphorus poisoning.

The initial stage of acute phosphorus poisoning through ingestion involves severe abdominal discomfort, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Excreta and breath have a garlicky odour. Luminescent faeces and vomit are characteristically seen (smoky stool syndrome). Direct contact with the skin can result in second and third-degree burns. Shock, hematemesis due to liver failure, and renal insufficiency are potential causes of death.

Regular inhalation of phosphorus fumes, leading to chronic phosphorus poisoning, results in necrosis of the lower jaw around a decayed tooth. This condition is known as phossy jaw and is associated with the discharge of foul-smelling pus from multiple sinuses.

Gastric lavage with potassium permanganate oxidizes phosphorus into phosphoric acid and phosphates. Activated charcoal can be used to adsorb the poison.

Stomach wash with 0.2% copper sulphate solution or 0.2 g of copper sulphate every 5 minutes until vomiting occurs. It coats the particles of phosphorus with a film of copper phosphide, which is relatively harmless. As copper has caustic properties and can cause acute poisoning, adequate care should be taken. Copper sulphate was also used for topical application in phosphorus poisoning. It is not recommended now.

Other options:

Option A: Aluminium Phosphide has no antidote. Magnesium sulphate is given in ALP poisoning to correct hypomagnesemia and arrhythmias and reduce organ toxicity.

Option B and D: British anti-Lewisite (BAL), also known as Dimercaprol, is used as an antidote for Mercury poisoning (except non-alkyl mercury) and Arsenic poisoning.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following condition seen in the image results from failure of fusion of :
options: Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence

Cleft lip is due to failure of fusion between the medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence.

Various defects of fusion of prominences in the face region are as follows:

* Cleft lip is due to the failure of the fusion of maxillary prominence with medial nasal prominence. It can be unilateral or bilateral. It can vary in severity from a small notch in the upper lip to a double cleft extending into both the nostrils. There is also associated underdevelopment of the part of the maxilla that bears the incisors.

* Median (midline) cleft lip is a rare defect occurring due to failure of fusion of the two medial nasal prominences in the midline.

* Oblique facial cleft is caused by the failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove. The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface in these cases.
