questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following does not stimulate catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperglycemia

Hyperglycemia does not stimulate catecholamine synthesis. Instead, hypoglycemia stimulates catecholamine synthesis.

Catecholamine synthesis is primarily stimulated by various physiological stressors and factors that activate the sympathetic nervous system, such as physical exertion(exercise), changes in posture, or certain external stimuli like smoking.

Other options:

Option B: Smoking stimulates catecholamine release through the activation of the sympathetic nervous system, which increases catecholamines like adrenaline and norepinephrine.

Option C: When a person stands up, it can lead to orthostatic hypotension, which triggers the release of catecholamines to help increase blood pressure and maintain adequate perfusion.

Option D: Exercise stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and increases catecholamine production to support increased heart rate, blood pressure, and metabolic demands.
questions.learning: Hyperglycemia Hyperglycemia does not stimulate catecholamine synthesis. Instead, hypoglycemia stimulates catecholamine synthesis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presented with diarrhea and dehydration. There was no blood in the stools. A stool examination revealed a spoke wheel pattern. Identify the causative organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rota virus

The given clinical scenario along with the electron micrograph image of the stool sample showing a spoke wheel pattern with complaints of non-bloody diarrhea and dehydration in a child is suggestive of rotavirus.

Rotavirus is a nonenveloped, double-stranded (ds) RNA virus. Rotaviruses appear as cartwheel-shaped structures with short spokes radiating from them. It has 11 segments of double-stranded RNA. They exhibit genetic reassortment due to the presence of this segmented RNA.

Rotavirus is the most common identifiable viral cause of diarrhea in children below the age of 5 years and is most frequent between 6-24 months of age. The incubation period is 1-3 days. Most cases are asymptomatic or with mild symptoms like watery diarrhea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and temporary lactose intolerance. Diagnosis can be made by rapid antigen detection of rotavirus in stool specimens.

Rotavirus vaccine is associated with a potential risk of intussusception, especially when the first dose of these vaccines is given to infants aged >12 weeks. Because of this risk, the rotavirus vaccine is not a part of catch-up immunization programs.

Symptoms associated with different levels of dehydration are classified into 3 types no/minimal dehydration, mild to moderate dehydration, and severe dehydration.

Other options:

Option A: Adenovirus contains double-stranded DNA. They have an icosahedral symmetry with structures known as fibers extruding from the vertices. They have a space vehicle-shaped appearance.

Option B: E coli are motile, facultative anaerobes in GIT. It is a gram-negative, flagellated rod. It is the most frequent cause of acute complicated urinary tract infections. It is a lactose fermenter and hence, grows on MacConkey medium to produce pink colonies.

Option C: Norwalk virus is a small, round, non-enveloped virion with a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome with icosahedral symmetry. When viewed under an electron microscope, it has a cup-shaped morphology. Clinical features include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea.
questions.learning: Rota virus — The given clinical scenario along with the electron micrograph image of the stool sample showing a spoke wheel pattern with complaints of non-bloody diarrhea and dehydration in a child is suggestive of rotavirus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Where are the Ito cells in the liver located?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Space of disse

Ito cells/Hepatic stellate cells are located in the space of Disse. They are mesenchymal in origin.

The space of Disse or the perisinusoidal space (or space of Disse) is a location in the liver between hepatocytes and the liver sinusoid.

Significance of Ito cells:

Ito cells are in a dormant state for the majority of the duration. They store the fat-soluble vitamin A in their lipid droplets and are a signiﬁcant source of growth factors involved in liver homeostasis and regeneration.

When there is liver injury, Ito cells get activated. They replace damaged hepatocytes with collagenous scar tissue and secrete intralobular matrix components, including collagen type III (reticular) ﬁbres. This leads to hepatic ﬁbrosis.

Note: A narrow space which separates limiting plate (a sleeve of modified hepatocytes) from the connective tissue of the portal area is known as space of moll.
questions.learning: Space of disse Ito cells/Hepatic stellate cells are located in the space of Disse. The space of Disse or the perisinusoidal space (or space of Disse) is a location in the liver between hepatocytes and the liver sinusoid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient complained of pain in one side of the neck. She is afraid of eating food as it worsens the pain. Ultrasound imaging of the salivary glands is done and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sialolithiasis

The given clinical scenario of pain on one side of the neck that worsens with food and the ultrasound image showing a stone within Wharton's duct is suggestive of sialolithiasis (salivary gland stone).

The submandibular gland has highly viscous secretions and hence forms the most common site for salivary gland stone formation. The two most common sites of stone impaction are near the punctum and the hilum of the gland where the duct bends over the mylohyoid muscle.

The patient usually presents with acute painful swelling in the submandibular region, which is aggravated with food intake. Symptoms resolve 1-2 hours after the meal is completed. On examination, a tender and enlarged submandibular gland can be noted on bimanual examination. Pus may be seen draining from the sublingual papilla or can be expressed on bimanual palpation of the gland.

Most submandibular stones are radio-opaque and visible in radiographs. Stones of size <4 mm are removed via a dormia basket using endoscopic or ultrasound-guided methods under local anesthesia. Stones of size >4 mm are broken first using intracorporeal or extracorporeal lithotripsy and then removed using a dormia basket.

Submandibular gland excision is done only when minimally invasive techniques have failed or there is evidence of a salivary gland tumor.

Nerves at risk during the removal of the submandibular gland:

• the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
• the lingual nerve
• the hypoglossal nerve
questions.learning: Sialolithiasis — The given clinical scenario of pain on one side of the neck that worsens with food and the ultrasound image showing a stone within Wharton's duct is suggestive of sialolithiasis (salivary gland stone).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under IDSP, which diseases are included under sentinel surveillance?
questions.explanation: The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) utilizes different levels of surveillance, including sentinel surveillance for specific chronic or complex conditions. Sentinel surveillance focuses on designated sites to track trends and prevalence in high-risk populations for diseases like HIV and Hepatitis B (HBV). Tuberculosis (Option B), while highly prevalent, is primarily monitored through the specialized NTEP program using routine surveillance. Malaria and Dengue (Option C) are vector-borne diseases that fall under active and passive surveillance protocols to capture outbreaks quickly. Measles and Diphtheria (Option D) are vaccine-preventable diseases monitored through routine reporting to detect immunization gaps. Therefore, HIV and HBV are the primary examples of diseases where sentinel sites are used to gather detailed longitudinal data that might be missed by standard clinical reporting systems
questions.learning: The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) utilizes different levels of surveillance, including sentinel surveillance for specific chronic or complex conditions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of molar pregnancy six months ago now presents with persistent abdominal pain and distension. Her β-hCG levels remain elevated, and a chest X-ray reveals cannon-ball lesions. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of a prior molar pregnancy combined with persistently elevated beta-hCG levels is highly suggestive of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), specifically choriocarcinoma. Choriocarcinoma is a malignant form of gestational trophoblastic disease that characteristically metastasizes early via the hematogenous route. The finding of "cannon-ball foci" on a chest X-ray is pathognomonic for pulmonary metastases from this malignancy. Endometriosis (Option B) typically presents with cyclical pelvic pain and does not involve elevated beta-hCG or lung nodules. Ovarian cysts (Option C) may cause distension but do not produce high hCG or metastatic lung patterns. Asherman’s syndrome (Option D) involves intrauterine adhesions leading to amenorrhea but is unrelated to trophoblastic tissue proliferation or hCG elevation. Therefore, given the specific history of molar gestation and the classic "cannon-ball" pulmonary metastases, the diagnosis is gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Treatment usually involves chemotherapy, often methotrexate or multi-agent regimens, and has a generally good prognosis if identified promptly
questions.learning: The patient’s history of a prior molar pregnancy combined with persistently elevated beta-hCG levels is highly suggestive of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), specifically choriocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient comes with acute chest pain for the past one hour. ECG shows ST segment elevation in the leads II, III and aVF. What is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary angioplasty

The patient given in the scenario with sudden onset chest pain and ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is suggestive of inferior wall MI and the most appropriate intervention is primary angioplasty. This intervention aims to restore blood flow to the affected coronary artery promptly and is associated with improved outcomes in acute STEMI compared to fibrinolytic therapy when performed.

Inferior wall MI mainly occurs due to blockage of the posterior descending branch of the right coronary artery. While anterior wall infarction shows sympathetic nervous system hyperactivity (tachycardia and hypertension), the inferior wall MI shows parasympathetic hyperactivity (bradycardia and hypotension).

Morphine and nitrates are contraindicated in an inferior wall MI due to the risk of further impairing the right ventricular preload.

Beta blockers (Option D) are generally not recommended either, due to the risk of the MI involving the AV node. Beta blockers can block the AV node which can lead to further AV blocks.

Other options:

Option B: Dabigatran is an anticoagulant medication commonly used for the prevention of stroke and systemic embolism in patients with atrial fibrillation and for the treatment and prevention of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. However, it is not indicated as the initial treatment for acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

Option C: Streptokinase is another fibrinolytic agent used for thrombolysis in the treatment of acute myocardial infarction, acute ischemic stroke, and acute pulmonary embolism. It is considered only an alternative reperfusion strategy in acute STEMI when primary angioplasty is unavailable or contraindicated.

The following protocol must be followed in the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome:

* Stabilization of airway, breathing and circulation.

* Administration of O2

* Give aspirin 325 mg and clopidogrel

* History and examination, assess cardiac biomarkers.

* Give up to three sublingual nitroglycerin tablets each 5 min apart till the pain subsides. Add IV nitroglycerin for the persistence of symptoms.

* Treat left heart failure if present with an after-load reducing agent or loop diuretic.

* Give beta blockers if there are no features of heart failure.

* Give morphine for the persistence of anxiety and discomfort related to MI.

* In patients with STEMI - Reperfusion with Percutaneous coronary intervention(PCI) or fibrinolysis (if PCI is unavailable within 120 min). is followed by antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. In patients with NSTEMI - antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is indicated.
questions.learning: Primary angioplasty — The patient given in the scenario with sudden onset chest pain and ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is suggestive of inferior wall MI and the most appropriate intervention is primary angioplasty.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: According to the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy due to contraceptive failure can be done up to what period of gestation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 20 weeks

According to the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy due to contraception failure can be done up to 20 weeks of gestation.

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of an obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state.

Consent:

Only the patient's consent is required for MTP; her partner's consent is not required. Consent of parent/guardian is needed if the age of the patient is <18 years or if the patient is mentally ill.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint be lodged with the police.

Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act with 2021 amendments

Indications:

* Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother

* Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure

* Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest

* Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives

Rules:

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Confidentiality:

A register for recording the details of MTP must be kept for at least 5 years. The patient's name must not be entered, only the reference number is used. Unlawful disclosure of patient's details is punishable with 1-year imprisonment ± fine.
questions.learning: 20 weeks According to the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy due to contraception failure can be done up to 20 weeks of gestation. Upper limit of MTP: * Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What are the characteristic laboratory findings in primary hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland itself is failing to produce adequate hormones. Because of the negative feedback loop, the pituitary gland compensates by increasing its secretion of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH). Therefore, the hallmark laboratory finding is an elevated TSH level coupled with low free T4 (thyroxine) levels. While T3 levels (Option B) also eventually drop, T4 is the primary hormone measured for diagnosis because T3 levels can remain within the normal range for a longer period. Elevated TSH with elevated T4 (Option C) is rare and could indicate TSH-producing pituitary tumors or thyroid hormone resistance. Low TSH with low T4 (Option D) is characteristic of "secondary" or "central" hypothyroidism, where the problem lies in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus. Patients with primary hypothyroidism typically present with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and bradycardia. Standard treatment involves lifelong replacement therapy with levothyroxine
questions.learning: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland itself is failing to produce adequate hormones. Because of the negative feedback loop, the pituitary gland compensates by increasing its secretion of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby assessed 5 minutes after birth, is found to be cyanosed with irregular gasping respiration. Heart rate is 60 beats/min, and a grimace is seen with some flexion of extremities. The APGAR score for this newborn is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

APGAR Score Calculation

| Sign | Finding | Score

| ---- | ------- | -----

| A – Appearance (color) | Cyanosed (blue/pale all over) | 0

| P – Pulse (heart rate) | 60/min (<100/min) | 1

| G – Grimace (reflex irritability) | Minimal response to stimulation | 1

| A – Activity (muscle tone) | Some flexion of extremities | 1

| R – Respiration | Irregular, gasping | 1

Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: If carbamazepine is added to ongoing valproate therapy, what adverse effect is risked?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatotoxicity

If carbamazepine is added to ongoing valproate therapy, it can result in hepatotoxicity.

A combination of valproate and carbamazepine increases hepatotoxicity. Valproic acid may inhibit carbamazepine clearance and increase steady-state carbamazepine blood levels.
questions.learning: Hepatotoxicity If carbamazepine is added to ongoing valproate therapy, it can result in hepatotoxicity. A combination of valproate and carbamazepine increases hepatotoxicity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A sexually active young woman presents with lower abdominal pain, high-grade fever, vomiting, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Her temperature is 103°F, pulse rate 109/min, and abdominal tenderness is noted. On pelvic examination, cervical motion tenderness is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?:
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a sexually active young female with lower abdominal pain, high-grade fever (103°F), tachycardia (109/min), vomiting, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge strongly suggests an acute ascending genital tract infection. The most significant diagnostic finding in this case is cervical motion tenderness, also known as the Chandelier sign, which is a hallmark clinical feature of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID). PID results from the ascending spread of microorganisms from the lower genital tract to the uterus, fallopian tubes, and adjacent pelvic structures. It is commonly polymicrobial, with Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae being frequent causative agents. The presence of systemic signs such as fever and tachycardia indicates active infection and inflammation. Endometriosis (Option B) and adenomyosis (Option C) typically present with chronic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea, not acute fever or purulent discharge. Appendicitis (Option D) may cause fever and abdominal tenderness but does not produce cervical motion tenderness or vaginal discharge. Prompt diagnosis and early antibiotic therapy are crucial in PID to prevent long-term complications such as infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and ectopic pregnancy
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a sexually active young female with lower abdominal pain, high-grade fever (103°F), tachycardia (109/min), vomiting, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge strongly suggests an acute ascending genital tract infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The height of the Jugular Venous Pulse is determined by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right atrial pressure

The Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) is a clinical indicator of right atrial pressure (RAP) because the internal jugular vein is in direct communication with the superior vena cava and right atrium, with no intervening valves.

Key points:

• Height of JVP = Right atrial pressure (Central Venous Pressure).
• Normal JVP is ≤3–4 cm above the sternal angle (approximately 6–8 cm H₂O above the right atrium).
• Raised JVP indicates elevated right atrial pressure, seen in:

• Right heart failure
• Constrictive pericarditis
• Cardiac tamponade
• Tricuspid regurgitation
• Superior vena cava obstruction (venous distension without pulsations)

• JVP reflects right-sided cardiac hemodynamics and does not directly indicate left atrial or left ventricular pressure.
questions.learning: Right atrial pressure — The Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) is a clinical indicator of right atrial pressure (RAP) because the internal jugular vein is in direct communication with the superior vena cava and right atrium, with no intervening valves.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following indications is not a standard therapeutic use of beta-blockers?
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers are not typically the preferred first-line choice for patients with Diabetes Mellitus and hypertension (Option B). This is because beta-blockers can mask the warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (like tachycardia and palpitations) and can impair glucose tolerance by inhibiting insulin release. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred in this demographic for their renoprotective effects. Essential tremors (Option A) are a classic indication for beta-blockers like Propranolol, as they reduce the amplitude of skeletal muscle tremors. Angina pectoris (Option C) is a major use, as they reduce myocardial oxygen demand by slowing the heart rate and contractility. Migraine prophylaxis (Option D) is another standard indication. While beta-blockers can be used in diabetics if necessary (especially cardioselective ones), they are not a "typical" or ideal first-line treatment compared to the other listed therapeutic uses. Therefore, Option B is the correct answer to this "not" question
questions.learning: Beta-blockers are not typically the preferred first-line choice for patients with Diabetes Mellitus and hypertension (Option B). This is because beta-blockers can mask the warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (like tachycardia and palpitations) and can impair…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding the anatomy of the adrenal glands?
options: The right adrenal gland is semi lunar in shape
The left adrenal gland is closely related with tail of pancreas and spleen
The adrenals are yellow on gross appearance
The adrenals are retroperitoneal in location
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The right adrenal gland is semi lunar in shape

Option A is false as the right adrenal gland is pyramidal in shape while the left adrenal gland is semi-lunar/crescent shaped.

The adrenal glands, also called the supra-renal glands, are endocrine glands which are located at the upper pole of each kidney. They are grossly yellow in appearance and are retroperitoneal in location. Both glands are surrounded by areolar tissue and perirenal fascia. The following are the key differences between the right and the left adrenal glands and their relations:

Right Adrenal Gland
Left Adrenal Gland

Shape
Pyramidal or triangular
Semi-lunar or crescenteric

Parts
Apex and base
Upper end and lower end

Superior relation
Bare area of liver
Spleen

Inferior relation
Right kidney
Left kidney and left supra-renal vein

Anterior relation
IVC, bare area of liver
Stomach and tail of pancreas with splenic artery

Posterior relation
Right crus of diaphragm, right kidney
Left crus of diaphragm, left kidney

Medial relation
Coeliac ganglion
Coeliac ganglion

Lateral relation
Liver
Stomach

Each gland is supplied by:

• Superior suprarenal artery - branch of the inferior phrenic artery.
• .Middle suprarenal artery - branch of the abdominal aorta.
• Inferior suprarenal artery - branch of the renal artery.

Each gland has one draining vein.

• The right suprarenal vein drains into the IVC.
• The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A man is brought to the hospital with bizarre behavior and an inability to recall his personal identity or the events surrounding his travel over a distance of 100 km. Collateral history reveals that he experienced a traumatic earthquake a few months earlier. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s inability to recall his identity combined with purposeful travel (100 km) and no memory of the journey constitutes dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue. This condition is directly linked to a recent severe traumatic stressor, such as the earthquake mentioned in the history. Dissociative identity disorder (Option B) involves two or more distinct personality states, which is not described here. Schizophrenia (Option C) is a psychotic disorder characterized by hallucinations and disorganized thought rather than isolated identity loss. Global amnesia (Option D) is typically caused by organic conditions like stroke and does not specifically follow trauma. Since the amnesia is localized to personal information following an identifiable psychological trauma, dissociative amnesia is the most specific diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s inability to recall his identity combined with purposeful travel (100 km) and no memory of the journey constitutes dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby presents with chronic diarrhoea along with a skin rash resembling acrodermatitis. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely nutritional deficiency?
questions.explanation: The combination of chronic diarrhea and a periorificial or acral rash is characteristic of zinc deficiency, often manifesting as the genetic disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica. This condition presents with a hallmark dermatitis around the mouth, hands, feet, and perineum, alongside alopecia and failure to thrive. It typically occurs due to impaired zinc absorption. Selenium deficiency (Option B) is associated with cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) but not acrodermatitis. Niacin deficiency (Option C) causes pellagra, featuring the "3 Ds" (diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia), but the resulting rash is usually photosensitive and occurs in sun-exposed areas rather than periorificial sites. Magnesium deficiency (Option D) causes neuromuscular issues like tetany and seizures rather than this specific rash pattern. Zinc plays a crucial role in intestinal integrity and immune function, so its deficiency leads to both the dermatological and gastrointestinal symptoms described
questions.learning: The combination of chronic diarrhea and a periorificial or acral rash is characteristic of zinc deficiency, often manifesting as the genetic disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common presenting symptom in patients with Multiple Sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sensory Disturbances

Multiple sclerosis most commonly presents initially with sensory disturbances such as numbness, paresthesia, or sensory loss.

These symptoms result from demyelination of sensory pathways in the CNS.

Motor deficits, ataxia, and cranial nerve involvement usually occur later in the disease course.

Thus, sensory symptoms are the earliest and most common presenting feature.

Classic Early Presentation Triad

1.     Sensory symptoms (most common)

2.     Optic neuritis (painful vision loss)

3.     Motor weakness

Initial Symptoms of Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
questions.learning: Sensory Disturbances Multiple sclerosis most commonly presents initially with sensory disturbances such as numbness, paresthesia, or sensory loss. These symptoms result from demyelination of sensory pathways in the CNS.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child immediately cries after breastfeeding, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Which enzyme deficiency might be responsible?
questions.explanation: Symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, and distress immediately following the ingestion of milk (including breast milk) in an infant or young child point toward Classic Galactosemia. Breast milk contains lactose, which is broken down into glucose and galactose. A deficiency in Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) leads to the toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate, causing immediate gastrointestinal distress and long-term organ damage. Aldolase B deficiency (Option A) causes Hereditary Fructose Intolerance, where symptoms start only after introducing fruits or juices, not with breastfeeding. Phenylalanine Hydroxylase deficiency (Option B) is PKU, which does not cause acute GI symptoms after feeding. Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Option D) is Gaucher's disease, which presents with hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain, not acute feeding intolerance. Because milk is the primary source of the offending sugar in this age group, GALT deficiency is the most likely enzymatic cause for these feeding-related symptoms
questions.learning: Symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, and distress immediately following the ingestion of milk (including breast milk) in an infant or young child point toward Classic Galactosemia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Inoculation loops are commonly sterilized by which method?
options: Heat till it become red hot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Heat till it become red hot

Inoculating loops are sterilized by direct flaming until they become red hot.

• Red heat ensures complete destruction of all microorganisms, including spores
• This is a method of dry heat sterilization
• The loop must be allowed to cool before touching the culture to avoid killing organisms

Why not others:

• Autoclaving is used for bulk instruments, not for immediate sterilization during procedures
• Microwave is not a standard sterilization method in microbiology labs
• Passing over flame a few times without achieving red heat is inadequate

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The Trapezoid of Disaster includes: (NEET PG 2015)
options: Triangle of death and circle of death
Triangle of doom and circle of death
Triangle of doom medially and triangle of pain laterally
Triangle of doom laterally and triangle of pain medially
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triangle of doom medially and triangle of pain laterally

During laparoscopic hernia repair, the surgeon must navigate important anatomical landmarks in the inguinal region. The "Trapezoid of Disaster" contains two important triangles that require careful attention during mesh placement. The Triangle of Doom is bounded medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the testicular vessels, containing the external iliac vessels and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve. The Triangle of Pain is located lateral to this, bounded medially by testicular vessels and laterally by the iliopubic tract, containing the femoral nerve, anterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, and lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh.
questions.learning: Triangle of doom medially and triangle of pain laterally During laparoscopic hernia repair, the surgeon must navigate important anatomical landmarks in the inguinal region.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is not included in the TNM stage T4b of breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Skin erythema involving > 1/3rd surface

T4b breast cancer includes:

• Peau d’orange (skin edema)
• Ulceration of skin
• Ipsilateral satellite skin nodules

These are features of direct skin involvement by breast carcinoma.

“Skin erythema involving >1/3 of breast surface” is a criterion for: Inflammatory breast cancer which is classified as T4d, not T4b.

| Stage | Feature

| ----- | -------

| T1 | Tumor < 2 cm

| T2 | Tumor 2 – 5 cm

| T3 | Tumor > 5 cm

| T4a | Chest wall invasion (ribs, intercostal muscles, serratus anterior; pectoralis major not included)

| T4b | Skin involvement – ulceration, satellite nodules, peau d’orange (< 1/3 of breast skin)

| T4c | Combination of T4a + T4b

| T4d | Inflammatory breast cancer – erythema/peau d’orange > 1/3 of breast skin

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the underlying embryological defect responsible for bicornuate uterus?
options: Failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts
Failure of descent of the Müllerian ducts
Failure of fusion of the Wolffian ducts
Failure of resorption of the Müllerian septum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts

A bicornuate uterus results from incomplete fusion of the two Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts, producing a uterus with two uterine horns and a deep fundal cleft (>1 cm).

| Embryological defect | Uterine anomaly

| -------------------- | ---------------

| Failure of Müllerian duct fusion | Bicornuate uterus, uterus didelphys

| Failure of resorption of Müllerian septum | Septate uterus (most common Müllerian anomaly)

| Failure of development of one Müllerian duct | Unicornuate uterus

| Complete agenesis of Müllerian ducts | Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the sign shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Popeye sign

The sign shown in the above image is the popeye sign, which occurs due to the rupture of the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii.

On flexing the elbow, the characteristic deformity appears due to the bulging of the muscle belly caused by the contraction of the unrestrained muscles.

Option B: Hill-Sachs sign refers to a defect in the postero-lateral surface of the humeral head due to repeated impact against anterior glenoid rim. It is a common complication of Anterior shoulder dislocation.

Option C: Griesinger sign refers to oedema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein. It is a complication of acute mastoiditis.

Option D: Rising sun sign , also known as Schwartze sign, is the otoscopic sign of active otospongiosis characterised by reddish discolouration of the cochlear promontory.
questions.learning: Popeye sign — The sign shown in the above image is the popeye sign, which occurs due to the rupture of the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The type of knot seen in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reef knot

The given image shows the suture material exiting the knot is on the same side as the entry i.e no cross-over is seen. This is seen in a reef knot.

A knot is a fastening made of threads intertwined together or on themselves. Each knot consists of- 2 half-hitches placed in sequential throws. Squaring refers to tightening the knot/half-hitch in a manner that the threads lay flat due to the alternating direction of half-hitches in adjacent layers.

Types of knots:

1. Granny knot: half-hitch over a half-hitch in the same direction. It has better-holding power than half-hitch
2. Reef knot: half-hitch followed by a second half-hitch after squaring.
3. Triple throw knot: Reef knot with another half-hitch knot for added security. Knots made with prolene sutures require 6-8 throws to prevent slippage.
4. Surgeon’s knot: Modification of the reef knot with two half-hitches in the first layer.
5. Slip knot: Modification of either granny/reef knot formed when one end of the thread is kept taut while tightening the knot.
questions.learning: Reef knot — The given image shows the suture material exiting the knot is on the same side as the entry i.e no cross-over is seen. A knot is a fastening made of threads intertwined together or on themselves.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs act on sodium channels and potentiate slow sodium inactivation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lacosamide

Lacosamide is a drug acting on sodium channel and potentiating slow sodium inactivation.

Lacosamide acts by blocking the voltage-gated sodium channels. It is used as adjunctive therapy for focal-onset seizures in patients older than 17 years.

It is the first anti-seizure medication that limits persistent repetitive firing, the neuronal firing pattern typical of focal seizures, and prolongs the gradual inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels. Additionally, lacosamide binds to the phosphoprotein collapsing response mediator protein-2 (CRMP-2), which is mostly expressed in the nervous system and has a role in controlling axonal outgrowth and neuronal differentiation.

The role of CRMP-2 binding in seizure control is unknown.

Therapeutic Uses:

• It is used for both monotherapy and add-on therapy for focal-onset seizures in patients 17 years and older.
• It is mostly beneficial in hospitalized patients because it is available in an intravenous formulation, has minimal hepatic metabolism, and has no adverse respiratory effects.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malignancy

Cancer is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients, whereas hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of hypercalcemia detected incidentally in outpatients. The causes of hypercalcemia in cancer :

• Cancers affecting bone like multiple myeloma, leukemia, bony metastasis - cause the bone to break down which releases excess calcium into the blood
• Pseudohyperparathyroidism - tumours producing parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) cause the bone to release calcium into the blood. The most common carcinoma associated is squamous cell carcinoma of lung.
• Cancers affecting kidneys - failure to remove excess calcium from the blood
• Dehydration caused by nausea and vomiting - difficult for the kidneys to remove calcium from the blood properly
• Lack of physical activity - causes bone breakdown, releasing calcium into the blood
questions.learning: Malignancy Cancer is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients, whereas hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of hypercalcemia detected incidentally in outpatients.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient, who is 2 months pregnant, reports to a hospital with complaints of increased vaginal bleeding and pain in lower abdomen. Internal examination reveals dilated internal os of cervix and products of conception are felt through it. What is her likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inevitable abortion

Inevitable abortion is defined as vaginal bleeding with cramp-like abdominal pain, cervical dilatation, and no expulsion of products of conception (POC). Once the internal os is dilated, continuation of pregnancy is no longer possible, and abortion is considered inevitable.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Threatened abortion: Vaginal bleeding occurs, but the cervical os remains closed, and the pregnancy may continue.
• C. Septic abortion: Characterized by fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, and signs of infection, which are absent here.
• D. Incomplete abortion: Occurs after partial expulsion of products of conception, with retained tissue in the uterus. In this case, the products are felt through the dilated cervix but have not yet been expelled.

| Type of Abortion | Bleeding | Cervical Os | Products of Conception (POC)

| ---------------- | -------- | ----------- | ----------------------------

| Threatened | Mild | Closed | Retained, fetus viable

| Inevitable | Moderate/Heavy | Open | Not expelled, felt through os

| Incomplete | Heavy | Open | Partially expelled, retained POC

| Complete | Minimal after expulsion | Closed | All POC expelled

| Missed | Minimal/Absent | Closed | Dead fetus retained

| Septic | Variable | Usually open | Infected retained POC
questions.learning: Inevitable abortion Inevitable abortion is defined as vaginal bleeding with cramp-like abdominal pain, cervical dilatation, and no expulsion of products of conception (POC).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 36-year-old man presents with dull aching epigastric pain. He gives a history of acute abdominal pain following a binge of alcohol 5 weeks back which was managed conservatively. On examination, he appears icteric and a firm mass was palpable in the epigastrium. His CT scan is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancreatic pseudocyst

The given clinical scenario with a history of acute pancreatitis, epigastric mass, and the CT image showing a cyst is suggestive of pancreatic pseudocyst. The capsule of the cyst is composed of collagen and granulation tissue, and it is not lined by epithelium. Hence, it is called a pseudocyst.

Pseudocysts are post-inflammatory cysts that arise following an attack of mild acute pancreatitis. Formation of a pseudocyst requires 4 weeks or more from the onset of acute pancreatitis. They are also the most common complication of chronic pancreatitis.

Pseudocysts are usually solitary and most commonly seen in the lesser omental sac. The most common artery involved is the splenic artery.

Complications of pancreatic pseudocyst include:

* Abscess

* Systemic sepsis

* GI bleeding

* Fistula formation

* Peritonitis

* Obstructive jaundice

* Bowel obstruction

* Hemorrhage into the cyst

* Hemoperitoneum

Pancreatic pseudocysts can be distinguished from cystic neoplasms by having high amylase levels and absence of mucin and low serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels.
questions.learning: Pancreatic pseudocyst — The given clinical scenario with a history of acute pancreatitis, epigastric mass, and the CT image showing a cyst is suggestive of pancreatic pseudocyst.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Marriage and mortality belongs under?
questions.explanation: Demography is the scientific study of human populations. The fundamental events that continuously change the size, structure, and distribution of a population are known as demographic processes. The five key processes are fertility (births), mortality (deaths), marriage, migration, and social mobility. Demographic dividend (Option B), bonus (Option C), and window (Option D) are related terms that describe the economic growth potential that results from shifts in a population's age structure, specifically when the working-age population is larger than the dependent population. However, the basic events of life and death themselves are classified as processes. Understanding these processes is vital for government planning, resource allocation, and predicting future public health needs. Mortality and marriage statistics are core components of a nation's vital registration system, which provides the raw data for all other demographic calculations
questions.learning: Demography is the scientific study of human populations. The fundamental events that continuously change the size, structure, and distribution of a population are known as demographic processes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Plasma sterilization makes use of ____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydrogen peroxide

A variety of hydrogen peroxide gas–based processes that use plasma as part of the sterilization process are known as "plasma sterilization."

The mechanisms of antimicrobial action in these processes are primarily due to hydrogen peroxide gas (or condensed gas) and not plasma, although the plasma generation phase of these processes is known to assist in the breakdown of residual peroxide in the chamber load.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In cystic fibrosis, which of the following structure is affected in pancreas?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

The part labeled ‘B’ in the image is the exocrine pancreas which is affected in cystic fibrosis.

Features of cystic fibrosis in the pancreas:

• Accumulation of mucus in the ducts leads to dilation of exocrine glands.
• Complete blockage of ducts with mucus leads to atrophy of the exocrine pancreas and progressive fibrosis
• Due to atrophy, there will be loss of exocrine secretions, which in turn leads to impaired absorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins
• Associated loss of vitamin A leads to squamous metaplasia of the pancreatic duct lining epithelium

Other options:

A- Endocrine pancreas

C- Pancreatic ducts

D- Blood vessels

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is given to prevent neural tube defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B9

Folic acid (Vitamin B9) is given to prevent the incidence of neural tube defects.

Folic acid deficiency is implicated in neural tube defects like spina bifida, encephalocele, and anencephaly.

Supplementation of folic acid, in doses of 400 μg/day, prior to conception has been shown to cause a significant reduction in the incidence of spina bifida and other neural tube defects.

Reduced activity of the enzyme 5,10-methylene-THF reductase (MTHFR) caused by a common C677T polymorphism in the MTHFR gene is one of the causes of neural tube defects in folate deficiency.

questions.text: Which statement regarding lamotrigine is not true?
options: Clearance reduced in severe hepatic impairment
Dizziness and ataxia are adverse effects

A. Primarily metabolized by glucuronidation: True. Lamotrigine is mainly metabolized via: Hepatic glucuronidation

B. Clearance reduced in severe hepatic impairment: True. Severe liver disease:

• Reduces clearance
• Requires dose adjustment

D. Dizziness and ataxia are adverse effects: True. Common adverse effects:

• Dizziness

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following statement regarding ranula are true except
options: Bluish, translucent, cystic swelling in the floor of mouth
Marsupialisation or excision is the treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arises from submandibular salivary gland

The incorrect statement regarding ranula is it arises from the submandibular salivary gland. It is a mucous extravasation cyst occurring as a result of obstruction of one of the sublingual salivary glands in the floor of the mouth.

Features :

* Translucent, bluish, soft, cystic fluctuant swelling present below the tongue pushing it upwards and medially thus interfering with speech, mastication, respiration, and swallowing.

* Plunging ranula presents as asymptomatic, enlarging neck mass.

Management:

* Marsupialisation – unroofing the cyst and tacking the edges of the cyst to adjacent tissues.

* Sclerosing agents like bleomycin.

* Sublingual gland excision – recurrence rate is very low.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What clinical test is depicted in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cottle’s test

The image representing a clinical test where the cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly is Cottle’s test.

This test is used to assess the patency of the nasal valve in patients with a deviated nasal septum. If the nasal airway improves on the test side, the test is positive and indicates an abnormality of the vestibular component of the nasal valve on that side.

Option A: Epley’s maneuver is used in the treatment of BPPV.

Option B: Heimlich manoeuvre is used in the treatment of accidental inhalation of foreign body.

Procedure: Stand behind the person and place your arms around his lower chest and give four abdominal thrusts. The residual air in the lungs can dislodge the foreign body providing some airway.

Option D: Trotter’s method is used in the treatment of epistaxis. In Trotter’s method, the patient is made to sit, leaning a little forward over a basin to spit any blood. He should pinch the nose firmly for 5 to 10 mins and breathe quietly from the mouth.
questions.learning: Cottle’s test — The image representing a clinical test where the cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly is Cottle’s test. This test is used to assess the patency of the nasal valve in patients with a deviated nasal septum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is admitted with high fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. The child was recently treated for acute otitis media. Lumbar puncture shows a predominance of polymorphs, protein level is raised, sugars reduced and chlorides diminished. Otoscopic examination reveals bulging of the tympanic membrane. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention to manage the underlying cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myringotomy

In a child with acute bacterial meningitis secondary to acute otitis media, the most important immediate step is drainage of the middle ear infection. Myringotomy is the treatment of choice because it:

• Provides immediate drainage of infected middle ear pus
• Reduces bacterial load and intracranial spread
• Allows culture of middle ear pus for targeted antibiotics
• Relieves pressure from bulging tympanic membrane

Radical/modified radical mastoidectomy → indicated only if mastoiditis, abscess, or complications persist despite myringotomy + antibiotics
questions.learning: Myringotomy — In a child with acute bacterial meningitis secondary to acute otitis media, the most important immediate step is drainage of the middle ear infection.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The child in the picture has large corneas, photophobia, and lacrimation. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital glaucoma

The given clinical scenario of an infant with large corneas, lacrimation and photophobia supported with the image is suggestive of congenital glaucoma.

Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) also known as developmental glaucoma refers to abnormally high intraocular pressure(IOP) which results from the developmental anomaly of the angle of the anterior chamber.

It can be classified as:

• True congenital or newborn glaucoma in which IOP is elevated during intrauterine life and the baby is born with ocular enlargement.
• Infantile glaucoma: which manifests prior to age 3 years.
• Juvenile glaucoma: IOP rises between 3 and 16 years of age.

Clinical findings include:

• Blepharospasm
• Buphthalmos: Large eyeball due to stretching of the globe from elevated IOP prior to the age of 3 years.
• Corneal enlargement:
• Corneal haze is due to corneal edema.
• Blue sclera - due to the shining of the underlying uveal tissue through the thinned-out sclera
• Haab striae are healed breaks in Descemet's membrane

Treatment:

• Goniotomy - when the angle of the anterior chamber is visible through the clear cornea.
• Trabeculectomy when the corneal clouding prevents visualization of the angle.
• Filtration procedures such as Trabeculectomy or combined trabeculectomy with trabeculectomy if the above procedures fail.
• Glaucoma drainage devices in unresponsive cases.

Other options:

Option A: Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood that is seen between 1-2 years.

Findings of Retinoblastoma include:

• Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex)- the most common manifestation
• Strabismus
• Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma
• An endophytic tumor grows into the vitreous as a white mass that may ‘seed’ into the gel. If calcification is present it gives a "cottage cheese appearance". An exophytic tumor grows outwards and causes overlying exudative retinal detachment.

The image below shows the leucocoria of the left eye.

Option C: Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) is an inherited corneal dystrophy that manifests since birth with endothelial degeneration. It appears as diffuse bilateral corneal edema in the absence of elevated IOP. The clinical features of the disease include corneal clouding, visual impairment, and nystagmus.

Option D: Megalocornea is a bilateral non-progressive X-linked condition that most commonly affects males. In this condition, the horizontal corneal diameter is ≥12mm(<2 years) and is ≥13 mm(>2 years). It is characterized by a clear cornea, normal corneal thickness, and no breaks in the descemet's membrane. Systemic associations of Megalocornea include Marfan's syndrome, Apert syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos, and Down syndrome.
questions.learning: Congenital glaucoma — The given clinical scenario of an infant with large corneas, lacrimation and photophobia supported with the image is suggestive of congenital glaucoma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The slogan coined by WHO 'Do it Right' in the first aid of a snake bite includes all of the following except?
options: Tell sequence of events in detail after the bite
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Incisions

Incisions are not a part of the management of a snake bite.

The first aid following a snake bite consists of the mnemonic: carry no right.

Carry: The victim is not allowed to walk, even for a short distance. Walking generates muscle-pumping activity which disperses the venom into the systemic circulation.

No: No tourniquet, no electrotherapy, no cutting, no pressure immobilization, no suction to the bite site

R: Reassure the patient since 70% of the bites are from non-venomous species.

I: Immobilize in the same way as a fractured limb. A splint can be applied to the bitten extremity to limit the movement and assist with positioning. The extremity should be maintained in a neutral position at approximately heart level.

GH: Get to a hospital immediately. The most important step is to rapidly transport the patient to a medical facility equipped to provide supportive management.

T: Tell the doctor of any systemic symptoms which may have appeared on the way to the hospital.

Note that elapid envenomations that are primarily neurotoxic and have no significant effects on local tissue may be managed by pressure immobilization. In this technique, the entire limb is immediately wrapped with a bandage and then immobilized. This technique restricts lymphatic drainage and has been shown to delay the absorption of venom into the systemic circulation. However, the offending snake should have been reliably identified as neurotoxic and the rescuer should be trained in applying this pressure bandage.
questions.learning: Incisions Incisions are not a part of the management of a snake bite. The first aid following a snake bite consists of the mnemonic: carry no right.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent profuse epistaxis and nasal obstruction. On examination, a reddish mass is seen in the nasopharynx. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Contrast-enhanced CT

The investigation of choice for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) is Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) because it best demonstrates bony anatomy and tumor extent.

• CECT findings:

• Intense contrast enhancement (high vascularity)
• Bony remodeling/destruction
• Holman–Miller sign (anterior bowing of posterior wall of maxillary sinus)

Why not other options:

• MRI: Better for soft tissue and intracranial extension, but not first-line
• DNE (Diagnostic nasal endoscopy): Helps visualize mass, but not definitive imaging
• Biopsy: Contraindicated due to risk of severe hemorrhage (highly vascular tumor)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following eye signs can be appreciated in the image?
questions.explanation: The image shows a dark brown–black horizontal band on the exposed sclera, with surrounding dryness. This is characteristic of tache noire, a postmortem change seen in eyes that remain partially open after death. It occurs due to drying of the sclera, leading to discoloration, typically appearing as two triangular patches or a horizontal band. Key feature: 1. Drying and pigmentation of exposed sclera 2. Seen in postmortem eyes, especially when eyelids are not fully closed Why other options are incorrect: (B) Kevorkian sign: Refers to retinal vessel segmentation (trucking), not visible externally (C) Corneal changes: Include opacity or clouding, not localized dark patches (D) Vitreous humour changes: Internal eye changes, not visible on external inspection The visible dark scleral band clearly indicates tache noire, a classic postmortem ocular sign

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Arrange the following bands in the sarcomere from the periphery to the center.

1. Z line
2. M line
3. A band
4. H zone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,3,4,2

The correct sequence of bands in the sarcomere from the periphery to the centre is: Z line→ A band→ H zone→ M line.

The sarcomere is the contractile unit of the skeletal muscle fibre.

• Z line provides attachment to actin filaments. The area between two adjacent Z lines is called the sarcomere. It is composed of thick and thin filaments:

• Thick filament: Myosin
• Thin filaments: Actin, tropomyosin and troponin

• I band is isotropic to light. It contains only actin filaments.
• A band is anisotropic to light. It contains myosin plus overlapped actin.
• H bands are the lighter areas in the centre of the A band. These are the areas where the the thick filaments do not overlap the thin filaments, when the muscle is relaxed.
• M line is present in the centre of H band. There are slender cross-connections that hold the thick filaments in proper array.
questions.learning: 1,3,4,2 The correct sequence of bands in the sarcomere from the periphery to the centre is: Z line→ A band→ H zone→ M line. The sarcomere is the contractile unit of the skeletal muscle fibre. • Z line provides attachment to actin filaments.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about viscoelastic substances?
options: Causes mechanical injury to corneal endothelium
Prevents the Anterior Chamber from collapsing during crucial steps like capsulorhexis and IOL placement
It is inert and can be left behind after surgery
Silicone oil, perfluoropropane, and SF6 are the most commonly used substances
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prevents the Anterior Chamber from collapsing during crucial steps like capsulorhexis and IOL placement

Viscoelastic substances prevent the anterior chamber from collapsing during crucial steps like capsulorhexis and IOL (Intra-ocular lens) placement.

Viscoelastic substances are commonly used in ocular surgery, particularly in cataract surgery, to maintain the anterior chamber (AC), protect the corneal endothelium, and facilitate surgical procedures. They prevent the collapse of the AC during crucial steps such as capsulorrhexis and IOL (intraocular lens) placement by providing a cushioning effect.

Other options

Option A:  Viscoelastic substances are typically used to protect the corneal endothelium, not to cause any mechanical injury.

Option C:  While some viscoelastics are inert, not all can be safely left behind. Some types of viscoelastic substances (especially those that are not fully biodegradable) should be removed from the eye after surgery to prevent complications.

Option D: Sodium hyaluronate and hydroxypropyl methylcellulose are the most commonly used viscoelastic substances, compared to silicone oil, perfluoropropane, and SF6.  Silicone oil, perfluoropropane, and SF6 are the substances used for vitreoretinal surgery (such as tamponade agents for retinal detachment), not for routine cataract surgery. Viscoelastic used in cataract surgery are typically substances like sodium hyaluronate and hydroxypropyl methylcellulose.
questions.learning: Prevents the Anterior Chamber from collapsing during crucial steps like capsulorhexis and IOL placement Viscoelastic substances prevent the anterior chamber from collapsing during crucial steps like capsulorhexis and IOL (Intra-ocular lens) placement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following findings is likely to be seen in this patient?
options: Decreased posterior tibial & dorsalis pedis pulsations
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Loss of sensation over foot

In the given image, the lesion present over the plantar surface of the foot is likely to be a neuropathic ulcer. Neuropathic ulcers can lead to loss of sensation over the foot.

A neuropathic ulcer is one that occurs as a result of peripheral neuropathy. In peripheral neuropathy, lack of sensation over the pressure points leads to cumulative microtrauma, minor wounds, or cuts that go unnoticed eventually developing into ulcers. They are painless ulcers that are punched out with regular margins. They are often located on the plantar surface of the foot. Ulcer margins show the presence of calluses.

Other options:

Option A: Decreased posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulsations are usually seen in peripheral arterial disease, which causes arterial ulcers that are usually found on the dorsal surface of the foot.

Option C: Positive Brodie-Trendelenburg test is seen in varicose veins. This condition leads to venous ulcers which are usually seen on the medial malleolus of the foot.

Option D: Pain on compression of calf is a sign of deep venous thrombosis.
questions.learning: Loss of sensation over foot — In the given image, the lesion present over the plantar surface of the foot is likely to be a neuropathic ulcer. Neuropathic ulcers can lead to loss of sensation over the foot.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with white, dandruff-like deposits on the anterior surface of the lens, observed during a slit-lamp examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome

Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is characterized by deposition of whitish, dandruff-like fibrillar material on the anterior lens capsule, typically seen in elderly patients.

Classic slit-lamp finding: Three-zone pattern on lens:

• Central disc
• Clear intermediate zone
• Associated with secondary open-angle glaucoma (pseudoexfoliative glaucoma)
• Causes zonular weakness → risk of lens subluxation and complications during cataract surgery

Why not others:

• Iris cyst: Localized cystic lesion, not diffuse deposits
• Persistent pupillary membrane: Congenital strands across pupil
• Pigment dispersion syndrome: Pigment deposition (not white flakes), seen in younger patients
questions.learning: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is characterized by deposition of whitish, dandruff-like fibrillar material on the anterior lens capsule, typically seen in elderly patients.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Droplet precaution and isolation is to be done for all of the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Localized varicella zoster

Droplet precaution and isolation is not done for localized varicella zoster, as it is only transmitted through direct contact.

Varicella-zoster localized in the patient with an intact immune system with a lesion that can be contained/covered do not require droplet precaution. Disseminated varicella in any patient requires airborne and contact precautions.

Diphtheria, pertussis, and mycoplasma are transmitted by droplets and hence require droplet precaution and isolation.

Although patients are not contagious starting 48 hours after antibiotic therapy, droplet precautions are typically maintained until the completion of the antibiotic course and are culture-negative on two cultures taken 24 hours apart. Droplet precautions include the use of masks, gowns, gloves and protective eye gear when providing direct patient care.
questions.learning: Localized varicella zoster Droplet precaution and isolation is not done for localized varicella zoster, as it is only transmitted through direct contact.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In psychiatry, it is important to differentiate between different types of perceptual disturbances, particularly true hallucinations and pseudohallucinations. Pseudohallucinations have distinct defining features. Which of the following statements does NOT correctly describe a characteristic of pseudohallucinations?
options: They are perceived in the outer objective space
They occur with an external stimulus
questions.explanation: In descriptive psychopathology, specifically Karl Jaspers' criteria, the defining difference between a true hallucination and a pseudohallucination is the location of the perception. True hallucinations are perceived in the outer objective space, whereas pseudohallucinations are characteristically perceived in internal subjective space (e.g., "voices in the head"). Therefore, Statement B is not accurate. Pseudohallucinations are also described as lacking the "concrete reality" or vividness (Option A) of true perceptions. Importantly, they are not voluntarily produced (Option C) and do not require an external stimulus (Option D); perceptions occurring with a stimulus are called illusions. Distinguishing these is vital; true hallucinations suggest a psychotic process (like schizophrenia), while pseudohallucinations may be seen in personality disorders or dissociative states. Recognizing that pseudohallucinations lack the quality of "external reality" helps clinicians accurately categorize a patient's perceptual disturbances and guide subsequent treatment
questions.learning: In descriptive psychopathology, specifically Karl Jaspers' criteria, the defining difference between a true hallucination and a pseudohallucination is the location of the perception.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the marked structure of the cochlear implant shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ground electrode

The marked structure in the radiology image of the cochlear implant is the ground electrode.

A cochlear implant is a medical device that uses electricity to stimulate the spiral ganglion cells of the auditory nerve to restore sensorineural hearing loss. It can be used in a patient with bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss.

It converts sound to an electrical signal (transduction) and delivers this to the hearing nerve, which bypasses the damaged hearing apparatus. It cannot be used in patients with cochlear aplasia or without the VIIIth cranial nerve.

Cochlear implant:

• An electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from a hearing aid.
• Principle- surgery to place the electrode array within the scala tympani of the cochlea.
• Indication- bilateral severe to profound deafness
• Prerequisites- intact 8th nerve and higher auditory pathway
• Surgical approach- facial recess (posterior tympanotomy) approach
• The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani. (Note: In the auditory brainstem implant, the site of the implant is the lateral recess of the 4th ventricle.)

The receiver-stimulator implanted during surgery (under the skin) and the electrode array (implanted in the scala tympani of the cochlea) are part of the internal component of the cochlear implant. The microphone, speech processor and transmitter are part of the external component of the cochlear implant, which remains outside the body.

Cochlear implants replace the non-functional transducer system of hair cells of the cochlea and convert the sound signal to electrical impulses, which directly stimulate the fibres of cranial nerve VIII.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A tall male presents with absent pubic and axillary hair, poorly developed genitalia, and markedly elevated levels of LH and FSH. Karyotype analysis reveals an XXY chromosomal pattern. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The 47,XXY karyotype is pathognomonic for Klinefelter's syndrome, the most common sex chromosome disorder in males. The extra X chromosome interferes with testicular development, leading to primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). This explains the elevated LH and FSH levels (lack of negative feedback) and the underdeveloped genitalia with poor secondary sexual characteristics. Affected individuals are characteristically tall with long limbs. Vanishing testis syndrome (Option A) involves the prenatal loss of testes in a 46,XY male. Noonan syndrome (Option C) is an autosomal dominant condition often called "male Turner syndrome," typically associated with short stature and heart defects. Adrenal hyperplasia (Option D) usually presents with virilization or salt-wasting, not a tall stature with underdeveloped male features. Testosterone replacement therapy is used to manage symptoms and improve bone density, although infertility is usually permanent
questions.learning: The 47,XXY karyotype is pathognomonic for Klinefelter's syndrome, the most common sex chromosome disorder in males. The extra X chromosome interferes with testicular development, leading to primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism).

questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to blood in his stool, which the parents noticed when changing his diaper. The infant has had no previous bleeding and has been eating and drinking normally. He has a history of recurrent otitis media, frequent herpes labialis, and 2 episodes of pneumonia. On examination, the patient is well developed, well nourished, and has a fair complexion. He has eczema on his cheeks, trunk, and extremities. Scattered petechiae are also visible on his lower extremities. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 24,000/mm³ and a leukocyte count of 9,000/mm³. Peripheral smear confirms the low platelet count and that the platelets are small. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following processes is most likely affected by this patient's gene mutation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cytoskeleton regulation

This child has features of Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked immunodeficiency characterized by the triad:

• Eczema
• Recurrent infections
• Thrombocytopenia with small platelets

The disease is caused by mutation in the WAS gene, which encodes the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP).

• WASP regulates actin cytoskeleton remodelling in hematopoietic cells.
• Defective cytoskeleton dynamics impair immune cell signalling, migration, and platelet formation, leading to immunodeficiency and microthrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following can be done to remove confounders except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blinding

Blinding does not eliminate confounding factors. Blinding is done to eliminate the bias (such as subject bias, observer bias, or investigator bias).

A confounding factor is defined as the one associated with both exposure and disease and is distributed unequally in study and control groups.

• For example, a prospective study is being conducted to know the effect of alcohol on the development of lung cancer.
• However, individuals who drink alcohol are most likely to smoke. So, smoking is associated with the exposure. Also, smoking is an independent causative factor for lung cancer. Thus, smoking is a confounding factor.
• In the above example, if the study is conducted without eliminating the confounding factor, then the result may falsely suggest that alcohol is a causative factor for lung cancer.

Techniques to eliminate confounding factors include

• Randomization
• Matching
• Stratified randomization
• Restriction

Randomization is the random allocation of the participants in experimental studies (Ex.randomized control trial) into the study group and control group.

Matching, which is usually done in analytical studies (for example, case–control and cohort studies), is the process where the participants in two groups are matched based on factors such as age, gender, race, smoking status, etc. to eliminate the potential confounders.

Stratified randomization, which is also known as prestratification or blocking, is the process that combines both randomization and matching techniques. In this method, the participants are first grouped into subgroups which internally match with potential confounding factors such as age, race, gender, etc. An equal number of participants form each subgroup are then allocated to the study and control groups.

Restriction: This method restricts the study to only those participants with particular characteristics. For example, a study can be restricted to participants of only one gender, race, age group, geographical area, disease severity, etc., thus eliminating the potential confounders.
questions.learning: Blinding Blinding does not eliminate confounding factors. Blinding is done to eliminate the bias (such as subject bias, observer bias, or investigator bias).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman, 10 years post-mastectomy, reports gradual swelling and heaviness in her right upper limb without pain. Examination reveals bluish skin nodules without signs of infection. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: A patient who develops Lymphangiosarcoma in the setting of chronic, long-standing lymphedema following a radical mastectomy is suffering from Stewart-Treves Syndrome. This is a rare but highly malignant vascular tumor. It characteristically presents approximately 10 years after the initial surgery as a gradual worsening of the swelling and the appearance of bluish-red nodules or plaques on the skin of the lymphedematous arm. Thoracic outlet syndrome (Option B) and venous insufficiency (Option C) can cause swelling but do not explain the localized bluish skin nodules in a post-mastectomy patient. Recurrent breast cancer (Option D) usually presents as a discrete mass or skin thickening (peau d'orange) rather than widespread vascular nodules. Stewart-Treves syndrome has an extremely poor prognosis due to early metastasis. The definitive treatment usually involves radical amputation of the limb, although results are often suboptimal. This condition highlights the importance of long-term monitoring for chronic lymphedema
questions.learning: A patient who develops Lymphangiosarcoma in the setting of chronic, long-standing lymphedema following a radical mastectomy is suffering from Stewart-Treves Syndrome.

questions.text: Which of the following is a tool used in gene editing:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CRISPR

Guide RNAs called CRISPRs help to selectively alter or correct DNA sequences.

CRISPR is Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats

• CRISPR-Cas9 is a genome editing tool and this system enables select bacteria to respond to and eliminate invading genetic material.
• CRISPRs are transcribed into an RNA sequence that directs the Cas9 to a sequence leading to its cleavage.
• Gene editing uses an artificial guide RNA that binds Cas9 and is complementary to a DNA sequence of interest and Cas9 induces the break of double-stranded DNA.

One of the first successful diseases used on experimental basis is Sickle Cell Anemia.

Other gene editing tools are:

• Zinc-finger nucleases (ZNFs)
• Transcription-Activator Like Effector Nucleases (TALEN)
• Meganucleases

Pearl PF0595: The Family as a Social Organization

* Types of families:

* A nuclear family or elementary family consists of only the married couple and their offspring while they are dependants.

* The term new family is applied when nuclear families are younger than 10 years and consist of parents and children.

* A joint family or extended family consists of a number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood. All property in joint families is held in common with the family income going into a common pocket. A senior male member is usually the head of the family who makes decisions.

* A three generation family is one where there are representatives from three different generations in one house.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Hand washing during COVID-19 is what level of prevention?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary prevention

Hand washing during COVID-19 is a method of Primary prevention.

COVID-19 is an infectious respiratory illness caused by the coronavirus. Infection control measures like immunization, hand washing, personal hygiene and public health measures such as sanitation serve as a holistic primary prevention strategy.

Primary prevention is defined as an action taken prior to the onset of a disease, whose aim is to prevent the disease from occurring. Its target population is healthy individuals. It commonly institutes activities that limit risk exposure or increase the immunity of individuals at risk to prevent a disease from progressing in a susceptible individual. The approaches can be as follows:

* Population (mass) strategy where the target group is the whole population

* A high-risk strategy is where the target group is limited to the people who are most at risk of developing a particular disease.
