questions.text: A man goes trekking at a high altitude. Due to the physiological response to decreased atmospheric oxygen tension, which of the following primary acid–base disturbances is most likely to develop in this individual?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory alkalosis

At high altitude, reduced atmospheric oxygen tension causes hypoxemia, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors. At High Altitude

| Parameter | Change

| --------- | ------

| pH | ↑ (alkalosis)

| pCO₂ | ↓

| HCO₃⁻ | Initially normal → later ↓ (renal compensation)

This leads to hyperventilation, resulting in excessive CO₂ washout.

The primary acid–base disturbance is therefore respiratory alkalosis.

| Phase | Mechanism | ABG

| ----- | --------- | ---

| Acute (hours) | Hyperventilation | Respiratory alkalosis

| Chronic (days) | Kidney excretes HCO₃⁻ | Compensated alkalosis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the process of antigenic drift?
options: There is a gradual sequential change in antigenic structure
Do not cause a sudden increase in the number of cases
The new antigens thus formed are totally unrelated to the previous antigens
Antigens to the predecessor viruses do not neutralize the new variants
questions.explanation: Antigenic drift refers to the gradual, sequential accumulation of point mutations in the genes encoding the surface antigens (hemagglutinin and neuraminidase) of the influenza virus. This process leads to minor changes in the antigenic structure over time. While small, these changes can eventually allow the virus to evade the host's existing immune response, leading to seasonal epidemics (Option B is incorrect as it can cause an increase in cases). In contrast to antigenic "shift" (Option C), the new antigens in drift are closely related to their predecessors. Pre-existing antibodies from prior infections or vaccines often provide some degree of partial "cross-neutralization" (Option D is incorrect), although their effectiveness decreases as the mutations accumulate. Therefore, statement A is the only accurate description of the gradual evolutionary mechanism underlying antigenic drift
questions.learning: Antigenic drift refers to the gradual, sequential accumulation of point mutations in the genes encoding the surface antigens (hemagglutinin and neuraminidase) of the influenza virus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A man working as a mason in a Kota stone factory presents with dyspnea and has following chest X-ray findings. Which occupational exposure is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Silicosis

A patient with dyspnea and eggshell calcifications on chest X-ray, combined with a history of occupational exposure to silica dust, is strongly suggestive of silicosis.

Silicosis is an occupational disease and is caused by exposure to silica. It is seen in people who work in mining, stone cutting, sandblasting, and quarrying.It is the most common pneumoconiosis in the world. In silicosis, macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that cause fibroblast recruitment.

In simple silicosis, the chest X-ray shows small rounded opacities in the upper lobes. When there is progressive nodular fibrosis, irregular masses >1 cm are seen, referred to as complicated silicosis. When these masses enlarge further, it is called progressive massive fibrosis (PMF). Calcification of hilar lymph nodes leads to the appearance of eggshell calcification. Silicosis increases the risk of lung cancer. It also increases susceptibility to tuberculosis as pulmonary macrophages are inhibited from killing the phagocytosed mycobacteria by crystalline silica.

Other options:

Option B: Asbestosis occurs due to the inhalation of crystalline hydrated silicates (asbestos). It is characterized by diffuse parenchymal interstitial fibrosis.

Option C:Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis

Option D: Tuberculosis is a specific infectious disease caused by M. tuberculosis. The disease primarily affects lungs and causes pulmonary tuberculosis. It can also affect intestine, meninges, bones and joints, lymph glands, skin and other tissues of the body.
questions.learning: Silicosis — A patient with dyspnea and eggshell calcifications on chest X-ray, combined with a history of occupational exposure to silica dust, is strongly suggestive of silicosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not correct regarding primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease)?
options: Orthostatic hypertension is a common clinical feature
Skin hyperpigmentation is seen due to elevated ACTH levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orthostatic hypertension is a common clinical feature

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) occurs due to destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone.

Because of volume depletion and low blood pressure, patients commonly develop orthostatic hypotension, not orthostatic hypertension.

Typical findings in Addison's disease:

• Hypotension / orthostatic hypotension
• Hyperkalemia
• Hyponatremia
• Hyperpigmentation of skin and mucosa
• Possible mild increase in serum creatinine due to dehydration
questions.learning: Orthostatic hypertension is a common clinical feature Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) occurs due to destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient, a known case of chronic alcoholism is brought to the emergency room with confusion and tremors. On examination, there is ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Deficiency of which of the following is responsible for the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin B1

This patient's clinical features are suggestive of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is seen due to the deficiency of thiamine/vitamin B1.

Wernicke's encephalopathy/alcoholic encephalopathy is an acute neurological disorder. Glucose infusions may precipitate Wernicke’s disease in a previously unaffected patient or cause a rapid worsening of an early form of the disease (as in this patient). For this reason, thiamine should be administered to all alcoholic patients requiring parenteral glucose.

The triad is (mnemonic - GOA):

* Global Confusion

* Ophthalmoplegia (first symptom to improve with thiamine +dextrose infusion)

* Ataxia

Alcohol abuse leads to thiamine deficiency by the following mechanisms:

* Poor nutritional habits

* Folate deficiency which reduces thiamine absorption from the gastrointestinal tract

* Direct damage of the intestinal mucosa

The initial treatment in a patient with Wernicke's disease should be emergent thiamine infusion, either IM or IV. This should be given daily until a normal diet is resumed and before treatment with IV glucose. Administration of glucose before thiamine can worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy.
questions.learning: Vitamin B1 — This patient's clinical features are suggestive of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is seen due to the deficiency of thiamine/vitamin B1.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which infection is typically associated with a creamy, fishy odor? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gardnerella

Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) caused by Gardnerella vaginalis produces a characteristic fishy odor vaginal discharge. This distinctive odor is one of the key diagnostic criteria for BV. The discharge is typically thin, homogeneous, gray-white that coats the vaginal walls. The fishy smell becomes more pronounced during the "Whiff test" when 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) is added to the discharge, releasing volatile amines.

Other Options:

Option A. Trichomonas: Trichomonas infection causes a greenish-yellowish discharge that is often frothy. It's associated with dysuria, dyspareunia, and the characteristic "strawberry cervix" appearance, but lacks the fishy odor.

Option C. Candida: Candida infection presents with thick curdy white discharge resembling cottage cheese or flakes adherent to the vaginal wall. It causes intense pruritus but has no fishy odor. The vaginal pH remains acidic (<4.5).

Option D. Chlamydia: Chlamydia typically causes mucopurulent cervical discharge but is not associated with fishy odor. It's often asymptomatic and is a common cause of cervicitis and PID when it ascends to the upper genital tract.
questions.learning: Gardnerella Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) caused by Gardnerella vaginalis produces a characteristic fishy odor vaginal discharge. This distinctive odor is one of the key diagnostic criteria for BV.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the probable cause of monocular diplopia in a young boy who has experienced trauma to his right eye?
questions.explanation: The provided image displays a classic iridodialysis, which is a separation of the iris root from its attachment to the ciliary body, usually resulting from blunt trauma. This separation creates a "second opening" or peripheral gap that allows light to enter the eye through a route other than the natural pupil. This results in monocular diplopia (double vision in one eye) as two images are formed on the retina. A festooned pupil (Option A) is irregularly shaped due to old inflammatory adhesions (synechiae). Iris bombe (Option B) is the forward bulging of the iris due to fluid trapped behind it, often seen in glaucoma. Iridodonesis (Option C) refers to a "tremulous iris" caused by a subluxated or absent lens. None of those options classically cause monocular diplopia as directly as the traumatic gap shown. Therefore, Iridodialysis is the definitive cause of the symptom and the diagnosis
questions.learning: The provided image displays a classic iridodialysis, which is a separation of the iris root from its attachment to the ciliary body, usually resulting from blunt trauma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following methods can detect the alterations in DNA sequence?

1. Restriction fragment length analysis
2. Flow cytometry
3. Pyrosequencing
4. FISH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 3

The alterations in DNA sequence can be detected by restriction fragment length analysis and pyrosequencing.

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) is also called cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS) assay. RFLP is a technique in which organisms may be differentiated by variations in their DNA sequence by restriction endonucleases. This technique involves cutting a particular region of DNA with known variability, with restriction enzymes, then separating the DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis and determining the number of fragments and relative sizes.

Pyrosequencing is a synthesis type of approach of DNA sequencing. This technique employs four enzymatic reactions in a single tube to monitor DNA synthesis. Nucleotides are incorporated into the reaction and pyrophosphate (PPi) is released. PPi triggers a series of reactions resulting in the production of light, which is proportional to the amount of DNA and number of incorporated nucleotides. The generated light is detected and recorded by a detector system in the form of a peak signal, which reflects the activity of all four enzymes in the reaction.

The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:

• Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
• Producing proteins such as:

• Interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
• Insulin, growth hormone
• Hepatitis B vaccine

• Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations.
• Restriction Fragment Length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
• Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
• Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation

Flow cytometry is a laser-based method that analyzes the cells and cell components based on the presence of certain cell surface molecules which are named as per cluster of differentiation (CD) nomenclature. It is very effective for the study of the immune system and its response to infectious diseases and cancer. It cannot detect the alterations in DNA sequence.

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique where cells are stained with fluorescent stains. It uses DNA probes that recognize sequences specific to particular chromosomal regions. It cannot detect the alterations in DNA sequence. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. Uses include :

• Numerical abnormalities of chromosomes e.g., aneuploidy.
• Subtle microdeletions and rearrangements.
• Complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping.
• Gene amplification of HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas.
questions.learning: 1 and 3 The alterations in DNA sequence can be detected by restriction fragment length analysis and pyrosequencing. Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) is also called cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS) assay.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parathyroid adenoma

Parathyroid adenoma is a benign tumor of the parathyroid gland, which causes primary hyperparathyroidism (not secondary).

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by high levels of parathyroid hormone, to compensate for the low levels of serum calcium, due to some other underlying condition.

Causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism, include:

• Chronic kidney disease: The damaged kidneys are unable to produce sufficient amounts of the active form of vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. This further causes hypocalcemia and triggers PTH secretion.
• Vitamin D deficiency: Causes hypocalcemia, which triggers the increased secretion of PTH.
• Lithium: May cause an increased set-point of calcium for parathyroid hormone suppression, which leads to parathyroid hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
In a PHC, which of the following initial screening tests are used to diagnose diabetes?

1. HbA1c >6.5
2. Fasting blood sugar >126mg/dL
3. Random blood sugar >200mg/dL
4. 2 hour post glucose load blood sugar
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 4

Fasting blood sugar >126 mg/dL and 2-hour postprandial blood sugar >200 mg/dl can be used as screening tests for diabetes in a primary health center (PHC).

HbA1c estimation is usually unavailable for screening at many PHCs due to low resources. In India, facilities for HbA1c estimation are usually available only at tertiary centers.

Random blood sugar >200 mg/dL can be used for diagnosis only if the patient presents with symptoms of diabetes, hence it is not a useful screening test.
questions.learning: 2 and 4 Fasting blood sugar >126 mg/dL and 2-hour postprandial blood sugar >200 mg/dl can be used as screening tests for diabetes in a primary health center (PHC).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In the WHO grading of astrocytomas, which grade does glioblastoma fall under?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IV

Glioblastoma multiforme falls under WHO Grade IV of astrocytomas. It has the worst long-term prognosis with a median survival of roughly 1 year.

Astrocytomas (Graded I to IV) are the most common primary CNS neoplasm. The term often is used to refer to astrocytomas specifically, excluding other glial tumours.

* Grade I - Pilocytic astrocytoma

* Grade II - Diffuse astrocytoma

* Grade III - Anaplastic astrocytoma

* Grade IV - Glioblastoma multiforme
questions.learning: IV Glioblastoma multiforme falls under WHO Grade IV of astrocytomas. It has the worst long-term prognosis with a median survival of roughly 1 year.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not classified as OCD as per ICD 11?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. PTSD

Post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD) is not classified as OCD under ICD 11.

Obsessive-compulsive or related disorders as per ICD 11

It refers to a group of disorders that are characterized by repetitive thoughts and behaviors that are similar in etiology and important diagnostic validators. Important features of these disorders are obsessions, intrusive thoughts, and preoccupations. It includes:

• Obsessive-compulsive disorder
• Body dysmorphic disorder
• Hypochondriasis
• Olfactory reference disorder
• Hoarding disorder
• Body focused repetitive behavior disorders (Skin pricking, hair pulling - Trichotillomania)

Important points regarding ICD-11

The ICD 11 was released by the WHO in June 2018 and will come into effect on 1 January 2022.

Its designations for antibiotic resistance align with the Global Antimicrobial Resistance System (GLASS).

New chapters on

• Traditional medicine
• Sexual health: Gender incongruence has been moved from mental health to sexual health.
• Immune system disorders
• Diseases of the Blood and Blood forming Organs
• Sleep-Wake Disorders
• Extension codes

Gaming disorder has been added under Addictive disorders.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is measured by the device shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oxygen saturation

The given image depicts a pulse oximeter. Pulse oximetry is used for monitoring pulse rate and oxygen saturation of a patient.

A small sensor is placed on the finger, toe, earlobe, or another convenient place. The relative absorption of light by oxyhemoglobin (HbO2) and deoxyhemoglobin is assessed by measuring the amount of red and infrared light emerging from tissues traversed by light rays and processed by the device, producing an oxygen saturation level.

Pulse oximetry does not measure the absolute content or the partial pressures of oxygen or carbon dioxide.

A pulse oximeter is not always reliable as it reads:

• Falsely high - carboxyhemoglobinemia
• Falsely low - severe anemia, low cardiac output states, hypovolemia, increased systemic vascular resistance
• 80% to 85%, irrespective of the arterial oxygen saturation - methemoglobinemia
questions.learning: Oxygen saturation — The given image depicts a pulse oximeter. Pulse oximetry is used for monitoring pulse rate and oxygen saturation of a patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with dilated, tortuous veins over the medial aspect of his left leg. He complains of heaviness that worsens by evening and improves on limb elevation. On examination, there is hyperpigmentation around the medial malleolus. A bedside test is performed: the leg is elevated, a tourniquet is applied just below the saphenofemoral junction, and the patient is asked to stand. The veins remain collapsed initially but rapidly fill after the tourniquet is released. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Incompetent perforators are the primary pathology
Deep venous thrombosis is the underlying cause
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saphenofemoral junction incompetence is present

Varicose veins are caused by valvular incompetence leading to venous reflux, most commonly at the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) in the great saphenous system.

Trendelenburg (Brodie–Trendelenburg) test helps localize the site of incompetence:

• Rapid filling before releasing tourniquet → incompetent perforators
• Rapid filling after releasing tourniquet → SFJ incompetence

Chronic venous insufficiency features:

• Medial malleolus involvement
• Hyperpigmentation (hemosiderin deposition)
• Edema, lipodermatosclerosis
questions.learning: Saphenofemoral junction incompetence is present Varicose veins are caused by valvular incompetence leading to venous reflux, most commonly at the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) in the great saphenous system.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under RBSK screening which one of the following diseases is not covered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital glaucoma

All of the above conditions are included in child health screening & early intervention services under RBSK (Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram) except congenital glaucoma.

The RBSK aims at the universal screening of the 4 ‘D’s i.e Defects at birth, Deficiencies, Diseases, Developmental delays including disabilities that would lead to early identification, timely management, and ultimately a reduction in morbidity, mortality, and lifelong disability in children.

Health conditions selected for the child (0-18 years) health screening and early intervention services are:

Defects:

• Neural tube defect
• Down’s syndrome
• Cleft lip and palate
• Talipes
• Developmental dysplasia of the hip
• Congenital cataract, congenital deafness, congenital heart disease
• Retinopathy of prematurity

Deficiencies:

• Anemia especially severe anemia
• Vitamin A deficiency
• Vitamin D deficiency
• Severe acute malnutrition
• Goitre

Diseases:

• Scabies, fungal infections, and eczema
• Otitis media
• Rheumatic heart disease
• Reactive airway disease
• Dental caries
• Convulsive disorders

Developmental delays and disabilities:

• Vision, hearing, and neuro-motor impairment
• Motor, cognitive and language delay
• Autism
• Learning disorder
• Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
questions.learning: Congenital glaucoma All of the above conditions are included in child health screening & early intervention services under RBSK (Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram) except congenital glaucoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image: ERCP- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography CBD- Common bile duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ERCP+CBD stenting

The image shown is of ERCP and CBD stenting.

This is an invasive procedure similar to Upper GI endoscopy. Ampulla of Vater is cannulated and then a contrast-filled dye is injected for evaluation of the biliary and pancreatic tree. After a pathology has been diagnosed in CBD, a CBD stent can be placed.
CBD stenting is useful in indicated in cases of

* CBD stones

* CBD strictures

* management of mild bile duct injury leaks

* palliative drainage of malignant bile duct obstructions.

* ERCP shows filling of the main pancreatic duct (MPD), and CBD. The MPD and CBD drain into the major papillary.

* The most common significant complication is acute pancreatitis.

Other options:

(Option A) The pancreatic duct is seen below.

Option B: PTBD is a form of external biliary drainage where either biliary ductal systems are drained outside percutaneously. It is not done endoscopically.

Option D: PEG is a minimally invasive procedure used for enteral feeding. Endoscopically, a light source is placed in the stomach and a percutaneous puncture is made. A tube is entered through the ostomy and secured to the skin. Enteral feeding can be through nasogastric and nasojejunal tubes. Surgically, tube gastrostomy and feeding jejunostomy can be done.
questions.learning: ERCP+CBD stenting — The image shown is of ERCP and CBD stenting. This is an invasive procedure similar to Upper GI endoscopy.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A gutter fracture of the skull is usually produced by which type of impact or force?
questions.explanation: A "gutter fracture" is a specific type of depressed skull fracture characteristically caused by a bullet or projectile that strikes the skull at a tangential angle. This creates a furrow or "gutter" in the outer table of the skull, often with comminution of the inner table. Sharp objects (Option A) typically cause incised or "cut" fractures. Blunt objects (Option B) or falls from a height (Option C) usually result in linear, stellate, or generalized depressed fractures depending on the force and surface area of the impact. Projectile-related fractures are distinct because the high velocity and energy lead to specific fragmentation patterns. Forensic identification of a gutter fracture is vital for determining the trajectory of a gunshot wound. These injuries are often associated with underlying dural tears and cortical contusions. Management requires neurosurgical evaluation to address intracranial pressure, remove fragments, and repair any underlying dural or brain injury
questions.learning: A "gutter fracture" is a specific type of depressed skull fracture characteristically caused by a bullet or projectile that strikes the skull at a tangential angle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman comes to the clinic. She already has twins by normal delivery. Which of the following is the correct representation of her obstetric score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. G2P1

The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1.

The obstetric score is used to summarize the past obstetric history as follows:

• G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one. It is irrespective of the period of gestation.
• P - Parity, denoting the total number of previous pregnancies crossing the period of viability, which is 28 weeks in India.

• This includes both live births and stillbirths
• The current pregnancy is not included

• A - Abortus or the number of pregnancies that were lost for any reason, including induced abortions or miscarriages.
• L - Living children

Both Gravida and para are the numbers of pregnancies rather than babies.

Terminology

• Nulligravida: One who is not and has never been pregnant
• Primigravida: One who is pregnant for the first time
• Multigravida: One who has previously been pregnant
• Nullipara: One who has never completed a pregnancy to the stage of viability
• Primipara: One who has delivered only once (fetuses born alive or dead after becoming viable)
• Multipara: One with 2 or more pregnancies to the stage of viability or more
• Parturient: A woman in labor
questions.learning: G2P1 — The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1. The obstetric score is used to summarize the past obstetric history as follows: • G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old female patient presented to emergency unconscious. A non-contrast CT revealed hydrocephalus, requiring urgent neurosurgical intervention. The patient had nobody accompanying or any identity proof. What should the doctor do ?
options: Take consent by calling the relatives
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Operate without consent

As the situation is an emergency, the person is unconscious and is not accompanied by anyone, the doctor can operate without consent.

Section 30 BNS (IPC 92) deals with acts done in good faith without consent.

The following situations would apply :

* Emergency (No need to take consent during emergencies)

* The person is incapable of giving consent

* The person has no guardian to give consent

Pearl PF1602: Consent

IPC Section

Provisions under the Act

87

Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent is not an offense.

88

Act done by consent in good faith for person’s benefit is not an offense.

89

Act done in good faith for the benefit of a child under 12 years of age or an insane person, with the consent of a parent or guardian is not an offense.

90

Consent is invalid if

• Given under fear or misconception.
• Given by an insane person

92

Act which is done in good faith without consent.

The following situations would apply :

• Emergency (No need to take consent during emergencies)
• The person is incapable of giving consent
• The person has no guardian to give consent

95

Act causing slight harm is not an offence
questions.learning: Operate without consent As the situation is an emergency, the person is unconscious and is not accompanied by anyone, the doctor can operate without consent.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A nerve conduction study is being conducted, as shown in the image. Electrodes are positioned near the wrist, and stimulation is used to evaluate motor and sensory function. Which nerve is most likely being monitored in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulnar nerve

In the given scenario, the ulnar nerve is being monitored. The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve. This assesses the contraction of the adductor pollicis muscle to monitor neuromuscular activity.

The procedure shown in the image is known as electromyography (EMG). It is the process of recording changes in muscle electric potential using surface or needle electrodes. An EMG test examines the electrical signals produced by muscles both at rest and while in use. A healthy muscle at rest does not emit any electrical signals. A damaged muscle may show electrical activity while at rest or in activity.

In order to avoid postoperative residual curarisation, an acceleromyograph can be used for neuromuscular monitoring during general anaesthesia with neuromuscular-blocking drugs.

In the image given below: (A) Placement of electrodes for physiological measurement of conduction of the ulnar nerve, based on standard surface Ag-AgCl electrodes applied differentially (21 mm centre-to-centre spacing) located along the ulnar nerve track. Centre distance: 18 cm between 5 and 4, all others 8 cm apart; (B) photo showing the location of the ulnar nerve track and the digiti minimi abductor muscle as well as the labelling of recording and triggering points.
questions.learning: Ulnar nerve — In the given scenario, the ulnar nerve is being monitored. The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn is brought to the hospital with an umbilical hernia, dry, rough skin, rough hair, and macroglossia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cretinism

The clinical vignette with umbilical hernia,  dry, rough skin, rough hair, and macroglossia is suggestive of Cretinism.

Congenital hypothyroidism, or cretinism, is an avoidable cause of intellectual disability.

Endemic cretinism occurs due to the nutritional deficiency of iodine. It can be neurological or myxedematous cretinism.

Newborn screening by measuring TSH in blood samples obtained by heelprick between 1 and 5 days of life is the most important method of diagnosis. Levothyroxine given orally is the treatment for congenital hypothyroidism.

Total serum T4 or free T4 levels and TSH should be monitored every 1-2 months in the first 6 months of life, and then every 2-4 months between 6 months and 3 years of age, to ensure treatment efficacy.

Other options :

Option A: Galactosemia: Classical galactosemia is an autosomal recessive disorder. The enzyme deficient here is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase. Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their calorie intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). Without GALT, the infant cannot metabolize galactose 1-phosphate, which accumulates and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain. Clinical features include vomiting, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, jaundice, congenital cataracts, aminoaciduria, and failure to thrive.

Option B - Edward syndrome is trisomy 18. It is characterised by low birth weight, prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feet, intellectual disability, and cardiac and renal malformations.

Option C - Prader-Willi syndrome is caused due to genomic imprinting, where there is the deletion of a part of the paternal chromosome 15. The clinical features include hypotonia, childhood obesity, growth failure, dysmorphic facial features, delayed puberty, and behavioural problems.

Pearl PF0119: Differences between the two types of endemic cretinism

Neurological type
Myxedematous type

Goiter
No goiter (USG shows thyroid atrophy)

Euthyroid
Permanent hypothyroidism

Intellectual disability, deaf-mutism, squint, proximal spasticity, and rigidity
Intellectual disability, Deaf, coarse facial features, and myxedema.

Normal pubertal development and adult stature
Delayed skeletal maturation and sexual development, severe short stature
questions.learning: Cretinism — The clinical vignette with umbilical hernia, dry, rough skin, rough hair, and macroglossia is suggestive of Cretinism. Congenital hypothyroidism, or cretinism, is an avoidable cause of intellectual disability.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with recurrent vomiting undergoes an X-ray (shown below). What is the most likely electrolyte imbalance in this patient?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays the "double bubble sign," which is pathognomonic for duodenal atresia or stenosis, leading to gastric and duodenal distension. This condition causes profuse, recurrent vomiting. Prolonged vomiting of gastric contents results in the loss of hydrogen ions (acid), chloride, and potassium. This leads to a state of hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. As the body tries to conserve hydrogen ions in the kidneys in exchange for potassium, potassium levels drop significantly. Hyperkalemia (Option B) and hypernatremia (Option D) are not typical outcomes of vomiting; they usually occur in renal failure or severe dehydration without fluid loss. While hyponatremia (Option C) can occur due to total body sodium loss, hypokalemia is the more hallmark and clinically significant electrolyte deficit associated with the metabolic alkalosis of high intestinal obstruction. Correcting these imbalances is essential before surgical intervention to repair the duodenal obstruction
questions.learning: The X-ray displays the "double bubble sign," which is pathognomonic for duodenal atresia or stenosis, leading to gastric and duodenal distension. This condition causes profuse, recurrent vomiting.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A surgical procedure is performed on the great saphenous vein, approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus. Which structure is most likely to be injured during this procedure?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein (GSV) is consistently located approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus at the ankle. At this level, the saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, runs in very close proximity to the vein. Surgical procedures such as venous cut-down or stripping of the GSV carry a high risk of injuring this nerve. Damage typically results in paresthesia or numbness along the medial aspect of the foot and leg. The sural nerve (Option B) runs with the small saphenous vein posterior to the lateral malleolus. The deep peroneal nerve (Option C) is found deep in the anterior compartment of the leg and supplies the first web space of the foot. The tibial nerve (Option D) passes posterior to the medial malleolus within the tarsal tunnel. Because of the intimate anatomical relationship between the GSV and the saphenous nerve at the ankle, it is the most vulnerable structure during distal venous interventions
questions.learning: The great saphenous vein (GSV) is consistently located approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus at the ankle. At this level, the saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, runs in very close proximity to the vein.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is deficient in breast milk?
questions.explanation: Human breast milk is a complete nutritional source for infants, but it is naturally deficient in Vitamin K (Option D). This deficiency, combined with the lack of intestinal flora in neonates to synthesize the vitamin, puts breastfed infants at high risk for Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding (VKDB), also known as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. To prevent this, a prophylactic dose of Vitamin K is administered to all newborns at birth. Breast milk is generally rich in Vitamin A (Option A), Vitamin C (Option B), and Vitamin E (Option C), providing sufficient amounts for the infant's needs. Vitamin D is also relatively low in breast milk, but Vitamin K is the classic academic answer for a "major" deficiency that mandates immediate intervention at birth. Therefore, the low concentrations of Vitamin K are a critical clinical consideration in neonatal care
questions.learning: Human breast milk is a complete nutritional source for infants, but it is naturally deficient in Vitamin K (Option D). This deficiency, combined with the lack of intestinal flora in neonates to synthesize the vitamin, puts breastfed infants at high risk…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient presents with agitation, confusion, and gait abnormalities. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is Vitamin B12 deficiency, which leads to Subacute Combined Degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord. This condition affects the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts, producing characteristic neurological features. Key clinical features: 1. Gait abnormalities (ataxia) due to loss of proprioception 2. Confusion and cognitive changes 3. Peripheral neuropathy (tingling, numbness) 4. Motor weakness These findings match the presentation of chronic neurological dysfunction, which is emphasized in exam interpretation. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Nicotinamide (B3): Causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia), not gait ataxia (B) Folate (B9): Causes megaloblastic anemia with minimal neurological involvement (D) Thiamine (B1): Causes Wernicke encephalopathy, but exam key focuses on chronic neurodegeneration of B12 deficiency Thus, according to the given explanation, the answer is Vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.learning: The diagnosis is Vitamin B12 deficiency, which leads to Subacute Combined Degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord. This condition affects the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts, producing characteristic neurological features.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 49-year-old female from Nagaland presented with right-sided hearing loss. On examination, a dull right tympanic membrane is noted. Enlarged lymph nodes are seen in the posterior triangle of the neck. Which of the following is the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radiotherapy

The given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with right-sided hearing loss, dull tympanic membrane (middle ear effusion leading to a conductive hearing loss) and enlarged lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck (cervical lymphadenopathy) is indicative of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is extremely radiosensitive, hence treatment of local and regional disease is invariably radiotherapy.

* Stage I and II are treated by radiotherapy alone while

* Stage III and IV require concomitant radiation and chemotherapy or radiation followed by chemotherapy.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking.

It has three types -

* Keratinizing carcinoma

* Nonkeratinizing differentiated carcinoma

* Nonkeratinizing undifferentiated carcinoma.

The most common presenting symptom is cervical lymphadenopathy, occurring in 60-90% of cases. The most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller. From here, it can spread extensively in any direction locally. It also can spread lymphatically to the cervical, retropharyngeal, or parapharyngeal lymph nodes.

Symptoms include:

* Nasal- Nasal obstruction, denasal speech, nasal discharge, epistaxis.

* Otologic- unilateral conductive hearing loss, and serous or suppurative otitis media.

* Facial pain and reduced corneal reflex- cranial nerve V. (most common cranial nerve to be involved)

* Squint and diplopia- involvement of cranial nerve VI.

* Exophthalmos and blindness- cranial nerve II.

* Horner's syndrome

* Cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common presenting symptom.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma can present with Trotter's triad, which includes:

* Conductive deafness (eustachian tube blockage),

* Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia due to involvement of CN V and

* Palatal paralysis due to involvement of CN X

Enlarged lateral retropharyngeal nodes compress the cranial nerve IX, X, and XI causing jugular foramen syndrome. High-resolution contrast-enhanced CT (HR-CECT) of nose and nasopharynx is the investigation of choice.

Other Options:

Option A: Grommet insertion + steroids would only treat the middle ear effusion symptomatically without addressing the underlying nasopharyngeal malignancy.

Option C: "Wait and watch" would be inappropriate for a suspected malignancy, as delayed treatment could lead to disease progression.

Option D: Radical neck dissection alone would be incorrect as it doesn't address the primary tumor in the nasopharynx, and NPC is primarily treated with radiotherapy rather than surgery due to its anatomical location and radiosensitivity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 43-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, shortness of breath, and bilateral lower limb swelling for 2 weeks. He reports decreased exercise tolerance and recent weight gain. On examination, blood pressure is 168/94 mm Hg, and there is bilateral pitting edema. Urinalysis reveals 2+ proteinuria and numerous red blood cells. A renal biopsy is performed. Immunofluorescence microscopy shown below. Which of the following is most likely to be observed on light microscopy in this patient?
options: Diffuse thickening of glomerular capillary walls
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffuse thickening of glomerular capillary walls

The key clue is granular (“lumpy-bumpy”) immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence, which is characteristic of immune complex–mediated glomerulonephritis, particularly membranous nephropathy in adults.

Light microscopy finding:

• Diffuse thickening of capillary walls
• “Spike and dome” appearance (on EM)

Why not other options?

A. Amyloid deposition → Congo red positivity with apple-green birefringence, not granular IF

B. Crescent formation → Seen in rapidly progressive GN (e.g., anti-GBM, ANCA), not typical granular IF

D. Nodular glomerulosclerosis → Diabetic nephropathy (Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules)
questions.learning: Diffuse thickening of glomerular capillary walls — The key clue is granular (“lumpy-bumpy”) immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence, which is characteristic of immune complex–mediated glomerulonephritis, particularly membranous nephropathy in adults.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Plethoric lung fields are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection

Plethoric lung fields are seen in Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC). In this condition, pulmonary venous obstruction results in pulmonary arterial hypertension, resulting in plethoric lung fields.

Increased pulmonary blood flow (pulmonary plethora)
Decreased pulmonary blood flow

Acyanotic
Ventricular septal defect, Atrial septal defect, Patent ductus arteriosus
—

Cyanotic
TAPVC
Ebstein anomaly, Tetrology of Fallot, Tricuspid atresia
questions.learning: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection Plethoric lung fields are seen in Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC). In this condition, pulmonary venous obstruction results in pulmonary arterial hypertension, resulting in plethoric lung fields.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the pathology in the child.
questions.explanation: The image shows a soft swelling protruding directly through the navel, which is characteristic of an umbilical hernia. This condition occurs in children due to the incomplete closure of the umbilical ring through which abdominal contents can bulge. The protrusion typically becomes more apparent when the child cries or strains. Spigelian hernia (Option B) occurs laterally along the semilunar line and is very rare in children. Inguinal hernia (Option C) presents as a swelling in the groin or scrotum due to a patent processus vaginalis. Femoral hernia (Option D) appears below the inguinal ligament and is mostly seen in adult females. Most pediatric umbilical hernias close spontaneously by age 2 to 3 years and require only observation unless they persist or become symptomatic. Therefore, based on the anatomical site, umbilical hernia is the correct identification
questions.learning: The image shows a soft swelling protruding directly through the navel, which is characteristic of an umbilical hernia. This condition occurs in children due to the incomplete closure of the umbilical ring through which abdominal contents can bulge.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following increases in COPD?

1. FRC
2. TLC
3. VC
4. FEV1/FVC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 2

In COPD, the functional residual capacity increases. Total lung capacity may be increased or normal. Hence, both 1 and 2 are correct.

• In obstructive lung diseases, both FEV1 and FVC reduces, where the decrease in FEV1 is more than the reduction in FVC. As a result, the ratio of FEV1/FVC also decreases.
• The total lung capacity is usually normal in chronic bronchitis, while increased in emphysema.
• Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air present in the lungs at the end of passive expiration. In COPD, FRC is increased.

Lung Capacities:

The total lung capacity can be broken down into alternative capacities that help to define functioning lungs.

• The vital lung capacity refers to the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung or maximum inspiratory level.
• The inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level.
• The functional residual capacity represents the volume of the air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath. Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.
questions.learning: 1 and 2 In COPD, the functional residual capacity increases. Total lung capacity may be increased or normal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Particulate matter 2.5 is an important component while calculating the AQI. If a person inhales a 2.5 particle, it gets deposited in which part of the airway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alveoli

PM2.5 particles have an aerodynamic diameter ≤2.5 µm, allowing them to bypass upper airway defences.

They penetrate deep into the respiratory tract and are deposited in the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.

This deep deposition explains their strong association with cardiopulmonary morbidity and mortality and their importance in AQI calculations.
questions.learning: Alveoli PM2.5 particles have an aerodynamic diameter ≤2.5 µm, allowing them to bypass upper airway defences. They penetrate deep into the respiratory tract and are deposited in the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following are features of otitis media with effusion EXCEPT?
options: Most cases have Ad type of curve on tympanometry and a conductive hearing loss
Resolves on its own after the symptoms subside
Usually occurs after an episode of common cold, but can occur de-novo
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Most cases have Ad type of curve on tympanometry and a conductive hearing loss

Type B tympanometry curve is obtained in otitis media with effusion.

Serous otitis media also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumors of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

• Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex
• Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus
• Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

• Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.
• Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Hearing tests suggestive of conductive hearing loss as seen in serous otitis media:

• Rinne negative (BC>AC).
• Weber - lateralized towards the worse ear
• Audiogram - AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present
• Impedance audiometry - flat curve (reduced compliance, shift to the negative side)

B-type tympanogram is expected in a case of serous otitis media.

Here, compliance decreases. The fluid accumulation causes decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve, this results in a B-type tympanogram, as shown below:

Note: Tympanograph is Flat when there is Fluid in the middle ear.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to cysticercosis: 1. It may present as personality change. 2. Subcutaneous nodule may be excised for histology. 3. Cerebral signs commonly do not occur until the larvae die, 5–20 years later. 4. Praziquantel can be given for 10 days. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Neurocysticercosis (larval infection by Taenia solium) commonly presents with seizures, but may also cause personality changes, raised intracranial pressure, and focal neurological deficits. Symptoms usually occur when the larvae degenerate and trigger an inflammatory response.

Why are the statements correct?

• 1. It may present as personality change ✔️: Can occur in neurocysticercosis.
• 2. Subcutaneous nodule may be excised for histology ✔️: Confirms diagnosis.
• 3. Cerebral signs commonly do not occur until the larvae die, 5–20 years later ✔️: Symptoms result from inflammation around dying cysts.
• 4. Praziquantel can be given for 10 days ✔️: Accepted treatment regimen (alternative: albendazole).
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 Neurocysticercosis (larval infection by Taenia solium) commonly presents with seizures, but may also cause personality changes, raised intracranial pressure, and focal neurological deficits.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient complains of a chronic morning cough with production of yellow sputum that becomes more pronounced when changing posture from the left side to the right. Based on this positional variation and symptom profile, what is the most likely underlying lung condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a chronic morning cough with copious "yellow" (purulent) sputum and postural variation (symptoms triggered or worsened by changing body positions) is highly suggestive of Bronchiectasis. In bronchiectasis, permanent dilation of the bronchi allows for the accumulation of large volumes of infected mucus. When the patient shifts positions, this pool of secretions moves and irritates different parts of the airway, triggering forceful coughing to clear the material. Lung cancer (Option A) usually presents with hemoptysis and weight loss. Bronchial asthma (Option C) is characterized by wheezing and reversible airway obstruction, usually worse at night rather than specifically tied to postural changes in sputum production. Pulmonary embolism (Option D) presents with acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, not chronic purulent morning cough. Therefore, the mechanical pooling of secretions that move with gravity makes bronchiectasis the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a chronic morning cough with copious "yellow" (purulent) sputum and postural variation (symptoms triggered or worsened by changing body positions) is highly suggestive of Bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which serotype of HPV is responsible for Ca Cervix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 16, 18, 31, 33

HPV – 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 52, 56, 58, 59, 68 are associated with Ca Cervix.

Human Papilloma Virus (DNA Virus):

* The most common serotype of HPV responsible for Ca.Cervix: HPV 16

* The most malignant serotype of HPV for Ca.Cervix: HPV 18

* HPV serotype most specific for Ca. Cervix is HPV 18.

* The most common serotype of HPV associated with Squamous Cell Carcinoma is HPV 16

* The most common serotype of HPV associated with Adenocarcinoma is HPV 18

* Viral proteins required for malignant transformation are E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

* The E6 gene acts through the p53 gene, and E7 acts through the Retinoblastoma gene.

* Viral proteins required for replication are E1 and E2.

* Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or southern blot or Hybrid capture technique is used for HPV DNA detection.

As per the December 2022 WHO Position on HPV vaccines, WHO recommends the following schedule:

* A one or two-dose schedule for girls aged 9-14

* A one or two-dose schedule for girls and women aged 15-20

* Two doses with a 6-month interval for women older than 21

A minimum of 2 doses and when feasible 3-doses remain necessary for those known to be immunocompromised and/or HIV-infected.

Note: Cervavac is India's first indigenously prepared quadrivalent HPV (qHPV) vaccine.

* Targeted strains: 6, 11, 16, and 18.

* Targeted group: 9-26 years of age

* Dose and route of administration: 0.5 ml, IM.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Positron emission tomography is based on which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucose metabolism

Positron emission tomography (PET) utilizes the mechanism of glucose metabolism.

PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer. It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron.

A glucose analog called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is used. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and thus accumulates within the cell. The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner.

Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose.
questions.learning: Glucose metabolism Positron emission tomography (PET) utilizes the mechanism of glucose metabolism. PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are essential steps of Fothergill’s operation? 1. Laparoscopic or vaginal ligation 2. Amputation of cervix 3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s ligaments in front of cervix 4. Anterior colporrhaphy Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Fothergill’s operation (Manchester operation) is a uterus-preserving surgery performed for uterine prolapse associated with cervical elongation in women who wish to retain the uterus but have completed childbearing. The operation corrects uterine descent by shortening and repositioning the cardinal (Mackenrodt’s) ligaments and removing the elongated cervix.

• 1. Laparoscopic or vaginal ligation ✗

• This is not a step of Fothergill’s operation.

• 2. Amputation of cervix ✓

• Amputation of the elongated cervix is the hallmark of the procedure.

• 3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s (cardinal) ligaments in front of the cervix ✓

• The cardinal ligaments are shortened and sutured anterior to the cervix to provide uterine support.

• 4. Anterior colporrhaphy ✓

• Anterior colporrhaphy is routinely performed to repair the associated cystocele.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Fothergill’s operation (Manchester operation) is a uterus-preserving surgery performed for uterine prolapse associated with cervical elongation in women who wish to retain the uterus but have completed childbearing.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in irreversible cell injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Large amorphous densities in mitochondria

The formation of large amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix is a feature of irreversible injury.

The presence of vacuoles and phospholipid-containing amorphous densities within mitochondria is typically a sign of irreversible injury, indicating a permanent loss of ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation.

Severe mitochondrial damage is marked by the influx of calcium ions and the formation of large flocculent densities within the mitochondria. These densities are typically observed in irreversibly injured myocardial cells following reperfusion after injury. Once mitochondrial damage becomes irreversible, cellular recovery is no longer possible.

Small amorphous densities are seen in reversible cell injury.

Reversible cell injury:

* Cellular swelling

* When there is adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion the sodium-potassium pump fails. Sodium and water accumulate within the cell.

* Fatty change

* Seen in cells involved in or dependent on fat metabolism, e.g., liver hepatocytes and myocardial cells.

* Ultrastructure findings (seen on electron microscopy):

* Mitochondrial swelling and small amorphous densities.

* Plasma membrane blebs (Option B).

* Swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).

* Detachment of ribosomes (Option D).

* Nuclear changes: disaggregation of granular and fibrillar filaments and clumping of chromatin (Option C).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Shifting fluid sign is seen in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Exudative RD

The presence of shifting fluid is a hallmark feature of serous or exudative retinal detachment.

In serous retinal detachment, there is a subretinal accumulation of the serous fluid mostly due to the breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier. When the position of the head is altered, the fluid shifts to the dependent portion. Serous retinal detachment has a smooth convex configuration. A retinal tear or preretinal traction is absent.

Other options:
Option B: Traction RD has a concave configuration and breaks are absent. Retinal mobility is severely reduced and shifting fluid is absent.
Option C: Rhegmatogenous RD presents with tobacco dust in anterior vitreous with substantial vitreous blood or inflammatory cells. Retinal breaks are also seen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman sustains a perineal tear during childbirth. Examination shows involvement of less than 50% of the external anal sphincter. According to the classification of perineal tears, how should this injury be described?
questions.explanation: Perineal tears are classified by the depth of tissue involvement. A Grade 3a tear involves less than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter (EAS). Grade 2 (Option A) involves only the perineal muscles but spares the anal sphincter entirely. Grade 3b (Option B) involves more than 50% of the EAS thickness. Grade 4 (Option D) is the most severe, involving the entire anal sphincter complex (both external and internal) and the anal epithelium (mucosa). Proper identification is crucial because Grade 3 and 4 tears require specialized surgical repair to prevent future fecal incontinence. Given the specific clinical finding of <50% EAS involvement, Grade 3a is the only correct classification
questions.learning: Perineal tears are classified by the depth of tissue involvement. A Grade 3a tear involves less than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter (EAS).

questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The solid line represents a normal individual, and the dotted line represents this patient. Which of the following conditions is most likely causing this patient’s findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Primary polydipsia

The diagram represents changes in body fluid compartments (ECF and ICF) comparing a normal individual (solid line) with the patient (dotted line).

In primary polydipsia (excess water intake):

• Plasma osmolality decreases (dilution of solutes).
• Water distributes into both ECF and ICF, causing expansion of both compartments.
• Solute concentration decreases in both compartments due to dilution.

Interpretation of the graph:

• Decreased concentration of solutes (↓ osmolarity)
• Increased total body water → expansion of both ICF and ECF volumes

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient with a history of head trauma presents with blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg, bradycardia, and elevated intracranial pressure. Which reflex best explains this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cushing's reflex

Cushing reflex (Cushing triad) is a physiological response to markedly increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Rising ICP reduces cerebral perfusion pressure, triggering sympathetic activation to increase systemic blood pressure and maintain cerebral blood flow. The resulting hypertension activates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia, while brainstem compression leads to irregular respirations.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bainbridge reflex: Reflex tachycardia in response to increased venous return and right atrial stretch.
• C. Bezold–Jarisch reflex: Causes hypotension, bradycardia, and vasodilation due to ventricular mechanoreceptor activation, commonly during inferior wall MI or spinal anesthesia.
• D. Baroreflex: Regulates short-term blood pressure but does not explain the characteristic triad associated with raised ICP.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which cells are responsible for graft rejection?
questions.explanation: The immunological rejection of an organ or tissue transplant is a complex process primarily driven by the adaptive immune system. T cells (both CD4+ helper and CD8+ cytotoxic cells) are the central mediators of graft rejection. They recognize foreign HLA (MHC) antigens on the donor tissue, leading to direct cell-mediated cytotoxicity and the release of cytokines that recruit inflammatory cells. Macrophages (Option A) act as effector cells that cause tissue damage but are recruited and activated by T cells rather than initiating the specific recognition. B cells (Option C) and plasma cells (Option D) are involved in chronic and hyperacute rejection through the production of donor-specific antibodies, but the cellular immune response led by T cells is the primary mechanism in most acute rejections. Therefore, because T cells are the primary orchestrators of the recognition and destruction of non-self grafts, they are the correct answer
questions.learning: The immunological rejection of an organ or tissue transplant is a complex process primarily driven by the adaptive immune system. T cells (both CD4+ helper and CD8+ cytotoxic cells) are the central mediators of graft rejection.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is deficient in the autosomal recessive type of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adenosine deaminase

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is the first immunodeficiency disease associated with enzyme deficiency in SCID (Severe combined immunodeficiency).

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)

* Defects in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses.

* Affected infants present with prominent thrush (oral candidiasis), extensive diaper rash, and failure to thrive.

* Some patients develop a morbilliform rash shortly after birth because maternal T cells are transferred across the placenta and attack the fetus, causing graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).

* Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including Candida albicans, Pneumocystis jiroveci, Pseudomonas species, cytomegalovirus, varicella, and a host of other bacteria.

Autosomal recessive

* The most common cause of autosomal-recessive SCID is a deficiency of the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA).

* Deficiency of ADA leads to the accumulation of deoxyadenosine and its derivatives (e.g., deoxy-ATP), which are toxic to rapidly dividing immature lymphocytes, especially those of the T-cell lineage. Hence, there may be a greater reduction in the number of T lymphocytes than of B lymphocytes.

* In the two most common forms (γc mutation and ADA deficiency), the thymus is small and devoid of lymphoid cells.

* In SCID caused by ADA deficiency, remnants of Hassall’s corpuscles can be found.

X-linked SCID.

* The most common form, accounting for 50% to 60% of cases, is X-linked, and hence, SCID is more common in boys than in girls.

* The genetic defect in the X-linked form is a mutation in the common γ-chain (γc) subunit of cytokine receptors.

* X-linked SCID is the first human disease in which gene therapy has been successful.

Other options:

Option A – Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency causes increased ammonia concentrations causing ataxia and death. It is one of the most common urea cycle disorders.

Option B– Phosphomannose isomerase deficiency is a disorder of glycosylation and features include failure to thrive, enteropathy, and hepatic fibrosis.

Option D-Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HPRT) enzyme deficiency leads to a disease called Lesch-Nyhan disease (LND)
questions.learning: Adenosine deaminase Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is the first immunodeficiency disease associated with enzyme deficiency in SCID (Severe combined immunodeficiency).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures passing via jugular foramen has a separate canal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glossopharyngeal nerve

The glossopharyngeal nerve passing through the jugular foramen has a separate canal.

The jugular foramen is formed by the occipital bone and the petrous part of the temporal bone. The spinal accessory nerve and vagus nerve also pass through this foramen.

The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves the skull through the anteromedial part of the jugular foramen in a separate dural sheath.

The branches of the nerve are tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar and lingual branches.

Infection, malignancy and postoperative inflammation of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa will cause referred pain in the ear. This is conducted through the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are:

• All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
• All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve)

Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc.

The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate etc.

The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx.

Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include:

• Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
• By assessing the strength of the cough

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Patient with high triglycerides esterified with long chain fatty acid (LCFA) presents with fatigue and biopsy of muscle shows fat vacuoles. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carnitine deficiency

Carnitine deficiency is a disorder of fatty acid oxidation in which long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) cannot be transported into mitochondria for β-oxidation. Carnitine is required for the carnitine shuttle

• LCFA cannot be utilized → accumulate as triglycerides in muscle
• Leads to lipid (fat) vacuoles in muscle biopsy
• ↓ energy production → especially during fasting/exercise

Clinical features:

• Muscle weakness & fatigue
• Hypoketotic hypoglycemia
• Myopathy with lipid accumulation

Why other options are incorrect:

• Fatty acid synthase defect: Affects synthesis, not oxidation
• Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) defect: Causes ↑ triglycerides in plasma (chylomicronemia), not muscle fat vacuoles
• LDL receptor defect: Causes hypercholesterolemia, not fatty acid oxidation defect

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl is seen for primary amenorrhea. She has not development of breasts or hair in the pubic or axillary region. Her height is 155cm and her weight is 48 kg. She has bilateral inguinal masses. On USG examination, rudimentary uterus with fallopian tubes is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism

The most likely diagnosis is: Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46,XY Swyer syndrome), which presents as hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

Why?

This patient has:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Absent breast development → estrogen deficiency
• Absent pubic and axillary hair (can occur with severe hypogonadism)
• Rudimentary uterus and fallopian tubes → Müllerian structures are present because there is no functional Sertoli cell secretion of AMH
• Bilateral inguinal masses → likely dysgenetic gonads (streak gonads) located in the inguinal canal

Diagnosis

• Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to gonadal dysgenesis (46,XY Swyer syndrome).

Expected hormonal profile

• ↑ FSH
• ↑ LH
• ↓ Estradiol
• Low testosterone

Why not Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS)?

AIS would have:

• Absent uterus and fallopian tubes (AMH from testes causes Müllerian regression)
• Normal breast development
• Sparse/absent pubic hair
• Testes in the inguinal canal or labia

The presence of a rudimentary uterus and fallopian tubes rules out AIS.

| Feature | Swyer syndrome (46,XY gonadal dysgenesis) | Complete AIS

| ------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------

| Karyotype | 46,XY | 46,XY

| Uterus | Present | Absent

| Breasts | Absent/poorly developed | Well developed

| Pubic hair | Reduced or absent | Sparse/absent

| Gonads | Dysgenetic streak gonads | Testes (inguinal/labial)

| Gonadotropins | ↑ FSH, ↑ LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) | Normal or mildly ↑ LH
questions.learning: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism — The most likely diagnosis is: Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46,XY Swyer syndrome), which presents as hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
