questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The electron transport chain is a series of redox reactions that result in ATP synthesis. Which of the following is a cytochrome complex IV inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cyanide

Cyanide is an inhibitor of cytochrome complex IV or cytochrome a+a3 (cytochrome c oxidase). It is a component of the electron transport chain.

The electron transport chain (ETC) is a specialized set of electron carriers that can accept electrons. Energy-rich molecules like glucose are oxidized to produce water and carbon dioxide. The intermediate substrates in these reactions can pass on electrons to certain coenzymes such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FADH2). The reduced forms can then donate electrons to the ETC by which they lose most of their free energy which is used to move H+ through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The H+ gradient thus produced results in the production of ATP. ATP synthesis together with electron transport is known as oxidative phosphorylation.

The reactions in oxidative phosphorylation and the arrangement of complexes that form the ETC are shown below.

These complexes can accept or donate electrons to coenzyme Q (CoQ) and cytochrome c, which are mobile electron carriers. Certain site-specific inhibitors can inhibit ATP synthesis.

Complexes of ETC
Inhibitors

Complex I
Piericidin A, amobarbital, rotenone

Complex II
TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III
BAL(British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV
Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Other options:

Option B - Carbon dioxide along with water is produced by the oxidation of energy-rich molecules in oxidative phosphorylation.

Option C - Oligomycin, an antibiotic, blocks the flow of protons through ATP synthase. This inhibits oxidative phosphorylation.

Option D - Ouabain is a cardiac drug that inhibits the Na+ - K+ ATPase of cell membranes by acting on the extracellular surface.
questions.learning: Cyanide Cyanide is an inhibitor of cytochrome complex IV or cytochrome a+a3 (cytochrome c oxidase). It is a component of the electron transport chain.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The average daily dietary nutrient intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97-98%) healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group is known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Recommended dietary allowance

The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is defined as the average daily intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97–98%) healthy individuals in a specific age and sex group.

It is derived from the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) and includes a safety margin to cover individual variability.

RDA=EAR+2SD

In contrast, Adequate Intake is used when RDA cannot be determined, and dietary goals are population-level recommendations rather than individual requirements.
questions.learning: Recommended dietary allowance — The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is defined as the average daily intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97–98%) healthy individuals in a specific age and sex group.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant has a scrotal swelling present since birth, which has now become acutely painful, erythematous, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The infant has a congenital scrotal mass (likely an inguinal hernia) that has suddenly become painful, erythematous, and irreducible, indicating that the blood supply to the trapped tissue is compromised. This is the definition of a strangulated hernia, a surgical emergency where delayed treatment leads to bowel necrosis. Acute epididymo-orchitis (Option A) is rare in infants and would not involve an irreducible groin mass. Testicular torsion (Option B) presents with acute pain but would not have been present from birth. An incarcerated hernia (Option D) is irreducible but does not yet have vascular compromise; therefore, it lacks the severe redness and systemic tenderness seen in strangulation. Physical examination shows a tense, extremely tender mass with no cough impulse. Immediate resuscitation followed by surgical exploration is mandatory
questions.learning: The infant has a congenital scrotal mass (likely an inguinal hernia) that has suddenly become painful, erythematous, and irreducible, indicating that the blood supply to the trapped tissue is compromised.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most appropriate diagnosis for a 3-month-old child presenting with cold, cough, and rapid breathing (RR 58/min) but no chest indrawing or danger signs according to IMNCI? RR-Respiratory Rate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumonia

The clinical presentation of a 3-month-old child with rapid breathing, cold, and cough suggests pneumonia. However, since there are no danger signs, it cannot be classified as severe pneumonia.

The revised classification of acute respiratory infections is simplified to include only two categories of pneumonia:

1. Pneumonia: with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, which requires home therapy with oral amoxicillin.

Age of child
Fast breathing RR

<2 months
>60 breaths/min

2-12 months
>50 breaths/min

1-5 years
>40 breaths/min

2. Severe pneumonia(Option B): Pneumonia with any general danger sign, which requires a referral and injectable therapy.

Danger signs of pneumonia in children include:

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions, lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition

If a child has only a fever, cough or cold, it is categorised as no pneumonia.

Other Options:

Option A: Cold and cough is not the correct answer beacuse the patient's respiratory rate is 58/min (>50/min) which steers towards the diagnosis of pneumonia.

Option B: Severe Pneumonia can't be the correct answer because there are no danger signs or even chest indrawing.

Option D: Allergy is not the correct option because there is niether history of exposure of any allergen nor symptoms supporting the diagnosis of allergy
questions.learning: Pneumonia — The clinical presentation of a 3-month-old child with rapid breathing, cold, and cough suggests pneumonia. However, since there are no danger signs, it cannot be classified as severe pneumonia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, what is the minimum number of antenatal visits recommended for a pregnant woman to achieve optimal maternal and fetal health outcomes?
questions.explanation: In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) updated its antenatal care (ANC) guidelines, increasing the recommended minimum number of visits from four to eight. This change was based on evidence showing that a higher frequency of contacts between a pregnant woman and healthcare providers is associated with a lower probability of stillbirths and improved overall maternal and neonatal health outcomes. The older "focused" ANC model, which recommended only four visits (Option B), is now considered the absolute baseline but no longer the ideal standard for comprehensive care. Options C (12 visits) and D (14 visits) represent even higher frequencies that may be utilized in high-risk pregnancies but are not the general WHO minimum recommendation. These eight contacts are strategically timed to screen for complications like pre-eclampsia, provide essential nutrition counseling, and prepare the mother for a safe birth. Adhering to the eight-visit model is a critical global health strategy for reducing preventable maternal and newborn morbidity and mortality
questions.learning: In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) updated its antenatal care (ANC) guidelines, increasing the recommended minimum number of visits from four to eight.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 36-year-old man undergoing treatment with antidepressant medication develops an acute hypertensive episode after consuming wine. Which antidepressant is he most likely taking?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes the classic "cheese reaction," a hypertensive crisis resulting from a dangerous food-drug interaction involving Monoamine Oxidase (MAO) inhibitors. MAO inhibitors (like phenelzine or tranylcypromine) block the enzyme responsible for breaking down tyramine, a naturally occurring sympathomimetic found in aged cheeses, processed meats, and wine. When a patient on MAOIs consumes tyramine-rich foods, the excess tyramine enters the circulation and triggers a massive release of norepinephrine from nerve endings, causing sudden and severe hypertension, headache, and palpitations. SSRIs (Option B), Trazodone (Option C), and Amitriptyline (Option D) do not interact with dietary tyramine in this manner. While MAOIs are effective for treatment-resistant depression, their use is limited by these severe dietary restrictions and the risk of intracranial hemorrhage if the protocol is breached. Patients must be meticulously counseled to avoid high-tyramine foods. Immediate management of the hypertensive crisis requires alpha-adrenergic blockers like phentolamine to rapidly lower blood pressure
questions.learning: The clinical scenario describes the classic "cheese reaction," a hypertensive crisis resulting from a dangerous food-drug interaction involving Monoamine Oxidase (MAO) inhibitors.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person was stabbed in the thigh with a knife, resulting in a wound measuring 1 cm in length and 3 cm in depth. How would you classify this wound?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Penetrating wound

In the given clinical scenario, a person is stabbed in the thigh with a knife, resulting in a wound measuring 1 cm in length and 3 cm in depth is suggestive of a penetrating wound.

A penetrating wound is an injury that occurs when an object, such as a knife, bullet, or any sharp instrument, breaks through the skin and enters deeper tissues of the body. These types of wounds can damage organs, blood vessels, and nerves, depending on the depth and location of the penetration. Penetrating wounds may lead to significant blood loss, infection, or trauma to vital structures, requiring prompt medical attention.

Treatment typically involves controlling bleeding, preventing infection, and repairing any internal damage, often requiring surgical intervention. The severity of a penetrating wound depends on the force of impact, the object involved, and the area affected.

Other options:

Option B: A perforating wound occurs when an object penetrates the body and exits, creating both an entry and an exit wound. These wounds can cause significant internal damage, including injury to organs, blood vessels, and tissues.

Option C: A crush injury occurs when a part of the body is subjected to intense pressure or force, typically from a heavy object. This can lead to tissue damage, fractures, nerve injury, and in severe cases, organ damage or compartment syndrome.

Option D: An incised wound is clean-cut, regular, well-defined caused by sharp lightweight weapons like a knife, razor, scalpel, etc. Incised wounds will have a characteristic head of wound and tailing of a wound.

The edges are well-defined and usually everted, free from contusions and abrasions. It is usually spindle-shaped. The depth is more at the commencement and progressively becomes shallower, known as tailing. Tailing determines the direction of the force applied when creating the wound.

questions.learning: Penetrating wound — In the given clinical scenario, a person is stabbed in the thigh with a knife, resulting in a wound measuring 1 cm in length and 3 cm in depth is suggestive of a penetrating wound.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female with a complaint of fatigue and dysphagia presents to the hospital with the peripheral blood smear given in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Plummer Vinson Syndrome

The above clinical scenario of a 30-year-old female with dysphagia and fatigue, and microcytic hypochromic anemia on PBS is consistent with the diagnosis of Plummer-Vinson Syndrome.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome is also known as Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome, and it predisposes to hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma and consists of four features with a higher incidence in women:

* Dysphagia

* Iron-deficiency anaemia

* Weight loss

* Esophageal webs.

Treatment includes correcting iron-deficiency anemia, which may improve dysphagia and pain. Oesophageal bougies can be used during upper endoscopy to dilate the post-cricoid webs and allow normal swallowing and passage of food.

The image below shows the endoscopic appearance of the post-cricoid esophageal web.

Other options:

Option A: B12 deficiency presents as megaloblastic anemia with neurological features, not as microcytic RBC with dysphagia. It is more common in pure vegetarian patients.

Option B: Hemolytic Anemia typically presents with jaundice, raised LDH, reduced haptoglobin with schistocytes in PBS.

Option D: Iron deficiency anemia presents with microcytic hypochromic RBC, but it does not present with dysphagia.
questions.learning: Plummer Vinson Syndrome — The above clinical scenario of a 30-year-old female with dysphagia and fatigue, and microcytic hypochromic anemia on PBS is consistent with the diagnosis of Plummer-Vinson Syndrome.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man is found unconscious in his backyard, surrounded by leaves from a plant resembling the one shown in the image. He is brought to the emergency department with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and cardiac arrhythmias. Based on the clinical features and the suspected plant exposure, which plant is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and specifically an irregular heartbeat (arrhythmia) strongly suggest cardiac glycoside poisoning. Yellow oleander (Thevetia peruviana) contains potent cardiac glycosides like thevetin A and B, which act similarly to digoxin by inhibiting the -ATPase pump. This lead to hyperkalemia and various heart blocks or bradyarrhythmias. The plant description (long, narrow leaves) and the clinical picture of cardiotoxicity are classic for Oleander. Ricinus communis (Option B) contains ricin, which causes severe hemorrhagic gastroenteritis but not primary cardiac arrhythmias. Datura (Option C) presents with anticholinergic symptoms—the "dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter" triad—including dilated pupils and tachycardia, rather than the gastrointestinal-cardiac mix seen here. Papaver somniferum (Option D), the opium poppy, causes CNS depression, pinpoint pupils, and respiratory depression. Given the presence of gastrointestinal distress coupled with life-threatening cardiac irregularities, Yellow Oleander is the most probable toxicological culprit

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: Whipple’s disease is characterized by the infiltration of small intestinal mucosa by foamy macrophages. Which one of the following histological stains is characteristically used to stain them?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Periodic acid Schiff

Whipple disease is a rare multisystem infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine, leading to malabsorption. The characteristic histopathological finding is the presence of foamy macrophages within the lamina propria that stain strongly positive with Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) due to the accumulation of glycoprotein-rich bacterial cell wall material.

Key points:

• Etiological agent: Tropheryma whipplei
• Histopathology: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant foamy macrophages in the small intestinal lamina propria
• Clinical features: Chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, arthralgia, fever, and lymphadenopathy
• Diagnosis: Duodenal biopsy with PAS staining, confirmed by PCR when required
questions.learning: Periodic acid Schiff Whipple disease is a rare multisystem infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine, leading to malabsorption.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following is true regarding inguinal hernia?

1. Medial border of the triangle of doom is bound by gonadal vessels
2. Medial border of the triangle of doom is bound by vas deferens
3. Medial border of myopectineal orifice is bound by rectus abdominis.
4. Medial border of myopectineal orifice is bound by iliopsoas
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3

The medial border of the triangle of doom is bounded by vas deferens and the medial border of the myopectineal orifice is bounded by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis.

The triangle of doom is bounded

• Medially by the vas deferens
• Laterally by the vessels of the spermatic cord (gonadal vessels)
• Inferiorly by peritoneal reflection

The myopectineal orifice of Fruchaud is an osseo-myo-aponeurotic tunnel through which all groin hernias occur.

It is bounded:

• Medially by the lateral border of the rectus sheath.
• Laterally by the iliopsoas muscle.
• Above by the arched fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscle.
• Below by the pectin pubis and fascia covering it.
questions.learning: 2 and 3 The medial border of the triangle of doom is bounded by vas deferens and the medial border of the myopectineal orifice is bounded by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During an upper GI endoscopy, a constriction was observed at 40 cm from the upper incisors. What is the most likely cause of this constriction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diaphragmatic opening

The esophagus has four normal anatomical constrictions, which are important landmarks during upper GI endoscopy, bronchoscopy, and for the common sites of foreign body impaction and corrosive injury.

Normal esophageal constrictions from the upper incisors:

| Constriction | Distance from Upper Incisors

| ------------ | ----------------------------

| Pharyngoesophageal junction (C6, cricopharyngeus) | 15 cm

| Arch of the aorta | 25 cm

| Left main bronchus | 28 cm

| Diaphragmatic hiatus (esophageal hiatus) | 40 cm
questions.learning: Diaphragmatic opening — The esophagus has four normal anatomical constrictions, which are important landmarks during upper GI endoscopy, bronchoscopy, and for the common sites of foreign body impaction and corrosive injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A health worker had a needle stick injury. While handling a chronic Hepatitis B case. She has taken 2 complete schedules (6 doses) of HBV vaccination. She was tested and was diagnosed as a non-responder to vaccination 3 months back, What is the most appropriate management in this case:
options: Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later
Give HBV vaccination starting now, after 4-6 weeks, check HBV titres and decide on giving HBIG
HBIG single dose with HBV vaccination (first dose beginning now)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later

A documented vaccine non-responder exposed to an HBsAg-positive source requires passive immunization only. Two doses of HBIG are given: one immediately and another at 1 month, as further vaccination is ineffective in proven non-responders. HBIG provides immediate anti-HBs protection after high-risk exposure. Revaccination strategies are used only in unknown or incomplete responders, not confirmed non-responders.

| Criteria | Meaning

| -------- | -------

| Anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL | No protective immunity

| After 2 full vaccine series | True non-responder

Non-responder : anti-HBs < 10 after 2 full series

What to do: HBIG × 2 doses: 4 weeks apart; No further vaccine
questions.learning: Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later A documented vaccine non-responder exposed to an HBsAg-positive source requires passive immunization only.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which organism is typically responsible for causing erythrasma?
questions.explanation: Erythrasma is a common, chronic, superficial bacterial infection that primarily affects intertriginous areas such as the axillae, groin, and between the toes. It is caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. Clinically, it appears as reddish-brown, scaly patches that are often asymptomatic. A pathognomonic diagnostic feature of erythrasma is its "coral-red fluorescence" when viewed under a Wood’s lamp, which is caused by the production of porphyrins by the bacteria. Corynebacterium diphtheriae (Option A) causes the serious respiratory or cutaneous disease known as diphtheria. Corynebacterium tenuis (Option C) is associated with trichomycosis axillaris, which affects hair shafts. Diphtheroids (Option D) is a general term for non-pathogenic Corynebacteria found as normal skin flora. Treatment for erythrasma typically involves topical antibiotics like fusidic acid or oral erythromycin. This condition is often misdiagnosed as a fungal infection (tinea cruris), making the Wood’s lamp examination a vital clinical tool
questions.learning: Erythrasma is a common, chronic, superficial bacterial infection that primarily affects intertriginous areas such as the axillae, groin, and between the toes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with renal tubular acidosis (RTA) presents with red-colored urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following findings is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of myoglobinuria following trauma indicates rhabdomyolysis, where massive muscle breakdown releases cell contents into the bloodstream. This includes myoglobin, which is highly nephrotoxic and often leads to acute tubular necrosis (ATN), and large amounts of intracellular potassium. Consequently, hyperkalemia is a hallmark feature of this condition due to both the direct release from damaged myocytes and impaired renal excretion from the subsequent kidney injury. Hypernatremia (Option A) and hyponatremia (Option C) are not typical hallmark findings in this clinical scenario. Hypokalemia (Option D) is seen in distal (Type 1) and proximal (Type 2) renal tubular acidosis (RTA), but rhabdomyolysis-induced kidney injury typically presents with hyperkalemia (often mirroring Type 4 RTA physiology). Therefore, monitoring and treating elevated potassium levels is a critical priority in patients with suspected rhabdomyolysis
questions.learning: The presence of myoglobinuria following trauma indicates rhabdomyolysis, where massive muscle breakdown releases cell contents into the bloodstream. This includes myoglobin, which is highly nephrotoxic and often leads to acute tubular necrosis (ATN), and…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a cause of the following finding shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypo-estrogenic state

The image shows palmar erythema which is not caused by a hypo-estrogenic state.

Palmar erythema is a condition due to increased dilation of surface capillaries in the hand. Vasodilation is mainly due to increased estrogen levels in the blood. The redness is blanchable, symmetrical, non-painful, non-itchy, and slightly warm. The centre of the palm is usually spared.

There is a physiological increase in estrogen during pregnancy.  Liver cirrhosis causes inadequate hepatic metabolism of steroid hormones leading to a hyperestrogenic state. The exact cause is not fully understood in the case of rheumatoid arthritis.

Causes of palmar erythema:

* Primary:

* Hereditary

* Pregnancy

* Idiopathic

* Secondary:

* Liver disease: Alcoholic cirrhosis, Wilson's

* Endocrine: Thyrotoxicosis, Diabetes

* Autoimmune: Rheumatoid arthritis, Kawasaki disease,

* Positioning

* Drug-induced palmar erythema.
questions.learning: Hypo-estrogenic state — The image shows palmar erythema which is not caused by a hypo-estrogenic state. Palmar erythema is a condition due to increased dilation of surface capillaries in the hand.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Isotype switching is seen in ____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Activated B cells

Isotype switching is seen in activated B cells.

Isotype switching: Conversion of one antibody class (isotype) to another resulting from the genetic rearrangement of heavy-chain constant-region genes in activated B cells.

Isotype switching is dependent on the presence of both antigens and cytokines secreted by T-cells.

Note: Defect in isotype switching can cause immunodeficiencies known as Hyper IgM syndrome.
questions.learning: Activated B cells Isotype switching is seen in activated B cells. Isotype switching: Conversion of one antibody class (isotype) to another resulting from the genetic rearrangement of heavy-chain constant-region genes in activated B cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true concerning the anatomy of the breast?
options: Inner quadrants contain most breast tissue
Ligaments of cooper are found only in lower quadrants
Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold

The tail of Spence extends across the anterior axillary fold and is a small extension of the upper lateral quadrant of the breast.

The breast lies in the superficial fascia of the pectoral region. It is divided into four quadrants, i.e. upper medial, upper lateral, lower medial and lower lateral.

Vertically, it extends from the second to the sixth ribs. Horizontally, it extends from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line. A small extension of the upper lateral quadrant, called the axillary tail of Spence, passes through an opening in the deep fascia and lies in the axilla. The opening is called the foramen of Langer.

The breast lies on the deep pectoral fascia covering the pectoralis major and serratus anterior superiorly, the external abdominal oblique and its aponeurosis inferiorly, and the clavipectoral fascia laterally. Fibrous strands or sheets consisting of condensations of connective tissue extend between the posterior lamina of the superficial fascia and the dermis. These suspensory ligaments (retinacula or Cooper’s ligaments) are often well-developed in the superior parts of the breast and support the breast tissue, helping to minimize drooping.

The breasts normally comprise up to 20 discrete lobes that contain ductal-glandular tissue consisting of branching ducts and terminal secretory lobules in a connective tissue stroma. Each lobe is derived by branching from one central lactiferous duct in the nipple. The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU or lobule) is the functional milk secretory component of the breast.

The upper outer quadrant of the breast contains a greater volume of tissue than the other quadrants. This is the reason for the majority of the carcinomas arising in the upper outer quadrant.
questions.learning: Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold The tail of Spence extends across the anterior axillary fold and is a small extension of the upper lateral quadrant of the breast.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25 year old woman comes for her regular antenatal check up. Which arterial gas abnormality is expected to be seen in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic respiratory alkalosis

Chronic respiratory alkalosis is a normal physiologic change seen in pregnancy.

Progesterone directly stimulates central respiratory centers to increase tidal volume and minute ventilation. This leads to increased PaO2 and decreased PaCO2. This paradoxically causes physiological dyspnea. It is an increased awareness of a desire to breathe.

This results in chronic respiratory alkalosis. Bicarbonate level is decreased from 26 to 22 mmol/L(approximately) in metabolic compensation of respiratory alkalosis.
questions.learning: Chronic respiratory alkalosis Chronic respiratory alkalosis is a normal physiologic change seen in pregnancy. Progesterone directly stimulates central respiratory centers to increase tidal volume and minute ventilation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man considering a vasectomy consults his physician to learn about the procedure and common misconceptions. Which of the following statements about vasectomy is incorrect?
options: The procedure is done under local anesthesia
Sterility is achieved 3 weeks after the procedure
A no-scalpel technique is being widely used now
The vas deferens is the structure that is divided in the procedure
questions.explanation: The statement that sterility is achieved 3 weeks after a vasectomy is incorrect (Option B) . After the procedure, viable sperm remain in the vas deferens distal to the ligation site. It typically takes approximately 12 to 16 weeks—or roughly 20 ejaculations—to clear these remaining sperm. The patient is NOT considered sterile until a follow-up semen analysis confirms azoospermia (zero sperm). All other statements are correct: the procedure is routinely performed under local anesthesia (Option A); the "no-scalpel" technique is indeed the modern standard of care (Option C); and the vas deferens is the target structure divided to prevent sperm transport (Option D). Therefore, patients must be strictly warned to use alternative contraception for at least 3 months following the surgery. Failure to adhere to this waiting period is a common cause of post-vasectomy unintended pregnancy
questions.learning: The statement that sterility is achieved 3 weeks after a vasectomy is incorrect (Option B) . After the procedure, viable sperm remain in the vas deferens distal to the ligation site.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A lesion in which lobe will lead to impairment of hand-eye coordination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parietal lobe

A lesion in the parietal lobe will lead to impairment of hand-eye coordination.

The somatic sensory area and related parts of the posterior parietal lobe project to the premotor cortex. Some of these neurons are concerned with aiming and manipulating the hands at an object, whereas other neurons are concerned with hand-eye coordination. Neurons in this posterior parietal cortex contribute to the descending pathways involved in motor control.

There are two parietal lobes, the dominant side, and the non-dominant side.

• The functions of the dominant side of the parietal lobe are calculation, language, planned movement, appreciation of size, shape, weight, and texture. A lesion here causes dyscalculia, dysphasia, dyslexia, apraxia, agnosia, homonymous hemianopia.
• The function of the non-dominant side is spatial orientation and constructional skills. Its lesion causes spatial disorientation, constructional apraxia, neglect of the non-dominant side, dressing apraxia, and homonymous hemianopia.

Other options:

Option B: The frontal lobe is responsible for personality, emotional response, social behavior. Any lesion in the frontal lobe causes disinhibition, antisocial behavior, impaired memory, incontinence, anosmia.

Option C: The temporal lobe has two lobes and is divided as dominant and non-dominant.

• The dominant temporal lobe has important functions like auditory perception, speech, language, verbal memory, smell. Lesions lead to dysphasia, dyslexia, poor memory, complex hallucinations (smell, sound, vision), impaired face recognition (Prosopagnosia) and homonymous hemianopia.
• The nondominant temporal lobe auditory perception, music, tone sequences, non-verbal memory (faces, shapes, music). Lesions here leads to poor non-verbal memory, loss of musical skills, complex hallucinations, and homonymous hemianopia.

Option D: The occipital lobe is responsible for the analysis of vision. A lesion in occipital lobe mainly affects vision leading to homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia, impaired face recognition (prosopagnosia), visual hallucinations (lights, lines and zigzags).
questions.learning: Parietal lobe — A lesion in the parietal lobe will lead to impairment of hand-eye coordination. The somatic sensory area and related parts of the posterior parietal lobe project to the premotor cortex.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: All of the following produce permanent alteration of fingerprints, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dermatitis

• Dermatitis causes only partial and temporary atrophy of fingerprint ridges.
• Permanent alterations occur after destruction of the dermal papillae.

Permanent alterations include:

• Leprosy
• Radiation
• Electrocution
• Deep burns

Temporary alterations:

• Dermatitis
• Eczema
• Superficial abrasions

| Condition | Effect on fingerprints

| --------- | ----------------------

| Dermatitis | Temporary

| Celiac disease | Complete atrophy

| Leprosy | Permanent

| Radiation | Permanent
questions.learning: Dermatitis • Dermatitis causes only partial and temporary atrophy of fingerprint ridges. • Permanent alterations occur after destruction of the dermal papillae.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged man with diabetes presents with progressive visual impairment. Fluorescein angiography findings are available for evaluation. Based on the typical angiographic features seen in such cases, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is the advanced stage of diabetic eye disease. The hallmark of PDR is "neovascularization"—the growth of new, fragile blood vessels from the retina into the vitreous. On fluorescein angiography (FA), these new vessels are identified by an intense, late-phase leakage of fluorescein dye because they lack a proper blood-retinal barrier. Options A and B (NPDR) are characterized by microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and exudates but not the growth of new vessels. Option C (Birdshot choroidopathy) is a rare autoimmune uveitis with different clinical features. PDR is caused by widespread retinal ischemia, which triggers the release of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF). These new vessels can lead to vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment, resulting in severe vision loss. Treatment involves Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation (PRP) or anti-VEGF injections to induce regression of the neovascularization and prevent blindness
questions.learning: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is the advanced stage of diabetic eye disease. The hallmark of PDR is "neovascularization"—the growth of new, fragile blood vessels from the retina into the vitreous.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, which of the following cell types exhibit decreased glucose uptake as a result of insulin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Skeletal Muscle

Correct answer is B because skeletal muscle requires insulin-dependent GLUT-4 transporters for glucose uptake, so insulin deficiency markedly reduces glucose entry into these cells.

RBCs and brain use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT-1/GLUT-3). Liver uptake via GLUT-2 is also insulin independent.
questions.learning: Skeletal Muscle Correct answer is B because skeletal muscle requires insulin-dependent GLUT-4 transporters for glucose uptake, so insulin deficiency markedly reduces glucose entry into these cells.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Egg shell calcification is seen in all the following, except _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metastatic lymph nodes

Eggshell calcification is not seen in the case of metastatic lymph nodes.

A ring of calcification at the periphery of a lymph node is known as eggshell calcification.
questions.learning: Metastatic lymph nodes Eggshell calcification is not seen in the case of metastatic lymph nodes. A ring of calcification at the periphery of a lymph node is known as eggshell calcification.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male soldier presents with a painful, erosive lesion near the earlobe that developed after returning from duty in a desert region. A punch biopsy taken from the advancing edge of the lesion shows characteristic findings. Which of the following organisms is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The history of a soldier returning from a desert area with a persistent skin lesion is highly suggestive of Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (often called "Oriental sore"). The biopsy image provided is definitive, showing macrophages filled with Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies, which are the amastigote form of the parasite. These organisms are transmitted through the bite of the sandfly. Trypanosoma brucei (Option A) causes sleeping sickness and presents with a chancre but is found in sub-Saharan Africa. Trypanosoma cruzi (Option B) causes Chagas disease in South America. Plasmodium vivax (Option D) is the cause of malaria and would be found in red blood cells, not as intracellular amastigotes in macrophages. LD bodies are characterized by a nucleus and a rod-shaped kinetoplast. This microscopic finding is a pathognomonic marker for leishmaniasis. Management includes local or systemic therapy with pentavalent antimonials
questions.learning: The history of a soldier returning from a desert area with a persistent skin lesion is highly suggestive of Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (often called "Oriental sore").

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with episodes of melena containing gastric mucosa and acute, intermittent pain in the right iliac fossa. On surgical exploration, a characteristic structure is identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of melena (bloody stool) containing ectopic gastric mucosa in a young child is pathognomonic for Meckel's diverticulum. Meckel's is a true diverticulum resulting from the incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct. The presence of gastric mucosa produces acid, leading to ulceration and painless bleeding. Intermittent pain can occur if the diverticulum causes intussusception. An appendicular lump (Option B) presents with fever and constant pain, not gastric-induced melena. Carcinoid tumors (Option C) are rare in children and present with systemic symptoms like flushing. Obstructed bowel (Option D) would show persistent vomiting and distension rather than isolated melena. Following the "Rule of 2s," Meckel's occurs in 2% of the population, is 2 inches long, and is located 2 feet from the ileocecal valve. Thus, the specific findings confirm Meckel's diverticulum
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of melena (bloody stool) containing ectopic gastric mucosa in a young child is pathognomonic for Meckel's diverticulum. Meckel's is a true diverticulum resulting from the incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to the treatment of vitamin A deficiency: I. Repeated high doses of retinol can cause liver damage and teratogenicity. II. Acute overdose of vitamin A may lead to increased intracranial pressure and skin desquamation. III. Regular vitamin A supplementation is also recommended for pregnant women even in countries where vitamin A deficiency is not endemic. IV. Excessive intake of carotene may cause harmless orange pigmentation of the skin. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Vitamin A (retinol) is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for vision, epithelial cell differentiation, immune function, reproduction, and growth. While supplementation is effective in treating deficiency, excessive intake can result in acute and chronic toxicity.

• I. Repeated high doses of retinol can cause liver damage and teratogenicity. ✅

• Chronic vitamin A toxicity causes hepatotoxicity, bone pain, alopecia, pseudotumor cerebri, and is teratogenic during pregnancy.

• II. Acute overdose of vitamin A may lead to increased intracranial pressure and skin desquamation. ✅

• Acute toxicity presents with headache, nausea, vomiting, raised intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri), blurred vision, and skin peeling/desquamation.

• III. Regular vitamin A supplementation is also recommended for pregnant women even in countries where vitamin A deficiency is not endemic. ❌

• Routine vitamin A supplementation is not recommended during pregnancy in non-endemic regions because excess vitamin A is teratogenic. Supplementation is reserved for women with documented deficiency or specific public health indications.

• IV. Excessive intake of carotene may cause harmless orange pigmentation of the skin. ✅

• Excess β-carotene causes carotenemia, characterized by yellow-orange discoloration of the skin (especially palms and soles) without scleral icterus. It is benign and reversible.
questions.learning: I, II and IV Vitamin — A (retinol) is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for vision, epithelial cell differentiation, immune function, reproduction, and growth.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and fatigue and has a past history of breast cancer treated with chemoradiation. Examination reveals a jugular venous pulse with prominent rapid x and y descents. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of chest radiation for breast cancer is a major risk factor for developing radiation-induced constrictive pericarditis. The key diagnostic physical sign is the jugular venous pulse (JVP) showing "rapid x and y descents". This "W" or "M" shaped JVP occurs because the rigid pericardium allows rapid early diastolic filling (steep y descent) but then abruptly halts it (the dip-and-plateau sign). Cardiac tamponade (Option B) typically shows a prominent x-descent but an absent or blunted y-descent. Dilated (Option C) and Restrictive (Option D) cardiomyopathies lack this specific rapid y-descent pattern. The provided X-ray (Option R) likely displays pericardial calcification, which is pathognomonic for constriction. Other classic findings include Kussmaul's sign and a pericardial knock. Management usually involves surgical pericardiectomy. Therefore, the clinical history and JVP morphology definitively point to constrictive pericarditis
questions.learning: The patient’s history of chest radiation for breast cancer is a major risk factor for developing radiation-induced constrictive pericarditis. The key diagnostic physical sign is the jugular venous pulse (JVP) showing "rapid x and y descents".

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 26-year-old man touches a hot metal surface and immediately withdraws his hand, experiencing a burning pain sensation. The receptor responsible for detecting this stimulus is most likely mediated by which of the following ion channels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. TRPV1

TRPV1 (Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1) is a nociceptive ion channel present on sensory nerve endings that detects noxious heat and burning pain.

• Activated by temperatures > 43°C, capsaicin (from chili peppers), and acidic conditions.
• Opening of the channel allows Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ influx, leading to depolarization of pain fibers (C fibers) and perception of burning pain.

Other channels:

A. TRPM8: Detects cold temperatures and menthol.

C. TRPA1: Detects chemical irritants and environmental toxins.

D. Piezo channels: Mechanoreceptors involved in touch and pressure sensation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is Net Reproduction Rate?
options: The average number of children who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
The average number of surviving children who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
The average number of daughters who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
The average number of surviving daughters who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The average number of surviving daughters who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan

The Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) is the average number of surviving daughters that a newborn girl is expected to bear during her reproductive years, taking into account both fertility and female mortality. An NRR of 1 indicates replacement-level fertility, where one generation of women exactly replaces itself.

Why not the other options?

• A. Average number of children: Describes Total Fertility Rate (TFR), not NRR.
• B. Average number of surviving children: Includes both sexes; NRR considers only surviving daughters.
• C. Average number of daughters: Equivalent to the Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR), which does not account for female mortality.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following spermicides is used in the contraceptive product "TODAY"?
questions.explanation: The contraceptive product "TODAY" is a vaginal sponge that acts as both a mechanical barrier and a chemical contraceptive. It contains the spermicide Nonoxynol-9 (Option C). Nonoxynol-9 is a surfactant that disrupts the cell membrane of the sperm, rendering them immobile and incapable of fertilization. NET-EN (Option A) and DMPA (Option B) are progestogen-only injectable contraceptives (norethisterone enanthate and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate). Norethisterone (Option D) is a common progestin used in oral birth control pills and HRT . Nonoxynol-9 is the most widely used spermicide globally and is also found in many contraceptive gels, foams, and pre-lubricated condoms. While effective as a spermicide, it does not provide protection against STIs and can occasionally cause vaginal irritation. Thus, for the "TODAY" vaginal sponge, Nonoxynol-9 is the active chemical agent
questions.learning: The contraceptive product "TODAY" is a vaginal sponge that acts as both a mechanical barrier and a chemical contraceptive. It contains the spermicide Nonoxynol-9 (Option C).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which aortic arch artery abnormality is responsible for producing the defect shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left 6th pharyngeal arch artery

The ductus arteriosus is derived from the left 6th aortic arch, and its persistence after birth results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

The right 6th arch largely regresses, while the 4th arch arteries contribute to the aortic arch and subclavian artery, not PDA.
questions.learning: Left 6th pharyngeal arch artery — The ductus arteriosus is derived from the left 6th aortic arch, and its persistence after birth results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old male patient presents with hematuria and a neovascular mass in bilateral kidney on a CT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal angiomyolipoma

The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypo-attenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years and there is a female predilection. It can present as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially with larger tumors. The patient can present with flank pain, palpable mass, hematuria, urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure.

Imaging in renal angiomyolipoma: Demonstration of macroscopic fat is the main part of making a diagnosis. USG may show hyperechoic lesions in the cortex with posterior acoustic shadowing. In patients with tuberous sclerosis, the entire kidney is affected and produces an echogenic appearance with loss of normal corticomedullary junction.

CT findings:

* Cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU)

* Absence of ossification or calcification

* The presence of macroscopic fat is strongly suggestive of this condition, but not pathognomonic as RCC may rarely demonstrate macroscopic fat.

* Approximately 5% may be fat-poor.

MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used:

* Fat-saturated techniques

* Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifacts at the junction between fat and non-fat components.

Digital subtraction angiography: They are hypervascular lesions showing a 'sunburst appearance' in the arterial phase and an 'onion peel appearance' in the venous phase.

They usually do not require any intervention. mTOR inhibitors like everolimus can be used to decrease the size of the lesion.

Other options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC): It is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions needs evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to the clinic by her mother with reduced hearing for the past 2-3 months. The otoscopy finding is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myringitis bullosa

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with hearing loss for the past 2-3 months and vesicles in the superficial layer of the tympanic membrane is suggestive of myringitis bullosa.

Bullous myringitis (myringitis bullosa haemorrhagica) is the finding of vesicles in the superficial layer of the tympanic membrane without affecting the contents of the external or middle ear. If the middle ear becomes involved, this would be consistent with acute otitis media. It occurs due to infection by influenza virus or by Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Bloody otorrhea can occur when a bulla rupture and is referred to as bullous hemorrhagic myringitis.

Option B: Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

It is often seen in children 5-8 years of age. They present with hearing loss not exceeding 40 dB, which is insidious in onset. Speech may be delayed and defective due to hearing loss. Mild earaches with a history of upper respiratory tract infection are usually seen.

On otoscopy,

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* If the tympanic membrane is transparent fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss. X-ray mastoid reveals clouding of air cells.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.

* Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy.

Option C: Acute otitis media is an acute infection of the middle ear by pyogenic organisms. It presents with marked earache and hearing loss is seen in later stages. Otoscopy shows a red and bulging tympanic membrane.

Option D: Myringitis granulosa is characterized by granulations on the outer surface of the tympanic membrane. It is associated with long-standing foreign body, wax impaction, and external ear infection.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 38-year-old man with depressive symptoms is concerned about sexual dysfunction as a side effect of treatment. Which antidepressant would be most appropriate given this concern?
questions.explanation: Sexual dysfunction is a very common and distressing side effect of most standard antidepressants, particularly SSRIs and SNRIs. For a patient prioritizing the avoidance of these side effects, Bupropion is the recommended choice. Bupropion is an atypical antidepressant that works by inhibiting the reuptake of Norepinephrine and Dopamine (NDRI). Unlike SSRIs, it has no significant effect on the serotonin system, which is the primary pathway responsible for antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction. In fact, bupropion is often used as an adjunct to reverse SSRI-induced sexual issues. Escitalopram (Option B) and Fluoxetine (Option D) are SSRIs, and Venlafaxine (Option C) is an SNRI; all three have high rates of sexual side effects like decreased libido or delayed orgasm. Bupropion is also useful for smoking cessation and weight loss but is strictly contraindicated in patients with a history of seizures or eating disorders. This "sexual-sparing" property makes it a valuable alternative for maintaining treatment adherence in young, sexually active patients
questions.learning: Sexual dysfunction is a very common and distressing side effect of most standard antidepressants, particularly SSRIs and SNRIs. For a patient prioritizing the avoidance of these side effects, Bupropion is the recommended choice.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which mental functions are examined in the Mental State Examination (100-7)?
questions.explanation: In a Mental State Examination (MSE), the specific test of asking a patient to perform "100-7" (serial subtractions of 7 starting from 100) is used to evaluate the patient's Concentration and sustained attention. This task requires the patient to hold a number in their memory while performing a calculation, making it a sensitive indicator of cognitive focus. Judgment (Option A) is assessed by asking the patient how they would react to a social scenario (e.g., finding a stamped letter). Orientation (Option C) is assessed by checking the patient's knowledge of time, place, and person. Language (Option B) is evaluated through general conversation, naming objects, and comprehension tasks. Impairment in the "serial 7s" task is commonly seen in patients with delirium, dementia, or severe depression (pseudo-dementia). It is a standard component of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Accurately identifying which cognitive domain is being tested allows the psychiatrist to localize the mental dysfunction during the clinical evaluation. AAns AAns AAns AAns
questions.learning: In a Mental State Examination (MSE), the specific test of asking a patient to perform "100-7" (serial subtractions of 7 starting from 100) is used to evaluate the patient's Concentration and sustained attention.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a post-transcriptional modification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycosylation

Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification; it is a post-translational modification.

A primary transcript is the initial, linear, RNA copy of a transcription unit. The collection of all the primary transcripts synthesized in the nucleus by RNA polymerase II is known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). The pre-mRNA components of hnRNA undergo extensive co- and posttranscriptional modification in the nucleus and become mature mRNA. These modifications usually include the following :

• Addition of a 5′ cap - This is the first of the processing reactions for pre-mRNA. The cap is a 7-methylguanosine attached to the 5′ terminal end of the mRNA and is resistant to most nucleases. Creation of the cap requires the removal of the γ-phosphoryl group from the 5′ triphosphate of the pre-mRNA, followed by the addition of guanosine monophosphate. Methylation of this terminal G occurs in the cytosol and is catalyzed by guanine- 7-methyltransferase. Additional methylation steps may occur (options A and B).
• Addition of a 3′-poly-A tail - Most eukaryotic mRNA have a chain of 40 to 250 adenylates (adenosine monophosphates) attached to the 3′ end. This poly-A tail is added by the nuclear enzyme, polyadenylate polymerase. The poly-A tail terminates eukaryotic transcription. In addition, it helps stabilize the mRNA, facilitates its exit from the nucleus, and aids in translation.
• Splicing - Maturation of eukaryotic mRNA usually involves removal from the primary transcript of RNA sequences (introns) that do not code for protein (endonuclease cleavage). The remaining coding (expressed) sequences, the exons, are joined together to form the mature mRNA. The process of removing introns and joining exons is called splicing. The molecular complex that accomplishes these tasks is known as the spliceosome (option D).
questions.learning: Glycosylation Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification; it is a post-translational modification. A primary transcript is the initial, linear, RNA copy of a transcription unit.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the primary purpose of using gamma radiation in sterilization?
questions.explanation: Gamma radiation is a form of ionizing radiation (usually from a Cobalt-60 source) used for "cold sterilization". Its primary clinical purpose is the industrial sterilization of "pre-packed, disposable, heat-sensitive" medical items like plastic syringes, needles, catheters, and surgical sutures. It is highly effective because gamma rays have deep penetrative power and can kill microorganisms without raising the temperature of the items. Contaminated clothes and carcasses (Option B) are usually disposed of via incineration. Gloves and aprons (Option C) can be sterilized with radiation, but they are more commonly treated with ethylene oxide gas or autoclaving depending on the material. Bacterial vaccines and IV solutions (Option D) are sterilized by filtration or careful heat processing, as radiation could damage the biological/chemical integrity of the product. Gamma radiation ensures that single-use medical devices are completely sterile before they reach the hospital setting
questions.learning: Gamma radiation is a form of ionizing radiation (usually from a Cobalt-60 source) used for "cold sterilization". Its primary clinical purpose is the industrial sterilization of "pre-packed, disposable, heat-sensitive" medical items like plastic syringes,…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which is not an obvious advantage of high pressure oxygen through nasal cannula:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreases need of intubation

High flow nasal cannula (HFNC), which delivers oxygen at high flow, and pressure through the nasal cannula.

Advantages of high-flow nasal cannula:

• Soft and pliable nasal prongs provide comfort to the patient.
• Warming and humidification of secretions: The heating of air to core temperature and humidification of the inspired air is better at high-flow. The humidification causes increased water content in the secretions, which facilitates the removal of secretions. It also decreases the work of breathing and avoids airway dessication and epithelial injury.
• Reduces dead space: The high flow of the oxygen delivered clears the upper airway of the expired air, which reduces dead space by a decrease of rebreathing and allows a higher fraction of minute ventilation to participate in alveolar gas exchange.
• Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP): HFNC increases the positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), and reduces the work of breathing.
• High flow rate causes decreased entrainment of room air, allowing more accurate delivery of oxygen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy undergoes bilateral adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma. On the third postoperative day, the boy feels lethargic and tired. Blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg, there is no sign of bleed. What could be the cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Addisonian crisis

The given clinical scenario of hypotension with no presence of bleeding and bilateral adrenalectomy is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life-threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones.

Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal or addisonian's crisis) is a medical emergency caused due to a precipitating illness unmasking insufficiency or trauma or severe sepsis causing adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) or surgical removal of the glands. It presents with non-specific symptoms such as shock with fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypocalcemia and electrolyte imbalances. It may be often misdiagnosed as an acute abdominal emergency.

Adrenal insufficiency can be primary (due to adrenal pathology), secondary (due to pituitary pathology- lack of ACTH) or tertiary (due to hypothalamus pathology- lack of CRH).

Autoimmune adrenalitis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency worldwide.

Tuberculosis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in India.

Adrenal crisis requires immediate intervention owing to its high mortality rate. Immediate rehydration is initiated with a saline infusion at 1 litre/hr with continuous cardiac monitoring. Glucocorticoid replacement is initiated with an initial bolus injection of hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg over 24 hours, preferably by continuous infusion or alternatively by IV or IM injections. Mineralocorticoid replacement is initiated once the daily dose of hydrocortisone has been reduced to <50 mg, since hydrocortisone at higher doses provides sufficient stimulation of mineralocorticoids.
questions.learning: Addisonian crisis — The given clinical scenario of hypotension with no presence of bleeding and bilateral adrenalectomy is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 17-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea but experiences abdominal pain every month. She has normal secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, an abdominal lump is noted, and a bluish bulge is observed when parting the labia. Considering the suspected diagnosis, what would be the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cruciate incision on the hymen

A history of primary amenorrhea, cyclical abdominal pain, presence of a palpable abdominal lump, and visualization of a tense bluish bulging membrane on the separation of the labia suggests the diagnosis of imperforate hymen and the appropriate management would be cruciate incision on the hymen.

Cryptomenorrhoea, also known as hematocolpos, is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract. The most common cause is an intact (imperforate) hymen or the presence of a vaginal septum. A vaginal septum is differentiated from the imperforate hymen by a pinkish concave covering in contrast to the bluish convex bulge in the latter. An ultrasound scan of the pelvis confirms the diagnosis.

Treatment: A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood, and leads to normal reproductive function, in cases of imperforate hymen.

Note:

In the case of a vaginal septum (i.e. atresia), more extensive dissection and vaginoplasty are required.
questions.learning: Cruciate incision on the hymen — A history of primary amenorrhea, cyclical abdominal pain, presence of a palpable abdominal lump, and visualization of a tense bluish bulging membrane on the separation of the labia suggests the diagnosis of imperforate…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the importance of the following manoeuvre?
options: To protect from tearing of the perineum
To pull the baby out faster
To facilitate controlled extension of the fetal head
To rotate the shoulders during delivery
questions.explanation: The image depicts the Ritgen manoeuvre (perineal support), where one hand supports the fetal head and the other applies controlled counter-pressure through the perineum. Its primary clinical importance is to protect the perineum from sudden overstretching and tearing by regulating the speed and angle of head extension during crowning. While it does involve controlled extension (Option C), the ultimate goal of that control is the prevention of trauma. This maneuver is not intended to accelerate delivery (Option B); in fact, it is used to slow down an abrupt expulsion. Shoulder rotation (Option D) is managed by distinct techniques after the head has been delivered. Thus, the maneuver is a protective strategy to minimize maternal perineal injury and neonatal scalp trauma during the final moments of the second stage of labor
questions.learning: The image depicts the Ritgen manoeuvre (perineal support), where one hand supports the fetal head and the other applies controlled counter-pressure through the perineum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a population with 4,050 total births, there are 50 stillbirths, 50 deaths within the first 7 days of life, and 150 deaths between 8 and 28 days of life. What is the Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) for this population?
questions.explanation: The Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) is defined as the number of deaths among live-born infants within the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births. Let us calculate step by step: 1. Total births = 4050 This includes 50 stillbirths, which must be excluded. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Option A (12.5): Represents only early neonatal mortality rate (50/4000 × 1000). 2. Option C (49.4): Incorrectly uses total births (4050) instead of live births as the denominator. 3. Option D (62.5): Not derived from the given data. Thus, the Neonatal Mortality Rate is 50 per 1,000 live births, making Option (B) correct
questions.learning: The Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) is defined as the number of deaths among live-born infants within the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births. Total births = 4050 This includes 50 stillbirths, which must be excluded.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following should not be included in the school health service?
questions.explanation: According to established public health guidelines for school health programs, it is not mandatory or standard practice to have a Doctor on the premises (Option B) at all times in every school. Instead, medical care is typically provided through periodic visits by mobile health teams or through a designated referral system to a nearby Primary Health Centre (PHC). The essential components that should be included are: the education and rehabilitation of handicapped children (Option A) to ensure inclusive learning; regular dental and eye health services (Option C) to detect vision and hearing problems early; and the maintenance of comprehensive School health records (Option D) for every student to track their growth and immunization status. Other key components include nutrition (Mid-Day Meal), environmental sanitation, and health education. While a nurse or first-aid provider may be present, the structural leadership of the school health service is community-based and integrated with the broader primary health care system rather than requiring an on-site full-time physician
questions.learning: According to established public health guidelines for school health programs, it is not mandatory or standard practice to have a Doctor on the premises (Option B) at all times in every school.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Instrument assisted delivery is not indicated in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cephalo pelvic disproportion

Instrument-assisted delivery is not indicated in cephalo pelvic disproportion. Ruling out CPD is a prerequisite before attempting instrument-assisted delivery.

Cephalo-pelvic disproportion (CPD) is a condition in which the baby’s head is too large, or the pelvis is too small, for the baby to pass through the birth canal. In such cases, instrument-assisted delivery is not indicated because vaginal birth is not feasible. The appropriate management for CPD is usually a cesarean section to avoid complications for both mother and baby.

Conditions where instrument-assisted delivery may be indicated:

1. Fetal distress: If the baby is showing signs of distress (such as decelerations in the heart rate), an instrument-assisted delivery may be needed to expedite delivery and reduce the risk of further harm. (Option A)
2. Maternal exhaustion: In cases of maternal fatigue, particularly after a prolonged second stage of labor, instruments may be used to assist in delivery if the mother is unable to continue pushing effectively. (Option B)
3. Prolonged second stage of labor: If the second stage of labor (when the cervix is fully dilated and the baby is descending) is prolonged, instruments can be used to assist in the delivery of the baby, especially if there are signs of fetal distress or maternal exhaustion. (Option C)

Prerequisites for instrumental vaginal delivery:

• Ruptured membranes vertex presentation
• Cephalopelvic disproportion not suspected
• No fetal coagulopathy or bone demineralization disorder
• Completely dilated cervix
• Precisely assessed fetal head position
• Engaged head
• Experienced operator
questions.learning: Cephalo pelvic disproportion Instrument-assisted delivery is not indicated in cephalo pelvic disproportion. Ruling out CPD is a prerequisite before attempting instrument-assisted delivery.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents to the dermatology clinic with a concerning mole on the back. The mole has changed in size, shape, and color over the past six months. The patient reports the lesion occasionally itches and bleeds. On examination, the mole is asymmetric, has irregular borders, varies in color from brown to black, and measures 8 mm in diameter. The patient has a history of extensive sun exposure and a family history of skin cancer. A biopsy of the lesion is performed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of the lesion fulfills the ABCDE criteria for the early detection of Malignant Melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation (brown to black), Diameter mm, and Evolution (change over 6 months). Symptoms like itching and bleeding in a pigmented lesion are also significant warning signs. Basal Cell Carcinoma (Option A) typically appears as a pearly nodule with rolled edges. Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Option B) often presents as a scaly, ulcerated plaque. Hepatocellular carcinoma (Option D) is a liver cancer unrelated to skin moles. Malignant melanoma arises from melanocytes and is the most lethal form of skin cancer due to its high potential for rapid metastasis. Chronic UV exposure and a positive family history are major risk factors. Management involves wide local excision with adequate margins, often guided by the Breslow depth of the tumor on biopsy. Early identification of suspicious moles is the most critical factor for improving survival in melanoma patients
questions.learning: The clinical description of the lesion fulfills the ABCDE criteria for the early detection of Malignant Melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation (brown to black), Diameter mm, and Evolution (change over 6 months).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is false about Anatomy of Adrenal gland?
options: Adrenals are yellow in gross appearance
Right adrenal is semilunar in shape
Left adrenal is related medially to coeliac ganglion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right adrenal is semilunar in shape

The adrenal (suprarenal) glands are paired endocrine glands located in the retroperitoneum on the superior poles of the kidneys.

• Color: Adrenal glands appear yellowish due to their high lipid content, especially in the cortex.
• Location: They are retroperitoneal structures situated within the renal fascia above the kidneys.
• Shape difference:

• Right adrenal gland → Pyramidal/triangular in shape.
• Left adrenal gland → Semilunar (crescentic) in shape.

Important Relations:

• The left adrenal gland is medially related to the coeliac ganglion and coeliac trunk.
• The right adrenal gland is related anteriorly to the inferior vena cava and liver.

Option C states that the right adrenal is semilunar, which is incorrect. The semilunar shape belongs to the left adrenal gland, while the right adrenal gland is pyramidal.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is used to diagnose the condition given in the below image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wood's lamp examination

The given image shows sharply demarcated hypopigmented macules coalescing into patches over the trunk, pointing to a likely diagnosis of tinea versicolor or pityriasis versicolor. A Wood's lamp is used to diagnose the condition. Lesions show a pale yellow fluorescence when examined under the lamp.

Tinea versicolor is characterized by asymptomatic hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules and patches and produces fine scales (branny/furfuraceous). The site most commonly affected is the upper trunk, but there is often spread to the upper arms, neck, and abdomen (seborrheic areas).

Pearl PF1216: Wood's lamp examination

Wood's Lamp Examination

Wood's lamp examination is a diagnostic test wherein the skin or hair is examined under exposure to the black light emitted by the Wood lamp. Black light is invisible to the naked eye because it is in the ultraviolet spectrum, with wavelength just shorter than the color violet. The lamp glows violet in a dark environment because it also emits some light in the violet part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

A traditional Wood lamp is a low-output mercury arc covered by a Wood filter (barium silicate and 9% nickel oxide) and emits light at wavelength 320–450 nm (peak 365 nm).

Most Trichophyton species, with the exception of T. schoenleinii, are non-fluorescent

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During recovery from anaesthesia, which of the following drugs is used for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neostigmine

Neostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor commonly used during reversal of anaesthesia.

Reversal agents commonly used in clinical practice:

Cholinesterase inhibitors - Neostigmine (most common), edrophonium, and pyridostigmine.
Sugammadex, a cyclodextrin, is the first selective relaxant binding agent for rocuronium and vecuronium.
L-cysteine causes the inactivation of gantacurium.

Other options:

Option B, C:  Anticholinergic drugs like glycopyrrolate and atropine are not used for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade. They only attenuate the undesirable muscarinic effects of anticholinesterase reversal agents.

Option D: Propofol is a barbiturate group of drug which is used for induction of anaesthesia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Pressure sores occur when the pressure exceeds ________ mmHg.
questions.explanation: Pressure sores (decubitus ulcers) develop due to localized ischemia when prolonged pressure is applied to soft tissue over bony prominences. Physiologically, the normal capillary filling pressure is approximately 25 to 32 mmHg. When external pressure exceeds 30 mmHg (Option A) for a significant duration, it overcomes the capillary pressure, leading to vessel collapse, tissue hypoxia, and eventually necrosis . Options B (40), C (50), and D (60) are much higher thresholds; while they would certainly cause damage, the fundamental threshold for initiating ischemic injury is the 30 mmHg mark. Prevention strategies in immobilized patients focus on frequent repositioning to ensure that no single area is subjected to pressure above this critical limit for more than two hours. Understanding this physiological threshold is essential for nursing and surgical care to prevent preventable skin breakdown. Therefore, 30 mmHg is the definitive value for the onset of pressure-induced tissue injury
questions.learning: Pressure sores (decubitus ulcers) develop due to localized ischemia when prolonged pressure is applied to soft tissue over bony prominences. Physiologically, the normal capillary filling pressure is approximately 25 to 32 mmHg.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True regarding mitochondrial genome:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Maternal inheritance

Mitochondrial genome is maternally inherited.

Mitochondrial inheritance:

• Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum) as an individual’s mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperms contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization.
• Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease.

Pedigree shows mitochondrial inheritance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle that adducts and medially rotates the arm at the shoulder is found arising from the inferior angle of the scapula and inserted into the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Which nerve supplies it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lower subscapular nerve

The muscle described is teres major.

• Origin: Inferior angle of the scapula
• Insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
• Actions:

o    Adduction of the arm

o    Medial rotation of the arm

o    Assists in extension of the shoulder

Nerve supply: Lower subscapular nerve (C5–C6) from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

Teres major forms part of the posterior axillary fold and the lower boundary of the quadrangular and triangular spaces in the axillary region.

Other options:

• Thoracodorsal nerve: supplies latissimus dorsi.
• Dorsal scapular nerve: supplies rhomboids and levator scapulae.
• Axillary nerve: supplies deltoid and teres minor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of Calot triangle are formed by all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gall bladder

The gall bladder does not form a boundary of the Calot’s triangle.

Calot's triangle is bounded by 3C's:

• Medially – Common hepatic duct
• Inferiorly – Cystic duct
• Superior – Cystic artery

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: GFR is increased by all except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ureteric stone

Ureteric stone causes a reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

Following ureteral obstruction, there is a progressive fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) due to a reduction in a single-nephron glomerular filtration rate (SNGFR) and a reduced number of filtering nephrons.

All the other factors/options increase GFR.
