questions.text: Which among the following aids in supination and pronation of the forearm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pivot joint

Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding and is diagnosed with stage IB carcinoma of the cervix. What type of hysterectomy is most commonly recommended for managing this condition?
questions.explanation: For stage IB carcinoma of the cervix, a Type 3 radical hysterectomy (Meigs' or Wertheim’s procedure) is the standard surgical management. This procedure involves the comprehensive removal of the uterus, cervix, upper vagina, and the entire parametria (parametrium and paracolpium) to ensure negative margins. In contrast, Type 1 hysterectomy (Option A) is a simple extrafascial hysterectomy indicated only for very early stage IA1 disease without lymphovascular space invasion. Type 2 hysterectomy (Option C), or modified radical hysterectomy, involves removing only the medial half of the parametria and is usually reserved for stage IA2 disease. Type 4 radical hysterectomy (Option D) is an extended procedure involving the removal of periureteral tissue and superior vesical arteries, typically utilized for more advanced or recurrent cases. Therefore, for a stage IB patient where the tumor is confined to the cervix but clinically visible, Type 3 radical hysterectomy provides the necessary oncological clearance

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A mason working in a stone factory in Kota, Rajasthan, presented with complaints of dry cough and shortness of breath. Chest X-ray revealed eggshell calcification, as shown in the image below. Which of the following conditions is he most likely suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Silicosis

Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes on chest X-ray is a classic radiologic sign of silicosis.

Chronic silica exposure (stone factory, mining) causes upper-lobe nodular fibrosis with calcified lymph nodes.

Asbestosis shows lower-lobe fibrosis with pleural plaques, bagassosis is hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and anthracosis is carbon deposition without eggshell calcification.

| Option | Exposure | Key Feature | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| A. Asbestosis | Asbestos | Lower lobe fibrosis | Shipyard, insulation | ❌ No eggshell calcification | Mesothelioma risk

| B. Bagassosis | Sugarcane dust | Hypersensitivity pneumonitis | Agricultural workers | ❌ No calcification | Organic dust disease

| C. Silicosis ✅ | Silica (stone, mining) | Eggshell calcification | ✔ Matches case | ✔ Correct | Upper lobe fibrosis

| D. Anthracosis | Coal dust | Carbon deposition | Coal workers | ❌ Mild disease, no calcification | “Black lung”

| Disease | Lobe Involvement | Key Clue

| ------- | ---------------- | --------

| Silicosis | Upper lobes | Eggshell calcification

| Asbestosis | Lower lobes | Pleural plaques

| Bagassosis | Diffuse | Hypersensitivity

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a patient with endometrial carcinoma receiving pelvic external beam radiation, which pelvic organ is most sensitive to radiation?
questions.explanation: Radio-sensitivity refers to the susceptibility of an organ or tissue to damage from ionizing radiation. Among the pelvic organs listed, the ovary (Option A) is definitively the most sensitive to radiation . Even very low doses of radiation can cause permanent damage to the ovarian follicles, leading to premature ovarian failure and sterility. In contrast, the vagina (Option B), bladder (Option C), and rectum (Option D) are relatively more radio-resistant, although they can still suffer from late-term radiation effects like cystitis or proctitis at higher cumulative doses. Because the oocytes are highly specialized and non-regenerative cells, the ovary serves as the limiting organ for dose planning in younger patients. Therefore, protecting the ovaries or performing an oophoropexy (moving the ovaries out of the radiation field) is a critical consideration in pelvic oncology to preserve endocrine function and fertility
questions.learning: Radio-sensitivity refers to the susceptibility of an organ or tissue to damage from ionizing radiation. Among the pelvic organs listed, the ovary (Option A) is definitively the most sensitive to radiation .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with massive abdominal swelling. Paracentesis fluid was sent for lab analysis and results show serum protein to be 3g/dL and ascitic fluid protein to be 1g/dL. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Late Budd Chiari syndrome

The likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario with serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1g/dL [calculated as serum albumin level - ascitic fluid albumin level, which in this case is 3-1=2g/dL] and ascitic fluid protein <2.5 g/dL is late Budd Chiari syndrome.

Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) can be used to differentiate between ascites due to portal hypertension and non-portal hypertensive ascites. It represents the pressure within the hepatic sinusoids and correlates with the hepatic venous pressure gradient.

It is given by the formula: SAAG = Serum albumin level - Ascitic fluid albumin level

Interpretation of SAAG:

• SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is due to increased pressure in the hepatic sinusoids. It reflects the presence of portal hypertension.
• SAAG <1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is not related to portal hypertension. It may be due to infection or malignancy.

In cases with high-SAAG (≥1.1), ascitic protein level analysis further helps in identifying the etiology:

• ≥2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids are normal and are allowing the passage of protein into the ascites as in early Budd-Chiari syndrome.
• <2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids have been damaged and scarred and no longer allow passage of protein as in late Budd-Chiari syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most common complication of ERCP?
questions.explanation: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a complex procedure used to manage biliary and pancreatic diseases. The most common complication following the procedure is Post-ERCP Pancreatitis (PEP), occurring in approximately 5-10% of cases. It is characterized by new-onset upper abdominal pain and an elevation of amylase/lipase within 24 hours of the procedure. Duodenal perforation (Option A), Cholangitis (Option B), and Hemorrhage (Option C) are serious potential complications, but they are significantly less frequent than pancreatitis. Risk factors for PEP include young age, female gender, and multiple cannulation attempts. Management involves aggressive hydration and supportive care. Prophylactic measures, such as rectal indomethacin and pancreatic stent placement in high-risk patients, have been shown to reduce the incidence of this complication. Clinicians must monitor all post-ERCP patients closely for signs of pain and distress during the first 24 hours of recovery
questions.learning: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a complex procedure used to manage biliary and pancreatic diseases. The most common complication following the procedure is Post-ERCP Pancreatitis (PEP), occurring in approximately 5-10% of cases.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 24-year-old male with a previous history of psychiatric disorder has become aggressive with neighbours. He is cheerful, speaking rapidly and also sleeping little. He exhibits hyperactive behaviour after discontinuing his prescribed medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bipolar disorder (Manic episode)

The given clinical vignette showing increased activity, energy, and euphoria with a decreased need for sleep is indicative of an acute manic episode in the setting of bipolar disorder.

Lithium is used in the management of bipolar disorder, and mania, and has anti-suicidal properties. It has a narrow therapeutic index, and blood levels in excess of this may cause symptoms of toxicity. Therapeutic drug monitoring is done by measuring lithium levels 12 hours after the last dose.

Lithium therapy for acute mania:

* Three individual 10-mg/kg doses of a sustained-release preparation administered at 2-h intervals.

* The sustained-release form is used to minimize GI adverse effects (e.g., nausea, diarrhea)

* Subsequent treatment may then be continued with Li+ carbonate.

Steady state-concentrations for therapy :

* For maintainance therapy in bipolar disorder - 0.5-0.8 mEq/L

* For episodes of acute mania - 0.8-1.2 mEq/L

* Toxic levels - >1.5 mEq/L

The blood sample for serum lithium estimation is to be collected after a time interval of 10-12 hours from the previous dose of lithium which is used to estimate the steady-state concentration.

Other Options:

Option A: Depression is consistent with feelings of hopelessness, hollowness, and low self-esteem lasting less than two-week intervals during which depressive episodes occur.

Option C: Diagnosis of Schizophrenia requires:

A 6-month period with at least 1-month overt psychotic symptoms where 2 or more of the following have to be present. And at least one must be delusion, hallucination or disorganised speech.

* Delusion

* Hallucination

* Disorganized speech (or formal thought disorder)

* Disorganized behaviour

* Affective flattening or other negative symptoms

Option D: The patient's history does not make mention of the use of any substances.
questions.learning: Bipolar disorder (Manic episode) — The given clinical vignette showing increased activity, energy, and euphoria with a decreased need for sleep is indicative of an acute manic episode in the setting of bipolar disorder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 54-year-old comes to the casualty with a history of massive hemoptysis. His routine investigation and chest X-ray were normal. Which of the following you will not do to prevent hemoptysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Procoagulant drugs

Procoagulant drugs are not used to prevent hemoptysis. Procoagulant drugs like vasopressin are indicated only if there is an abnormal coagulation profile.

Massive hemoptysis is generally defined as the expectoration of over 600 mL of blood within a 24-h period.

Treatment priorities in the management of massive hemoptysis:

• First priorities are to secure the airway, optimize oxygenation and stabilize the hemodynamic status by administering IV fluids.
• Chest X-ray is the first investigation of choice. CT scan is done only in hemodynamically stable patients.
• If the bleeding site is known, the patient should be placed in a lateral decubitus position with the bleeding side down to prevent aspiration into the unaffected lung. Supplemental oxygen should be given.
• If large-volume bleeding continues or the airway is compromised, the patient should be intubated and undergo an emergency bronchoscopy.
• The bleeding site is localized using flexible/rigid bronchoscopy.
• Control the hemorrhage:

• Endobronchially with Nd: YAG laser or bronchial occlusion
• Endovascularly with bronchial and/or pulmonary artery embolization
• Electrocauterization
• Surgically with resection of the involved lobe

The cause of the hemoptysis must be determined to definitively prevent a recurrence.
questions.learning: Procoagulant drugs Procoagulant drugs are not used to prevent hemoptysis. Procoagulant drugs like vasopressin are indicated only if there is an abnormal coagulation profile.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is typically elevated in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: Acid phosphatase, specifically the prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) isoenzyme, is characteristically elevated in patients with prostate cancer, particularly when the disease is advanced or has metastasized to the bone. While prostatic acid phosphatase was historically the primary tumor marker for this condition, it has largely been replaced in clinical practice by the more sensitive prostate-specific antigen (PSA). Regarding the distractors, alkaline phosphatase (Option B) may increase during bone metastasis but is non-specific, as it also rises in liver diseases and other bone disorders. Lactate dehydrogenase (Option C) is a general marker of high cell turnover seen in many malignancies and is not specific to the prostate. Alpha-fetoprotein (Option D) serves as a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and certain germ cell tumors rather than prostate cancer. Therefore, acid phosphatase remains a classic biochemical marker associated with prostatic malignancy in medical examinations
questions.learning: Acid phosphatase, specifically the prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) isoenzyme, is characteristically elevated in patients with prostate cancer, particularly when the disease is advanced or has metastasized to the bone.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The glycosaminoglycan present in the cornea responsible for transparency is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratan sulfate

Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency.

Note:

Keratan sulfate is made of repeating units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose. 2 types of keratan sulfate are seen:

* Keratan sulfate I is present in the cornea.

* Keratan sulfate II is mainly present in the cartilage.

Both keratan sulfate I and dermatan sulfate (KS I and DS) play roles in corneal transparency. However, DS is widely distributed in the body, mainly in the skin. Hence, KS I is the single best choice for this question.

Other factors contributing to transparency of cornea are:

* Peculiar arrangement of corneal lamellae (Maurice theory)

* Peculiar refractive index of corneal lamellae (Goldmann theory)

* Avascularity of cornea

* Corneal crystallins

* Balance between intraocular pressure and swelling pressure
questions.learning: Keratan sulfate Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency. Note: Keratan sulfate is made of repeating units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the refractive error.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myopia

In the above image, parallel rays are focused in front of the retina and hence the refractive error shown is Myopia.

Myopia, also known as short sightedness, is that dioptric condition of the eye in which, with the accommodation at rest, incident parallel rays come to a focus anterior to the light-sensitive layer of the retina. In myopia the defect in vision is more for objects present at a distance.

American Optometric Association (AOA) Grading of Myopia:

• Low myopia, when the error is ≤ –3D.
• Moderate myopia, when the error is between -3D to -6D.
• High myopia, when the error is ≥ –6D.

Option B: Presbyopia is used to define physiological insufficiency of accommodation that causes progressive loss of near vision. It is commonly seen in elderly due to age-related decline in ciliary muscle power. Bifocals spectacles are prescribed in presbyopia.

Option C: In hypermetropia, parallel rays of light are focussed behind the retina causing defective vision which is more for near objects.

Option D: In astigmatism, the rays of light entering the eye fail to converge at a point focus but they form focal lines. Strum’s connoid of astigmatism represents the configuration of a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic(toric) surface and helps in understanding the optics of regular astigmatism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman was prescribed a diuretic by a doctor for the management of hypertension. Which of the following diuretic acts on the site 'A' marked in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrochlorothiazide

The site 'A' in the given image represents a distal convoluted tubule. Hydrochlorothiazide, thiazide type of diuretuic act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT).

They block the Na+/Cl- symport in the DCT leading to an increase in Na+ and Cl− excretion. Thiazides are the diuretic of choice for uncomplicated hypertension. They are also used for the treatment of edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, chronic renal failure, and acute glomerulonephritis.

The advantages of thiazide as an antihypertensive are:

* It can be given as once a day dose and has a flat dose-response curve

* Decreased incidence of postural hypotension and relative freedom from CNS side effects

* No tolerance

* No fluid retention

* Decreased risk of osteoporotic fractures due to its hypocalciuric action

* Low cost

The adverse effects include extracellular volume depletion, hypotension, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, and hyperuricemia.

Other options:

Option A: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits Na+-K+-2Cl– symport. They are used in acute pulmonary edema, edema associated with congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, and nephrotic syndrome.

Option C: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and primarily acts in the proximal tubule. It is used in glaucoma, altitude sickness, diuretic resistance, and metabolic alkalosis.

Option D: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that acts primarily in the loop of Henle. It also acts in the proximal tubule. It is used in elevated intraocular pressure and elevated intracranial pressure.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old child presents with enuresis. The parents mention that he had a fall from the bed once during early childhood, but there is no other significant medical history. There are no signs of urinary tract infection or neurological deficits. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Behavioral modification

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nocturnal enuresis. The next most appropriate management option is behavioral modification.

Nocturnal enuresis refers to the occurrence of involuntary voiding at night after 5 years of age. It may be a normal phenomenon in children up to 5 years of age.

If there are no daytime symptoms and physical and urine examinations are normal, then further evaluation for urinary tract pathology is not warranted. USG is done in an older child (usually >7 years) with enuresis or in those who do not respond to therapy.

Causes of Nocturnal Enuresis:

* Delayed maturation of cortical mechanisms that control voluntary micturition reflex.

* Defective sleep arousal, making it difficult for the child to awaken when the bladder is full.

* Reduced antidiuretic hormone production at night, leading to increased nocturnal urine output (nocturnal polyuria).

* Genetic predisposition, with associations noted on chromosomes 12 and 13, and a strong family history link.

* Bladder factors such as reduced capacity, overactivity, or lack of inhibition.

* Constipation, which can aggravate bladder dysfunction.

* Organic causes like urinary tract infection, obstructive uropathy, or sickle cell anemia nephropathy.

* Sleep disorders, including sleep-disordered breathing due to enlarged adenoids.

Treatment:

* Behavioral therapy with positive reinforcement and bladder alarms. It helps the child to deal with enuresis psychologically and motivates the child to void at night if he wakes up with a full bladder. Bedwetting alarms make a loud tone when they sense moisture. This helps to condition the child to wake at the sensation of a full bladder.

* Pharmacological therapy, including imipramine and desmopressin is reserved for cases resistant to behavioral therapy. It is intended to treat the symptoms of enuresis and thus is regarded as second-line and is not curative. In children above 5 years, Imipramine 25 mg at bedtime is effective for nocturnal enuresis. Intranasal desmopressin is also effective in the treatment of nocturnal enuresis.
questions.learning: Behavioral modification — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nocturnal enuresis. The next most appropriate management option is behavioral modification.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When quarantine was introduced in the 14th century for plague, how many days were people who were suspected to have the infection quarantined for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 40 days

In the 14th century, quarantine was used for plague and the suspects were quarantined for 40 days.

The idea of quarantine when it was initially introduced was that, the disease would remain dormant in the quarantine period and die out. But the 40 day period caused inconveniences and was based on a lack of scientific knowledge regarding the causation and spread of the disease.

Quarantine is the restriction on the movement of people, animals, and goods that may have been exposed to a communicable disease. It is intended to prevent the spread of communicable diseases.

Quarantine is distinct from medical isolation, in which those confirmed to be infected with a communicable disease are isolated from the healthy population.

It is a primary level of prevention and falls under specific protection measures. The various types of quarantine are:

* Absolute - Complete limitation of movement

* Modified - Selective partial limitation of movement

* Segregation - Observation of a group of persons in a population after separation

Note:

With respect to the COVID-19 pandemic, home quarantine is advised when a person comes in contact with a COVID-19 positive patient.
questions.learning: 40 days In the 14th century, quarantine was used for plague and the suspects were quarantined for 40 days. The idea of quarantine when it was initially introduced was that, the disease would remain dormant in the quarantine period and die out.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: ‘Tumour Plop’ is a characteristic auscultatory finding seen in which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrial myxoma

A tumor plop is a characteristic low-pitched diastolic sound produced when an atrial myxoma moves through the atrioventricular valve during ventricular filling. It is classically associated with left atrial myxoma, where the tumor intermittently obstructs the mitral valve.

Why not the other options?

• B. Arrhythmogenic ventricular cardiomyopathy: Characterized by ventricular arrhythmias and right ventricular structural abnormalities; tumor plop is not a feature.
• C. Constrictive pericarditis: Classically produces a pericardial knock, an early diastolic sound due to abrupt cessation of ventricular filling.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: May produce S3 gallop due to volume overload and ventricular dilation, but not a tumor plop.
questions.learning: Atrial myxoma — A tumor plop is a characteristic low-pitched diastolic sound produced when an atrial myxoma moves through the atrioventricular valve during ventricular filling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 23-year-old medical student with a 2-month history of palpitations, sweating, and restlessness. He also complains of a sweaty palm. His appearance is as shown in the picture. What is the next step in evaluation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ultrasensitive TSH

Ultrasensitive TSH is the best initial test in suspected hyperthyroidism because it is the most sensitive marker of thyroid axis status. Thyrotoxicosis typically shows suppressed TSH before T3/T4 become markedly elevated. Antibody tests and radioactive uptake are used later to determine etiology. Screening always begins with TSH.

A. Thyroid receptor antibody

• Used to confirm Graves disease

B. Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU)

• Used to differentiate causes

D. Anti-TPO antibody

• Seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the given image is correct?
options: Albendazole is the drug of choice
Majority of infections are asymptomatic in humans
Infection is acquired by ingestion of aquatic plants
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Majority of infections are asymptomatic in humans

The given image shows a spherical or ovoid, non-bile stained egg which is diagnostic of Hymenolepis nana infection. It has a thin colorless outer membrane and a thin embryophore covering the hexacanth embryo. The majority of infections are asymptomatic and are more commonly seen in children.

H. Nana or dwarf tapeworm is the smallest and most common cestode that infects man. There is no intermediate host. The infection is acquired by ingestion of food and water contaminated with eggs.

Patients with heavy infections may present with nausea, abdominal pain, anorexia, diarrhea, and irritability. An allergic response to the parasite can cause pruritus as well.

A single dose of Praziquantel given at the rate of 25mg/kg is the drug of choice. Nitazoxanide (500 mg twice daily for 3 days) may be given as an alternative.

Image below shows egg of H. Nana.

Other options:

Option C - Following are the parasites with aquatic plants as the source of infection :

• Fasciola hepatica

• Fasciolopsis buski

• Watsonius watsoni.
• Gastrodiscoides hominis

Option D - The adult worm of Fasciola hepatica is a flat leaf-shaped liver fluke.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 39 year old patient presents to the OPD with complaints of pain over his ear lobule. He also complains of difficulty in eating food and the inability to close his eyes completely. On examination, there is a swelling below his ear. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facial nerve

The clinical scenario of pain over the ear lobule, inability to close eyes, and difficulty in eating point toward an injury to the facial nerve. The swelling could possibly be a parotid swelling injuring the facial nerve. The course of facial nerve is given below

Nerve supply of external ear

Pinna

* Greater/Great auricular nerve - medial surface and posterior part of lateral surface (lobule, posterior part of helix and anti helix).

* Lesser occipital nerve - upper part of medial surface.

* Auriculotemporal nerve - tragus, crus of helix and adjacent part of helix.

* Auricular branch of vagus (Arnold's nerve or Alderman's nerve) - concha on the lateral surface and post auricular groove medially.

* Facial nerve - concha and post auricular groove along with Arnold's nerve.

External Auditory Canal

* Auriculotemporal nerve - anterior wall and roof

* Auricular branch of vagus - posterior wall and floor

* Facial nerve - sensory supply to the posterior wall through the vagus

Tympanic Membrane

* Auriculotemporal nerve - anterior half of lateral surface

* Auricular branch of vagus - posterior half of lateral surface

* Tympanic branch of Glossopharyngeal - medial surface

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is admitted to the ICU with a 4-day history of fever and recent onset of breathlessness. Despite increasing the oxygen flow rate, the patient remains hypoxic with progressively falling oxygen saturation. Chest X-ray shows characteristic abnormalities, and the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio is 204 mmHg. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of acute breathlessness following an infection (fever), refractory hypoxemia (unresponsiveness to oxygen), and a ratio between 200–300 mmHg satisfies the Berlin definition for mild Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). ARDS is characterized by diffuse alveolar damage leading to non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Atelectasis (Option A) involves the collapse of lung tissue, usually localized rather than diffuse. Mediastinitis (Option B) is an inflammation of the mediastinum, typically presenting with chest pain rather than primary lung failure. Pulmonary fibrosis (Option C) is a chronic, progressive restrictive lung disease, not an acute condition occurring over four days. ARDS chest X-rays typically show bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Management focuses on treating the underlying cause (e.g., sepsis or pneumonia) and providing lung-protective mechanical ventilation with low tidal volumes to prevent further lung injury
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of acute breathlessness following an infection (fever), refractory hypoxemia (unresponsiveness to oxygen), and a ratio between 200–300 mmHg satisfies the Berlin definition for mild Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents within 2 days of birth with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. An abdominal X-ray has been performed (as shown). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of bilious vomiting in a newborn within the first 48 hours of life is a red flag for high intestinal obstruction. The provided X-ray demonstrates the classic "double bubble" sign, which consists of two large air-filled spaces in the upper abdomen—one representing the stomach and the other the dilated proximal duodenum. This finding is pathognomonic for duodenal atresia. Bilious vomiting occurs because the obstruction is typically distal to the ampulla of Vater where bile enters the gut. Esophageal atresia (Option B) would present with drooling and inability to feed from birth, often with a gasless abdomen on X-ray. Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (Option C) presents later (3–6 weeks) with non-bilious projectile vomiting. "Gas in bowel" (Option A) is a normal finding and does not explain bilious vomiting. Duodenal atresia is frequently associated with Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), making it a critical pediatric diagnostic pattern to recognize

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following jugular venous pressure (JVP) waves corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. c wave

The c wave of jugular venous pressure wave corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase in the cardiac cycle.

During isovolumetric contraction, the ventricles start contracting with valves closed. This leads to bulging of the tricuspid valve. This bulging increases pressure in the right atrium which is transmitted to the right internal jugular vein. This appears as a c wave in jugular venous pressure (JVP) tracing.
JVP measured in the internal jugular vein (IJV) is a reflection of the right atrial pressure. IJV is preferred because it is not valved and is in direct line with superior vena cava and right atrium.

The waveforms seen in a normal JVP are:

• a wave corresponds to atrial contraction and occurs just after the P wave (on ECG) and just before the first heart sound.
• c wave represents the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during ventricular systole.
• x descent corresponds to the atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.
• v wave represents atrial filling during ventricular systole and peaks at the second heart sound.
• y descent represents passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after tricuspid valve opening.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Spread of prostate cancer to lumbar vertebra is via?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer characteristically metastasizes to the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis through venous spread. This occurs via Batson’s venous plexus, which is a system of valveless veins connecting the prostatic venous plexus to the internal vertebral venous system. Because these veins lack valves, changes in intra-abdominal pressure can cause retrograde blood flow, allowing malignant cells to travel directly from the prostate to the spine. Regarding the distractors, arterial spread (Option A) is less common and usually occurs late in the disease. Local spread (Option B) involves direct invasion of the bladder or seminal vesicles. Lymphatic spread (Option C) primarily affects the pelvic lymph nodes, such as the obturator and internal iliac nodes. Therefore, the unique valveless venous communication is the primary anatomical route responsible for the classic osteoblastic vertebral metastases seen in prostate cancer patients

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: BIPAP cannot be considered in patients with which of the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Unconscious patients

Patients being unconscious in considered a contraindication for BiPAP.

BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) therapy is a non-invasive ventilation technique that requires patient cooperation and the ability to breathe spontaneously. It relies on the patient's ability to initiate and maintain breathing efforts while receiving pressure support from the device. An unconscious patient, by definition, lacks the ability to consciously control their breathing and cannot actively participate in the breathing process. Therefore, BiPAP therapy is contraindicated in unconscious patients as they cannot tolerate the interface and settings required for this type of ventilation.

In such cases, invasive mechanical ventilation, which provides full ventilatory support, is typically necessary to maintain adequate gas exchange and support respiratory function.

Positive-pressure ventilation helps with stiff lungs and high airway resistance. Here, gas flow and pressure can be adjusted to improve inflation. Disadvantages include poor ventilation-perfusion matching, lower cardiac output, and lung injury. Increased chest pressure reduces blood return to the heart. Barotrauma results from high pressures, and volutrauma occurs from repeated alveolar collapse and reopening. Air flows to the upper lung areas, while blood flows to the lower regions, increasing the dead space.

Other Options:

Option (a) Low pO2 levels: BiPAP therapy is often utilized to improve oxygenation in patients with hypoxemia (low blood oxygen levels). By delivering positive airway pressure, BiPAP helps to recruit collapsed alveoli, improve lung ventilation-perfusion matching, and enhance oxygen diffusion into the bloodstream. Therefore, low pO2 levels are not a contraindication for BiPAP therapy; instead, they may indicate the need for BiPAP to support oxygenation.

Option (c) High CO2 levels: BiPAP therapy can also be beneficial for patients with hypercapnia (elevated blood carbon dioxide levels), such as those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation or obesity hypoventilation syndrome. By providing inspiratory pressure support and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), BiPAP assists ventilation, enhances alveolar ventilation, and helps to eliminate excess carbon dioxide from the body. Therefore, high CO2 levels alone do not contraindicate the use of BiPAP therapy; rather, BiPAP may be indicated to improve ventilation and reduce CO2 levels.

Option (d) Obstructive sleep apnea: BiPAP therapy is commonly employed as a non-invasive treatment for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a sleep disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway collapse during sleep. By delivering two levels of pressure – higher pressure during inspiration (IPAP) and lower pressure during expiration (EPAP) – BiPAP helps to keep the upper airway open, prevent apnea events, and improve sleep quality. Therefore, obstructive sleep apnea is not a contraindication for BiPAP therapy; rather, BiPAP is a recommended treatment modality for managing this condition.

questions.text: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) of the cervix and no obvious macroscopic growth. What is the next line of management?

Correct answer: C. Colposcopy and biopsy

In a woman diagnosed with a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), the next step in management is to perform a colposcopy and biopsy.

Patients who are found to have HSIL are further subjected to biopsy. This is done by colposcopic study for the visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) for aceto-white areas and taking biopsies of abnormal areas.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the segment with the bolus of food during peristalsis is because of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VIP

The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the segment of a bolus of food during peristalsis is due to Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP).

Peristaltic contractions in the small intestine are designed to propel the food towards the large intestine.

The food bolus in the small intestine is sensed by enterochromaffin cells of the intestinal mucosa, which release 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT)(serotonin). The 5-HT then binds to the receptors on intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs), which when activated, initiate the peristaltic reflex in that segment of the small intestine. Behind the bolus, excitatory transmitters like acetylcholine, Substance P, neuropeptide Y are released in the circular muscle, while these pathways are inhibited in the longitudinal muscle; thus this segment of small intestine (behind the bolus) contracts and lengthens.

(Recall that contraction of circular muscle decreases the diameter of that small intestinal segment whereas contraction of the longitudinal muscle decreases the length of that segment. To prevent the conflict that would occur if circular and longitudinal are contracted at the same time, they are reciprocally innervated)

In front of the bolus, inhibitory pathways like vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and nitric oxide (NO) are activated in the circular muscle, while excitatory pathways are activated in the longitudinal muscle;thereby relaxing and shortening this segment of small intestine.
questions.learning: VIP — The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the segment of a bolus of food during peristalsis is due to Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP).
